A brain lesion with no known cancer
Sudden aphasia: from the emergency department to prevention
Prolonged convulsion in the emergency department
Painful red eye in a cinema

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man is brought to the emergency department 1 hour after his wife noticed that his speech was slurred and the left corner of his mouth was drooping. On examination, he cannot bare his teeth on the left side, but he wrinkles his forehead symmetrically when asked to look up. His left hand grip is weak. A lesion in which of the following locations best explains his facial findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Left facial nerve in the facial canal

options.label: B
options.html: Left facial nucleus in the pons

items.explanationHtml:
Lower-face weakness with a preserved forehead is an upper motor neuron pattern. The part of the facial nucleus that drives the forehead receives input from both hemispheres, so one cortical or capsular lesion leaves the forehead working. The weak left face and weak left hand point to a lesion of the right corticobulbar and corticospinal fibres, which run together in the posterior limb of the right internal capsule.

Takeaway: a spared forehead means a central lesion on the side opposite the facial droop.

whyNot.A: A facial canal lesion is lower motor neuron and would weaken the left forehead as well, without hand weakness.
whyNot.B: A lesion of the left facial nucleus weakens the whole left face, forehead included.
whyNot.D: A right cerebellopontine angle lesion would weaken the right side of the face and usually affects hearing.
whyNot.E: A lesion at the left stylomastoid foramen paralyses the entire left face, including the forehead.

items.objective: Localise facial weakness that spares the forehead to the contralateral upper motor neuron pathway.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman comes to the clinic because she woke up this morning unable to close her right eye. Yesterday she had an ache behind her right ear. She has no rash, hearing loss or limb symptoms. She lives in a city and has not travelled or noticed tick bites. Temperature is 36.8°C (98.2°F) and blood pressure is 118/74 mm Hg. She cannot raise her right eyebrow, close her right eye fully or lift the right corner of her mouth. The ear canals and tympanic membranes are normal. The rest of the neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: MRI of the brain with gadolinium

options.label: B
options.html: Oral prednisone and eye lubrication with nighttime taping

options.label: E
options.html: Nerve conduction studies of the facial nerve

items.explanationHtml:
This is a typical Bell palsy: sudden, whole-hemiface lower motor neuron weakness with retroauricular pain and no other deficit. An oral corticosteroid started within 72 hours raises the chance of complete recovery. The eye cannot close, so protect the cornea with lubricating drops, ointment and taping at night.

Takeaway: typical Bell palsy needs a steroid within 72 hours and eye protection; it does not need tests.

whyNot.A: Imaging is reserved for atypical features: gradual onset, recurrence, other cranial nerve or limb signs.
whyNot.C: An antiviral alone has not been shown to help; at most it is added to a corticosteroid in severe cases.
whyNot.D: She has no tick exposure or endemic-area risk, and treatment should not wait for serology.
whyNot.E: Electrodiagnostic testing is a prognostic option for complete palsy after the first days, not a first step.

items.objective: Treat typical Bell palsy with an early oral corticosteroid and eye protection, without routine testing.

items.stemHtml: A 10-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department because of fever, poor feeding and irritability for 1 day. He was born at term by vaginal delivery after prolonged rupture of membranes. His temperature is 38.9°C (102°F). The anterior fontanelle is bulging. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 1,800 leukocytes/mm3 (90% neutrophils). Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains. Which of the following organisms is most likely responsible?
items.explanationHtml:
Group B streptococcus, acquired from the maternal genital tract during delivery, is the leading cause of meningitis in the first weeks of life. Prolonged rupture of membranes raises the risk. On Gram stain it forms gram-positive cocci in chains.

Takeaway: gram-positive cocci in chains in neonatal CSF mean group B streptococcus.

whyNot.A: Listeria is a gram-positive rod, not a coccus in chains.
whyNot.C: E. coli is a common neonatal cause but is a gram-negative rod.
whyNot.D: Pneumococcus appears as lancet-shaped diplococci and is uncommon in the first month of life.
whyNot.E: Meningococcus is a gram-negative diplococcus and rarely causes neonatal meningitis.

items.objective: Identify group B streptococcus as the cause of neonatal meningitis from host age and Gram stain.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old college student is brought to the emergency department 6 hours after the onset of fever, headache and a spreading non-blanching rash on his legs. Blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg. Platelet count is 42,000/mm3 and the INR is 2.4. Gram stain of cerebrospinal fluid shows gram-negative diplococci. Which of the following bacterial components is most responsible for his hypotension and coagulopathy?

options.label: E
options.html: Heat-labile exotoxin that ADP-ribosylates G proteins

items.explanationHtml:
Neisseria meningitidis releases large amounts of lipooligosaccharide (its endotoxin) in membrane blebs. Through TLR4 it drives a cytokine storm, vascular leak, shock and disseminated intravascular coagulation, which produces the purpuric rash.

Takeaway: meningococcal shock and DIC are driven by endotoxin (lipooligosaccharide).

whyNot.A: The capsule helps the organism evade phagocytosis and complement but does not itself trigger shock.
whyNot.B: IgA protease helps mucosal colonisation by cleaving secretory IgA.
whyNot.C: Pili mediate adhesion to nasopharyngeal epithelium and endothelium.
whyNot.E: This mechanism belongs to toxins such as cholera toxin; meningococcus does not make it.
whyNot.F: Protein A is a Staphylococcus aureus factor that binds the Fc portion of IgG.

items.objective: Link meningococcal septic shock and DIC to lipooligosaccharide endotoxin.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman is admitted with fever, confusion and strange smells that no one else notices. MRI shows asymmetric T2 hyperintensity in the left medial temporal lobe. CSF PCR is positive for herpes simplex virus type 1. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the first-line drug for her condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Phosphorylation by viral thymidine kinase, then inhibition of viral DNA polymerase with chain termination

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of viral neuraminidase, blocking release of new virions

options.label: C
options.html: Direct pyrophosphate-site inhibition of viral DNA polymerase without prior activation

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of viral uncoating by blocking an M2 ion channel

options.label: E
options.html: Phosphorylation by a viral protein kinase encoded by UL97, then polymerase inhibition

items.explanationHtml:
Acyclovir is a guanosine analogue. HSV thymidine kinase adds the first phosphate, so the drug is activated mainly in infected cells; host kinases complete the triphosphate, which competes with dGTP, inhibits viral DNA polymerase and terminates the chain.

Takeaway: acyclovir needs viral thymidine kinase; resistance comes from thymidine kinase mutations.

whyNot.B: Neuraminidase inhibitors such as oseltamivir act on influenza.
whyNot.C: This is foscarnet, which is reserved for acyclovir-resistant virus.
whyNot.D: This describes amantadine, an influenza drug no longer used for that purpose.
whyNot.E: UL97-dependent activation is how ganciclovir works against cytomegalovirus.

items.objective: Describe the activation and mechanism of acyclovir in HSV encephalitis.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man is brought for evaluation of memory loss and unsteadiness that have progressed over 4 months. He now needs help to dress. Loud noises make his limbs jerk suddenly. EEG shows periodic sharp-wave complexes. He dies 3 months later. Brain tissue shows neuronal loss and vacuoles in the grey matter without inflammatory cells. Which of the following best describes the pathogenesis of his disease?

options.label: A
options.html: Latent DNA virus reactivates in oligodendrocytes

options.label: B
options.html: Extracellular deposition of amyloid-β cleaved from amyloid precursor protein

options.label: C
options.html: A host protein refolds into a protease-resistant β-sheet-rich form that converts more normal protein

options.label: D
options.html: Hyperphosphorylated α-synuclein accumulates in cortical neurons

options.label: E
options.html: Persistent measles virus infection triggers chronic inflammation

items.explanationHtml:
Rapid dementia with startle myoclonus and periodic sharp-wave complexes is sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease. Normal prion protein (PrPC) is converted into PrPSc, which is rich in β-pleated sheets, resists proteases and acts as a template for further conversion. Neuronal loss and spongiform vacuolation occur without inflammation.

Takeaway: prion disease is self-propagating misfolding of PrP into a β-sheet form, with spongiform change and no inflammation.

whyNot.A: This describes JC virus in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy, which damages white matter.
whyNot.B: Alzheimer disease progresses over years, not months, and does not cause spongiform change.
whyNot.D: Cortical α-synuclein aggregates (Lewy bodies) cause dementia with Lewy bodies, which progresses over years with fluctuations and hallucinations and no spongiform change.
whyNot.E: Subacute sclerosing panencephalitis occurs in children and adolescents and shows marked inflammation and inclusions.

items.objective: Explain the pathogenesis of Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man with untreated HIV infection comes to the emergency department because of a 2-week history of headache and fever. CD4 count is 38/mm3. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 34 cm H2O. India ink staining of the cerebrospinal fluid is positive. Which of the following best describes the organism causing his illness?

options.label: A
options.html: Dimorphic fungus with broad-based budding yeasts

options.label: B
options.html: Septate hyphae branching at acute angles

options.label: C
options.html: Non-septate hyphae branching at wide angles

options.label: E
options.html: Yeast with a thick polysaccharide capsule and narrow-based budding

items.explanationHtml:
Cryptococcus neoformans is an encapsulated yeast acquired by inhalation (soil, pigeon droppings). Its polysaccharide capsule excludes India ink, and it is also detected by cryptococcal antigen testing. Narrow-based budding and a high opening pressure are characteristic.

Takeaway: India ink-positive meningitis with high opening pressure in advanced HIV is Cryptococcus, an encapsulated yeast.

whyNot.A: Broad-based budding is the hallmark of Blastomyces.
whyNot.B: This describes Aspergillus, which causes angioinvasive disease rather than chronic meningitis.
whyNot.C: This describes the Mucorales, which cause rhinocerebral mucormycosis.
whyNot.D: Spherules belong to Coccidioides, which can cause basilar meningitis but is not seen with India ink.

items.objective: Identify Cryptococcus neoformans from its morphology in an HIV-associated meningitis.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman with relapsing multiple sclerosis has taken natalizumab for 3 years. Over 6 weeks she develops progressive right arm weakness and difficulty finding words. MRI shows confluent T2-hyperintense lesions in the left frontal and parietal subcortical white matter that do not enhance and have no mass effect. PCR of cerebrospinal fluid detects JC virus DNA. Which of the following cell types is the primary target of this virus?
items.explanationHtml:
This is progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy. JC polyomavirus reactivates when cell-mediated immunity fails or, with natalizumab, when lymphocyte surveillance of the CNS is blocked. It lytically infects oligodendrocytes, causing demyelination; infected oligodendrocytes have enlarged nuclei with viral inclusions.

Takeaway: PML is JC virus destruction of oligodendrocytes, a known risk of natalizumab.

whyNot.A: Astrocytes can show bizarre reactive changes in this disease, but myelin loss follows infection of the myelin-forming cell.
whyNot.C: Microglia respond to injury but are not the cells the virus destroys to cause demyelination.
whyNot.D: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and are not targeted.
whyNot.E: Schwann cells myelinate peripheral nerves, which are not involved.
whyNot.F: The lesions are in white matter, and cortical neurons are not the main target.

items.objective: Identify oligodendrocytes as the target cell in progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has had shooting pains in his legs for a year and now staggers in the dark. Vibration and joint-position sense are absent in both feet, ankle reflexes are absent and the Romberg sign is positive. Both pupils are small and irregular; they constrict when he looks at a near object but not in response to light. Serum treponemal antibody is positive. Degeneration of which of the following structures best explains his gait disorder?
items.explanationHtml:
This is tabes dorsalis, a late form of neurosyphilis. Inflammation of the dorsal roots leads to degeneration of the dorsal columns. Loss of proprioception produces a sensory ataxia that worsens without vision (a positive Romberg sign); loss of the afferent limb abolishes reflexes; root irritation produces lightning pains. Argyll Robertson pupils accommodate but do not react to light.

Takeaway: tabes dorsalis destroys dorsal roots and columns: sensory ataxia, positive Romberg, areflexia, Argyll Robertson pupils.

whyNot.A: Corticospinal damage gives weakness, spasticity and hyperreflexia, not sensory ataxia with lost reflexes.
whyNot.B: Anterior horn loss gives weakness and wasting, not loss of position sense.
whyNot.C: Cerebellar ataxia is present with the eyes open and does not cause a positive Romberg sign.
whyNot.E: Spinothalamic damage causes loss of pain and temperature, not of vibration and position sense.

items.objective: Localise the lesion of tabes dorsalis to the dorsal roots and dorsal columns.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has had frontal headaches for 2 weeks and a generalised seizure today. One month ago he had acute frontal sinusitis that was treated with a short course of antibiotics. His temperature is 37.9°C (100.2°F). MRI shows a 3-cm ring-enhancing lesion in the right frontal lobe with surrounding oedema and restricted diffusion in its centre. Which of the following organisms is most likely to be isolated from the lesion?
items.explanationHtml:
An abscess next to an infected frontal sinus forms by contiguous spread. The usual organisms are viridans streptococci, especially the S. anginosus (milleri) group, often mixed with anaerobes. These streptococci are notable for forming abscesses.

Takeaway: brain abscess from a sinus or tooth: viridans streptococci (S. anginosus group) and anaerobes.

whyNot.A: Toxoplasma causes ring lesions in immunosuppressed patients, usually multiple and at the basal ganglia.
whyNot.B: Pseudomonas is a cause after neurosurgery or chronic ear infection, not after frontal sinusitis.
whyNot.D: Listeria causes meningitis and rhombencephalitis, not abscesses spreading from a sinus.
whyNot.E: Neurocysticercosis produces cysts in people from endemic areas, not an abscess after sinusitis.

items.objective: Predict the organisms of a brain abscess from its source of spread.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is brought to the emergency department by his roommate because he has become increasingly confused over the past 8 hours after a day of fever and severe headache. Temperature is 39.6°C (103.3°F), pulse is 122/min and blood pressure is 104/62 mm Hg. He is drowsy and oriented only to person. The neck is stiff. There are a few petechiae on his ankles. Fundoscopy is not possible because he will not cooperate. There is no focal weakness. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the head, then lumbar puncture, then antibiotics

options.label: B
options.html: Lumbar puncture immediately, then antibiotics once the Gram stain is available

options.label: C
options.html: Vancomycin, ceftriaxone and ampicillin without dexamethasone, then lumbar puncture

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain blood cultures, give dexamethasone, vancomycin and ceftriaxone, then CT of the head

options.label: E
options.html: Intravenous acyclovir alone while awaiting MRI

items.explanationHtml:
He has suspected bacterial (probably meningococcal) meningitis with altered consciousness, an indication for CT before lumbar puncture. Imaging must not delay treatment: draw blood cultures, give dexamethasone with the first antibiotic dose and start vancomycin plus ceftriaxone (the regimen for ages 1 month to 50 years), then image and perform the LP if safe.

Takeaway: if CT must come before LP, give cultures, dexamethasone and antibiotics first.

whyNot.A: His reduced consciousness means imaging is needed before LP, but antibiotics must not wait for CT.
whyNot.B: Altered consciousness is an indication for CT before LP, and waiting for the Gram stain delays treatment.
whyNot.C: Ampicillin is not needed at his age, dexamethasone should be given, and LP before imaging is unsafe here.
whyNot.E: Neck stiffness, petechiae and high fever point to bacterial meningitis, which needs antibacterial therapy now.

items.objective: Sequence blood cultures, dexamethasone, empirical antibiotics and imaging in suspected bacterial meningitis.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item received dexamethasone, vancomycin and ceftriaxone, and CT of the head was normal. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 3,200 leukocytes/mm3 (94% neutrophils), protein 260 mg/dL (reference 15–45 mg/dL) and glucose 18 mg/dL (reference 40–70 mg/dL); Gram stain shows gram-negative diplococci. His roommate, who shares their apartment, is well. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for the roommate?

options.label: A
options.html: A single oral dose of ciprofloxacin

options.label: B
options.html: No action unless he develops fever

options.label: E
options.html: Throat culture, with treatment only if it grows the organism

items.explanationHtml:
Gram-negative diplococci confirm meningococcal meningitis. Household and other close contacts should receive chemoprophylaxis as soon as possible: a single oral dose of ciprofloxacin, a 2-day course of rifampin, or a single intramuscular dose of ceftriaxone. Public health should be notified.

Takeaway: close contacts of meningococcal disease get chemoprophylaxis (ciprofloxacin, rifampin or ceftriaxone) without waiting.

whyNot.B: Close contacts of meningococcal disease are at high risk and should receive chemoprophylaxis within 24 hours.
whyNot.C: Vaccination does not protect quickly enough after an exposure; chemoprophylaxis is required.
whyNot.D: Amoxicillin does not reliably eradicate nasopharyngeal carriage of meningococcus.
whyNot.E: Prophylaxis is given to all close contacts without waiting for carriage testing.
whyNot.F: A full treatment course is not needed; a single intramuscular dose is one prophylaxis option.

items.objective: Recommend chemoprophylaxis for close contacts of a patient with meningococcal meningitis.

items.stemHtml:
A 31-year-old man who moved to the United States from a country with a high prevalence of tuberculosis 6 months ago has had headache, low-grade fever, night sweats and weight loss for 3 weeks. Today he has double vision. His temperature is 38.1°C (100.6°F). He cannot abduct the left eye. HIV testing is negative. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis shows:

CSF testResultReference range
Opening pressure290 mm H2O70–180 mm H2O
Leukocytes240/mm3 (85% lymphocytes)0–5/mm3
Protein230 mg/dL15–45 mg/dL
Glucose24 mg/dL (serum 104 mg/dL)40–70 mg/dL
Gram stainNo organisms

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A subacute illness over weeks, constitutional symptoms, a cranial nerve palsy (the abducens nerve is often affected by basal exudate and raised pressure), lymphocytic CSF with a very high protein and a low glucose point to tuberculous meningitis. Send CSF for acid-fast stain, mycobacterial culture and nucleic acid amplification, and start four-drug therapy plus dexamethasone without waiting for confirmation.

Takeaway: lymphocytic CSF with very high protein and low glucose over weeks suggests tuberculous meningitis.

whyNot.A: Viral meningitis is acute and has a normal CSF glucose.
whyNot.B: He has had no antibiotics, and the 3-week course with weight loss does not fit.
whyNot.C: GBS raises CSF protein without pleocytosis (albuminocytologic dissociation) and causes ascending weakness.
whyNot.D: Subarachnoid haemorrhage causes a sudden severe headache, with red cells or xanthochromia in the CSF.

items.objective: Interpret a cerebrospinal fluid profile to diagnose tuberculous meningitis.

items.stemHtml: A 54-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because he has been confused and has spoken in jumbled sentences since this morning. He has had fever and headache for 3 days. Temperature is 38.8°C (101.8°F). He is disoriented and has a fluent aphasia; there is no neck stiffness or rash. CT of the head is normal. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 110 leukocytes/mm3 (88% lymphocytes), 340 erythrocytes/mm3, protein 82 mg/dL (reference 15–45 mg/dL) and glucose 64 mg/dL (reference 40–70 mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Wait for the CSF HSV PCR result before treating

options.label: E
options.html: Brain biopsy of the left temporal lobe

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, acute confusion and a language disturbance with lymphocytic CSF containing red cells suggests HSV encephalitis of the dominant temporal lobe. Untreated mortality is high, and early acyclovir improves survival and function, so start it immediately and then confirm with CSF PCR and MRI.

Takeaway: suspected encephalitis means intravenous acyclovir now, before the PCR result returns.

whyNot.A: Delaying acyclovir worsens outcome; treatment starts on suspicion.
whyNot.C: Encephalitis needs admission and intravenous acyclovir.
whyNot.D: The lymphocytic CSF with normal glucose points to a viral cause, and antibacterials alone do not cover HSV.
whyNot.E: Biopsy is no longer needed for diagnosis now that CSF PCR is available.

items.objective: Start empirical intravenous acyclovir in suspected HSV encephalitis.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of fever, headache and confusion that began yesterday. Temperature is 39.2°C (102.6°F). She has neck stiffness and is oriented only to person. She has no immunosuppressive conditions and takes no medications. CT of the head is normal, blood cultures are drawn and lumbar puncture is performed. Which of the following is the most appropriate empirical regimen to give with dexamethasone?
items.explanationHtml:
Over age 50, Listeria monocytogenes joins pneumococcus and meningococcus as a likely cause. Cephalosporins do not cover Listeria, so ampicillin is added to vancomycin and ceftriaxone.

Takeaway: add ampicillin for Listeria in meningitis over age 50, in pregnancy and with impaired cellular immunity.

whyNot.A: Ceftriaxone alone misses penicillin-resistant pneumococcus and Listeria.
whyNot.B: This is adequate under age 50 but omits Listeria cover, which she needs at 72.
whyNot.D: This neonatal regimen does not cover resistant pneumococcus or meningococcus reliably.
whyNot.E: This post-neurosurgical regimen is broader than needed and still lacks a reliable anti-Listeria agent at standard use.

items.objective: Choose empirical antibiotics for bacterial meningitis in an older adult.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old woman with HIV infection, not taking antiretroviral therapy, is admitted with 3 weeks of worsening headache and blurred vision. CD4 count is 22/mm3. MRI of the brain is normal. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 380 mm H2O (reference 70–180 mm H2O), 12 leukocytes/mm3, and a positive cryptococcal antigen. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine, with repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures

options.label: B
options.html: Fluconazole alone, with acetazolamide for the raised pressure

options.label: C
options.html: Start antiretroviral therapy today alongside antifungal therapy

options.label: D
options.html: Amphotericin B plus flucytosine, with high-dose dexamethasone

options.label: E
options.html: Ventriculoperitoneal shunt placement before antifungal therapy

items.explanationHtml:
Cryptococcal meningitis is treated with induction therapy of amphotericin B (liposomal preferred) plus flucytosine, then fluconazole. Raised intracranial pressure, common and lethal, is controlled with repeated therapeutic lumbar punctures. Antiretroviral therapy is started after about 4–6 weeks of antifungal therapy.

Takeaway: cryptococcal meningitis: amphotericin plus flucytosine, therapeutic LPs for pressure, and delayed ART.

whyNot.B: Fluconazole alone is weaker induction therapy, and acetazolamide is harmful in cryptococcal meningitis.
whyNot.C: Starting ART immediately raises mortality from immune reconstitution; it is deferred for about 4–6 weeks.
whyNot.D: Adjunctive corticosteroids increased harm in trials of cryptococcal meningitis.
whyNot.E: Antifungal therapy and serial LPs come first; a shunt is reserved for persistent raised pressure.

items.objective: Manage cryptococcal meningitis in advanced HIV, including intracranial pressure and timing of antiretroviral therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old man with HIV infection who stopped antiretroviral therapy 2 years ago comes to the emergency department with headache and left arm weakness that have worsened over 10 days. CD4 count is 64/mm3. Serum Toxoplasma IgG is positive. MRI shows four ring-enhancing lesions, the largest in the right basal ganglia, with surrounding oedema. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Multiple ring-enhancing lesions at the basal ganglia and grey–white junction, a CD4 count below 100/mm3 and positive Toxoplasma IgG make cerebral toxoplasmosis most likely. Treat empirically with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and leucovorin (which protects the marrow from pyrimethamine), then repeat imaging in about 2 weeks.

Takeaway: multiple ring lesions with positive Toxoplasma IgG in advanced HIV: treat empirically and re-image.

whyNot.A: Biopsy is reserved for lesions that do not improve after about 2 weeks of empirical therapy.
whyNot.B: Radiation treats lymphoma, which usually presents as a single periventricular lesion.
whyNot.C: Amphotericin treats cryptococcal infection, which does not cause multiple ring lesions.
whyNot.D: Methotrexate is chemotherapy for primary CNS lymphoma, not the first step here.

items.objective: Treat suspected cerebral toxoplasmosis empirically in advanced HIV.

items.stemHtml: A 51-year-old man is evaluated for memory problems and irritability that have developed over a year. His serum RPR is reactive at a titre of 1:64 and the treponemal antibody test is positive. HIV testing is negative. Cerebrospinal fluid shows 28 leukocytes/mm3 (lymphocytes), protein 70 mg/dL (reference 15–45 mg/dL) and a reactive VDRL. He reports no drug allergies. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: A single intramuscular dose of benzathine penicillin G

options.label: B
options.html: Intramuscular benzathine penicillin G weekly for 3 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Intravenous aqueous penicillin G for 10–14 days

options.label: E
options.html: A single oral dose of azithromycin

items.explanationHtml:
A reactive CSF VDRL with lymphocytic pleocytosis and cognitive decline confirms neurosyphilis (general paresis). The treatment is intravenous aqueous crystalline penicillin G for 10–14 days. Repeat CSF examination and serology at intervals to confirm response.

Takeaway: neurosyphilis needs intravenous penicillin G for 10–14 days; benzathine penicillin is inadequate.

whyNot.A: Benzathine penicillin does not reach treponemicidal levels in the CSF.
whyNot.B: This treats late latent syphilis, not neurosyphilis.
whyNot.C: Doxycycline is not first-line for neurosyphilis and is reserved for special situations.
whyNot.E: Azithromycin is not an effective treatment for neurosyphilis, and resistance is widespread.

items.objective: Treat neurosyphilis with intravenous penicillin G.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had two episodes of neurological symptoms: painful loss of vision in the right eye 2 years ago and numbness of both legs this month, each improving over weeks. MRI shows ovoid T2-hyperintense lesions next to the lateral ventricles and in the cervical cord. Which of the following findings in the cerebrospinal fluid is most likely?

options.label: B
options.html: IgG oligoclonal bands that are not present in serum

options.label: D
options.html: Albuminocytologic dissociation with protein above 300 mg/dL

items.explanationHtml:
Relapsing episodes in different CNS locations with periventricular and cord lesions indicate multiple sclerosis. B cells within the CNS make IgG, detected as oligoclonal bands present in CSF but absent from serum, with a raised IgG index.

Takeaway: CSF-specific oligoclonal IgG bands reflect antibody synthesis inside the CNS in MS.

whyNot.A: MS causes at most a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis.
whyNot.C: CSF glucose is normal in MS.
whyNot.D: This pattern suggests Guillain-Barré syndrome; protein in MS is normal or mildly raised.
whyNot.E: Xanthochromia indicates prior bleeding into the subarachnoid space.
whyNot.F: 14-3-3 protein suggests rapid neuronal destruction, as in prion disease.

items.objective: Recognise the CSF findings of multiple sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has double vision when she looks to the right. On right gaze, the left eye does not move past the midline, and the right eye shows horizontal nystagmus. Convergence is normal. She had optic neuritis a year ago. A lesion in which of the following structures best explains her eye findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Failure of adduction of the left eye on right gaze, with nystagmus in the abducting right eye and normal convergence, is a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The lesion is in the left medial longitudinal fasciculus, which carries signals from the right abducens nucleus to the left oculomotor nucleus. Convergence uses a separate pathway, so it is spared. In a young adult, MS is the usual cause.

Takeaway: INO is named for the side of the eye that fails to adduct, which is the side of the MLF lesion.

whyNot.A: An abducens nucleus lesion causes a gaze palsy to the same side in both eyes.
whyNot.B: A right MLF lesion would impair adduction of the right eye on left gaze.
whyNot.C: A third nerve palsy would also impair convergence and cause ptosis and a dilated pupil.
whyNot.D: A right PPRF lesion causes failure of both eyes to look to the right.

items.objective: Localise internuclear ophthalmoplegia to the medial longitudinal fasciculus.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old woman has severe visual loss in both eyes and, 3 months later, weakness of both legs with a sensory level at T4. For 2 weeks between these episodes she had constant hiccups and vomiting. MRI shows a T2-hyperintense lesion running continuously from C7 to T6. Antibodies against which of the following targets are most likely to be found in her serum?

options.label: C
options.html: Acetylcholine receptor at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: D
options.html: GluN1 subunit of the NMDA receptor

options.label: E
options.html: Voltage-gated calcium channel on presynaptic nerve terminals

items.explanationHtml:
Severe optic neuritis, longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis (3 or more segments) and an area postrema syndrome are characteristic of NMOSD. Most patients have IgG against aquaporin-4, the water channel on astrocyte foot processes; complement-mediated astrocyte injury leads to secondary demyelination.

Takeaway: NMOSD: aquaporin-4 IgG attacks astrocytes; optic neuritis, long cord lesions, intractable hiccups.

whyNot.B: Antibodies to myelin basic protein are not a diagnostic test for any of these disorders.
whyNot.C: These antibodies cause myasthenia gravis, a disorder of fatigable weakness.
whyNot.D: These antibodies cause an encephalitis with psychiatric symptoms and dyskinesias.
whyNot.E: These antibodies cause Lambert-Eaton syndrome.
whyNot.F: These antibodies are associated with the Miller Fisher variant of Guillain-Barré syndrome.

items.objective: Identify aquaporin-4 as the target antigen in neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman with highly active relapsing multiple sclerosis starts a monthly intravenous monoclonal antibody. Before starting, she is tested for antibodies against JC virus. Which of the following best describes how this drug works?

options.label: A
options.html: It depletes B cells by binding CD20

options.label: B
options.html: It traps lymphocytes in lymph nodes by modulating sphingosine-1-phosphate receptors

options.label: C
options.html: It blocks α4-integrin on lymphocytes and prevents their adhesion to brain endothelium

options.label: D
options.html: It inhibits dihydroorotate dehydrogenase in activated lymphocytes

options.label: E
options.html: It depletes T and B cells by binding CD52

items.explanationHtml:
Natalizumab binds α4-integrin (VLA-4) on lymphocytes, preventing their adhesion to VCAM-1 on cerebral endothelium and their migration into the CNS. Because CNS immune surveillance falls, JC virus can cause progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy; the risk is highest in patients with JC virus antibodies, long treatment and prior immunosuppression.

Takeaway: natalizumab blocks α4-integrin; screen for JC virus antibodies because of PML risk.

whyNot.A: Anti-CD20 antibodies (ocrelizumab) deplete B cells; JC virus testing is not their defining safety test.
whyNot.B: S1P modulators such as fingolimod are oral drugs.
whyNot.D: This is teriflunomide, an oral drug.
whyNot.E: Anti-CD52 therapy (alemtuzumab) is given as yearly courses and is known for secondary autoimmunity.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism and main risk of natalizumab.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with relapsing multiple sclerosis starts a new oral disease-modifying drug. Six hours after the first dose his pulse falls from 72/min to 48/min. Over the following months his blood lymphocyte count falls sharply, although lymphocytes are not destroyed. Which of the following drugs did he most likely start?
items.explanationHtml:
Fingolimod is a sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator. It causes internalisation of S1P1 receptors on lymphocytes, which then cannot leave lymph nodes, so blood lymphocyte counts fall. S1P receptors on atrial myocytes explain first-dose bradycardia and AV block; macular oedema is another adverse effect.

Takeaway: S1P receptor modulators trap lymphocytes in nodes and can cause first-dose bradycardia.

whyNot.A: Dimethyl fumarate causes flushing and lymphopenia, but not first-dose bradycardia.
whyNot.B: Teriflunomide causes hepatotoxicity and hair thinning, not bradycardia.
whyNot.C: Cladribine kills lymphocytes as a purine analogue rather than redistributing them.
whyNot.E: Dalfampridine is a potassium channel blocker that improves walking and does not alter lymphocyte counts.

items.objective: Recognise fingolimod from its mechanism and adverse effects.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after 2 weeks of anxiety, insomnia and paranoid ideas, followed by a generalised seizure today. She makes repetitive chewing and lip-smacking movements, her blood pressure fluctuates between 90/50 and 170/100 mm Hg, and she has periods of shallow breathing. CSF shows a mild lymphocytic pleocytosis. Which of the following conditions is most likely to be found on further evaluation?
items.explanationHtml:
Psychiatric symptoms progressing to seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability and hypoventilation in a young woman are typical of anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. IgG against the GluN1 subunit causes receptor internalisation. An ovarian teratoma, which contains neural tissue expressing NMDA receptors, is found in a large share of adult women with the disease.

Takeaway: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in a young woman: look for an ovarian teratoma.

whyNot.A: Small cell carcinoma is associated with other paraneoplastic antibodies (for example anti-Hu) and is rare at her age.
whyNot.C: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis.
whyNot.D: Neuroblastoma is associated with opsoclonus-myoclonus in young children.
whyNot.E: Medullary thyroid carcinoma is not a recognised trigger of autoimmune encephalitis.

items.objective: Associate anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis with ovarian teratoma.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl is brought to the emergency department because she has become drowsy and unsteady over 3 days. Two weeks ago she had a febrile upper respiratory infection. She has bilateral leg weakness, ataxia and brisk reflexes. MRI shows multiple large, poorly marginated T2-hyperintense lesions in the subcortical white matter, thalami and brainstem, all of similar age. CSF shows 18 lymphocytes/mm3 and no oligoclonal bands. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A child with encephalopathy and multifocal deficits days to weeks after an infection, with widespread lesions of the same age, has acute disseminated encephalomyelitis. It is an immune response, thought to involve molecular mimicry, that is usually monophasic; some children have MOG antibodies. Treatment is high-dose corticosteroids.

Takeaway: ADEM: post-infectious, monophasic, encephalopathy plus multifocal lesions of the same age, usually in a child.

whyNot.A: MS lesions are typically of different ages, and encephalopathy is unusual at onset.
whyNot.B: HSV targets the temporal lobes and causes fever with cortical signs, not multifocal white matter lesions.
whyNot.C: PML occurs with immunosuppression and progresses over weeks without a preceding infection.
whyNot.D: This X-linked disorder progresses over months, affects boys and produces symmetric posterior white matter changes.

items.objective: Distinguish ADEM from multiple sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 33-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis notices that her left leg becomes weak and her vision blurs whenever she takes a hot shower or jogs; the symptoms resolve within an hour of cooling down. Which of the following best explains this phenomenon?

options.label: A
options.html: Heat triggers a new inflammatory lesion in the optic nerve and spinal cord

options.label: B
options.html: Exercise lowers serum potassium and hyperpolarises motor neurons

options.label: C
options.html: Higher temperature makes action potentials fail at demyelinated segments of axons

options.label: D
options.html: Vasodilation in the skin diverts blood flow away from the brainstem

options.label: E
options.html: Heat increases acetylcholinesterase activity at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: F
options.html: Sweating causes dehydration and cerebral hypoperfusion

items.explanationHtml:
This is the Uhthoff phenomenon. Demyelinated axons conduct with a low safety factor. A rise in temperature shortens the action potential (sodium channels inactivate faster), so the current reaching the next node can fall below threshold and conduction blocks. Old deficits reappear transiently and resolve with cooling.

Takeaway: heat-induced, reversible return of old MS symptoms is conduction block in demyelinated axons, not a relapse.

whyNot.A: Symptoms resolve within an hour, which rules out a new inflammatory lesion.
whyNot.B: Exercise raises, not lowers, extracellular potassium, and the vision change is not explained.
whyNot.D: Cutaneous vasodilation does not cause focal deficits in a pattern matching old lesions.
whyNot.E: The neuromuscular junction is not involved in MS.
whyNot.F: Mild dehydration does not reproduce focal deficits that match previous lesions.

items.objective: Explain the Uhthoff phenomenon in multiple sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman comes to the clinic because of 4 days of blurred vision in her left eye and pain when she moves it. Visual acuity is 20/20 in the right eye and 20/80 in the left. She cannot distinguish colours well with the left eye, and there is a left relative afferent pupillary defect. The optic disc looks normal. She has had no previous neurological symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to guide long-term management?

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain with gadolinium

options.label: C
options.html: Lumbar puncture for oligoclonal bands as the first test

items.explanationHtml:
Painful monocular vision loss with poor colour vision, a relative afferent pupillary defect and a normal disc is optic neuritis (retrobulbar). MRI of the brain with gadolinium is the most useful test: typical white matter lesions mean a high risk of multiple sclerosis and may establish the diagnosis, which leads to early disease-modifying therapy.

Takeaway: after a first episode of optic neuritis, brain MRI with gadolinium sets MS risk and management.

whyNot.A: Giant cell arteritis affects people over 50 and causes painless vision loss with a swollen pale disc.
whyNot.C: CSF can support the diagnosis but MRI is the key first test to estimate MS risk.
whyNot.D: Carotid disease causes painless transient monocular vision loss, not painful optic neuritis.
whyNot.E: CT does not show white matter demyelinating lesions and adds radiation without benefit.
whyNot.F: The retina is normal in optic neuritis; the problem is in the optic nerve.

items.objective: Order brain MRI after a first episode of optic neuritis.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman with relapsing multiple sclerosis, stable for 3 years on ocrelizumab, comes to the clinic because the numbness and weakness in her right leg, which she had after a relapse 4 years ago, have returned over 2 days. She has also had burning when she urinates and needs to urinate frequently. Temperature is 38.0°C (100.4°F). Strength is 4/5 in the right leg, as it was at its worst after the old relapse. There are no new deficits. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Intravenous methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3–5 days

options.label: E
options.html: Urgent MRI of the brain and spinal cord with gadolinium

items.explanationHtml:
Return of an old deficit with fever and urinary symptoms suggests a pseudo-relapse: infection and fever impair conduction in previously damaged pathways. Confirm and treat the urinary tract infection; symptoms should resolve as the fever settles. Steroids are not indicated and could worsen the infection.

Takeaway: before treating an MS relapse, exclude infection and fever (pseudo-relapse).

whyNot.B: Steroids are for a true relapse; infection-induced worsening should be treated by treating the infection.
whyNot.C: Plasma exchange is for severe relapses that do not respond to steroids.
whyNot.D: A pseudo-relapse does not mean treatment failure.
whyNot.E: Imaging may be considered later, but the likely trigger, infection, should be confirmed and treated first.

items.objective: Distinguish an infection-triggered pseudo-relapse from a true MS relapse.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old man with relapsing multiple sclerosis develops weakness of his left arm and leg over 4 days, so that he now needs a cane to walk. He has no fever and urinalysis is normal. MRI shows a new gadolinium-enhancing lesion in the right corona radiata. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment for this episode?

options.label: A
options.html: Oral prednisone 60 mg daily tapered over 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Observation only, because steroids do not alter long-term disability

items.explanationHtml:
A new disabling deficit lasting more than 24 hours without fever or infection, with a new enhancing lesion, is an MS relapse. High-dose corticosteroids (for example methylprednisolone 1 g daily intravenously for 3–5 days) speed recovery. Plasma exchange is the next step if the response is poor. Review whether his disease-modifying therapy needs escalating.

Takeaway: a disabling MS relapse is treated with high-dose methylprednisolone; plasma exchange if refractory.

whyNot.A: Low-to-moderate oral doses are not the standard; high doses are needed.
whyNot.B: IVIG has not been shown to help MS relapses.
whyNot.D: Dalfampridine is a symptomatic treatment for chronic walking difficulty, not for an acute relapse.
whyNot.E: Steroids do not change long-term disability, but they speed recovery from a disabling relapse.

items.objective: Treat an acute disabling relapse of multiple sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman is recovering from a first episode of transverse myelitis. MRI showed a central cord lesion extending from C3 to T2. During the same month she had 10 days of intractable hiccups and vomiting. Serum aquaporin-4 IgG is positive. Brain MRI shows no periventricular lesions. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term therapy to prevent further attacks?
items.explanationHtml:
A long cord lesion, an area postrema syndrome and aquaporin-4 IgG confirm NMOSD. Attacks cause cumulative disability, so long-term immunotherapy is started after the first attack. Approved options include inebilizumab (anti-CD19), eculizumab or ravulizumab (C5 inhibitors) and satralizumab (anti-IL-6 receptor); rituximab is also used. Several MS drugs make NMOSD worse.

Takeaway: NMOSD is not MS: use B-cell, complement or IL-6 receptor therapy and avoid interferon, natalizumab and fingolimod.

whyNot.A: Interferon-β can worsen NMOSD.
whyNot.B: Natalizumab has been associated with severe attacks in NMOSD.
whyNot.C: Fingolimod can provoke NMOSD relapses.
whyNot.E: Glatiramer has no proven benefit in NMOSD.

items.objective: Choose maintenance immunotherapy for aquaporin-4 IgG-positive NMOSD.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman is admitted with a week of agitation, paranoia and insomnia, followed by two seizures. She now has abnormal writhing movements of her mouth and fluctuating blood pressure. MRI of the brain is normal. CSF shows 22 lymphocytes/mm3 with a normal glucose; HSV PCR is negative. Antibodies against the NMDA receptor are detected in the CSF. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Start haloperidol for agitation and observe

options.label: C
options.html: CT of the chest for small cell carcinoma

options.label: D
options.html: Repeat lumbar puncture in 2 weeks before treating

options.label: E
options.html: Ultrasonography or MRI of the pelvis

items.explanationHtml:
This is anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Search for an ovarian teratoma with pelvic ultrasound or MRI, and start first-line immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange). Removing a teratoma speeds recovery and lowers relapse risk.

Takeaway: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: image the pelvis for a teratoma and start immunotherapy.

whyNot.A: Antipsychotics are poorly tolerated and do not treat the cause; immunotherapy and a tumour search are needed.
whyNot.B: ECT does not address the underlying autoimmune process and is not a first step.
whyNot.C: Small cell carcinoma is not the associated tumour in a young woman with this syndrome.
whyNot.D: Treatment should start now; delays worsen outcome.

items.objective: Investigate for an ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old woman with newly diagnosed, highly active relapsing multiple sclerosis is going to start ocrelizumab. Which of the following tests is most important to perform before the first infusion?

options.label: A
options.html: Hepatitis B surface antigen and core antibody

options.label: D
options.html: Optical coherence tomography for macular oedema

items.explanationHtml:
Anti-CD20 antibodies deplete B cells and can cause fatal hepatitis B reactivation, so screening for hepatitis B (surface antigen and core antibody) is required before starting. Vaccines should also be brought up to date, because B-cell depletion blunts the response to vaccines given afterwards.

Takeaway: screen for hepatitis B before anti-CD20 therapy.

whyNot.B: Thyroid monitoring matters for alemtuzumab, which causes autoimmune thyroid disease.
whyNot.C: An ECG and first-dose monitoring are needed before sphingosine-1-phosphate modulators.
whyNot.D: Macular oedema is a concern with fingolimod, not anti-CD20 therapy.
whyNot.E: JC virus antibody status guides natalizumab risk.

items.objective: Identify pre-treatment screening required for anti-CD20 therapy in multiple sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman with multiple sclerosis reports urinary urgency and two episodes of urge incontinence a week for 3 months. She has no fever or dysuria. Urinalysis is normal. Ultrasonography shows a post-void residual volume of 30 mL. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
MS often causes neurogenic detrusor overactivity. With a small post-void residual, treatment is behavioural measures and an antimuscarinic such as oxybutynin (or the β3-agonist mirabegron). Always measure the residual volume first: if it is large, antimuscarinics could cause retention, and intermittent catheterisation is needed.

Takeaway: MS urgency with a small residual: antimuscarinic or mirabegron; large residual: intermittent catheterisation.

whyNot.A: Catheterisation treats incomplete emptying with a large residual volume, which she does not have.
whyNot.C: α-Blockers help outflow obstruction and incomplete emptying, not urgency from an overactive bladder.
whyNot.D: Bethanechol stimulates bladder contraction and would worsen urgency.
whyNot.E: A long-term catheter is a last resort and is not needed for an overactive bladder that empties.

items.objective: Manage neurogenic bladder overactivity in multiple sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has had progressive difficulty walking for 2 years, with stiffness in both legs and urinary urgency. He has never had a sudden episode of neurological symptoms. Examination shows spastic paraparesis with brisk reflexes and bilateral extensor plantar responses. MRI shows several periventricular and cervical cord T2 lesions, none enhancing, and CSF contains oligoclonal bands. Vitamin B12 and copper levels are normal. Which of the following disease-modifying therapies has been shown to slow disability progression in this condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Steady progression from onset without relapses, with typical MRI lesions and CSF oligoclonal bands, is primary progressive multiple sclerosis. The anti-CD20 antibody ocrelizumab modestly slows disability progression, especially in younger patients with active (enhancing) disease; the other agents listed treat relapsing MS only.

Takeaway: ocrelizumab is the agent shown to slow disability in primary progressive MS.

whyNot.A: Interferon-β has not shown benefit in primary progressive MS.
whyNot.B: Glatiramer failed to slow progression in primary progressive MS.
whyNot.D: Dimethyl fumarate is approved only for relapsing forms of MS.
whyNot.E: Teriflunomide is approved only for relapsing forms of MS.

items.objective: Select disease-modifying therapy for primary progressive multiple sclerosis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman has a fetal ultrasound at 18 weeks' gestation because of a markedly raised maternal serum α-fetoprotein. The fetus has no skull vault above the orbits and no recognisable cerebral hemispheres. Polyhydramnios develops later in pregnancy. Failure of which of the following processes during the fourth week of development caused this anomaly?

options.label: C
options.html: Division of the prosencephalon into two hemispheres

options.label: F
options.html: Fusion of the posterior vertebral arches

items.explanationHtml:
This is anencephaly, caused by failure of the rostral (cranial) neuropore to close around day 25. Exposed neural tissue leaks AFP into the amniotic fluid and maternal serum. The fetus cannot swallow normally, so amniotic fluid accumulates (polyhydramnios).

Takeaway: anencephaly = rostral neuropore failure; raised AFP and polyhydramnios.

whyNot.B: Failed caudal closure causes lumbosacral myelomeningocele, not absence of the forebrain.
whyNot.C: Failed forebrain division causes holoprosencephaly, a disorder of the fifth to sixth week.
whyNot.D: Vermis hypoplasia occurs in Dandy-Walker malformation.
whyNot.E: Neural crest defects cause disorders such as Hirschsprung disease, not anencephaly.
whyNot.F: Failed arch fusion alone causes spina bifida occulta.

items.objective: Explain the embryological failure in anencephaly.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman who has a child with spina bifida asks how she can lower the chance of the same problem in her next pregnancy. Supplementation with which of the following, begun before conception, has been shown to reduce the recurrence of this defect?
items.explanationHtml:
Neural tube closure needs folate for one-carbon transfer in nucleotide synthesis and methylation during rapid cell division. Taking folic acid from before conception through the first trimester greatly reduces both first occurrence and recurrence of neural tube defects; a higher dose is recommended after an affected pregnancy.

Takeaway: periconceptional folic acid prevents most neural tube defects; the dose is higher after an affected pregnancy.

whyNot.A: Vitamin B12 deficiency is linked to neural tube defects in some studies but its supplementation is not the proven preventive measure.
whyNot.B: Iodine deficiency causes congenital hypothyroidism, not neural tube defects.
whyNot.C: High-dose vitamin A is teratogenic and does not prevent neural tube defects.
whyNot.D: Iron prevents maternal anaemia but does not affect neural tube closure.

items.objective: Identify folic acid as the nutrient that prevents neural tube defects.

items.stemHtml: A newborn girl has a lesion on her lower back like the one shown in panel 4 of the figure: a sac containing meninges, cerebrospinal fluid, spinal cord and nerve roots, with no skin covering. She has weak legs and a patulous anus. Which of the following associated abnormalities is she most likely to have?

options.label: A
options.html: Cystic enlargement of the fourth ventricle with an absent vermis

options.label: C
options.html: Herniation of the cerebellar vermis and medulla through the foramen magnum

options.label: D
options.html: Isolated cerebellar tonsillar descent presenting in adulthood

options.label: E
options.html: Absence of the cerebral hemispheres and skull vault

items.explanationHtml:
Panel 4 shows a myelomeningocele. It is almost always accompanied by a Chiari II malformation: the vermis, fourth ventricle and medulla are displaced through the foramen magnum, which obstructs CSF flow and causes hydrocephalus in most infants.

Takeaway: myelomeningocele comes with Chiari II and hydrocephalus.

whyNot.A: This describes Dandy-Walker malformation, which is not typically associated with myelomeningocele.
whyNot.B: This describes holoprosencephaly, a forebrain cleavage defect.
whyNot.D: This describes Chiari I, which is not associated with myelomeningocele.
whyNot.E: This describes anencephaly, a rostral neuropore defect.

items.objective: Associate myelomeningocele with the Chiari II malformation.

items.stemHtml: A newborn has closely set eyes, a single nostril, a midline cleft lip and a single central upper incisor bud. MRI shows a single large ventricle with fused frontal lobes. Karyotype shows trisomy 13. Disruption of which of the following signalling pathways is most directly responsible for the brain malformation?
items.explanationHtml:
This is holoprosencephaly, failure of the forebrain to divide into two hemispheres, with midline facial defects. Sonic hedgehog from the prechordal plate drives ventral midline patterning. It is affected by SHH mutations, trisomy 13, maternal diabetes, prenatal alcohol, and defects of cholesterol synthesis (cholesterol modifies the SHH protein).

Takeaway: holoprosencephaly reflects defective sonic hedgehog signalling; trisomy 13 is a classic cause.

whyNot.A: Wnt signalling patterns the dorsal neural tube and limbs; it is not the classic cause of this malformation.
whyNot.C: Activating FGFR3 mutations cause achondroplasia.
whyNot.D: HOX genes pattern the body axis segment by segment; their disruption gives limb and vertebral anomalies.
whyNot.E: Excess retinoic acid causes ear, heart and neural crest anomalies.

items.objective: Link holoprosencephaly to the sonic hedgehog pathway.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had occipital headaches for 2 years that come on when she coughs or laughs. Recently she burned her hand on a stove without noticing. She has lost pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders and the backs of both arms, with normal light touch and vibration sense. MRI shows the cerebellar tonsils 9 mm below the foramen magnum and a fluid-filled cavity in the centre of the cervical cord. Damage to which of the following structures best explains her sensory findings?

options.label: B
options.html: Lateral spinothalamic tracts at the cord surface

items.explanationHtml:
A Chiari I malformation with a cervical syrinx expands from the centre of the cord. It first interrupts the second-order pain and temperature fibres as they cross in the anterior white commissure, causing a bilateral, cape-like loss of pain and temperature at the affected levels. Touch and vibration, which ascend in the dorsal columns, are spared.

Takeaway: a central cord syrinx causes cape-like loss of pain and temperature by cutting crossing fibres in the anterior white commissure.

whyNot.A: Dorsal column damage would impair vibration and position sense, which are normal.
whyNot.B: Surface spinothalamic damage would cause loss below the lesion, not a band over the shoulders and arms.
whyNot.C: Anterior horn damage causes weakness and wasting, not sensory loss.
whyNot.E: Ganglion damage affects all sensory modalities in the involved dermatomes.

items.objective: Localise dissociated sensory loss from a syrinx to the anterior white commissure.

items.stemHtml: An 8-month-old boy has clusters of brief flexion spasms of the trunk and arms. He has several hypopigmented oval macules on his trunk that fluoresce under a Wood lamp, and prenatal ultrasound had shown a cardiac mass. MRI shows cortical tubers and calcified subependymal nodules. The protein encoded by the most commonly mutated gene in this disorder normally has which of the following functions?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibits mTOR signalling by acting as a GTPase-activating protein for Rheb

options.label: B
options.html: Inactivates Ras by acting as its GTPase-activating protein

options.label: C
options.html: Targets hypoxia-inducible factor for proteasomal degradation

options.label: D
options.html: Links membrane proteins to the actin cytoskeleton to restrain growth

options.label: E
options.html: Activates a heterotrimeric G-protein α subunit

items.explanationHtml:
Infantile spasms, hypomelanotic macules, a cardiac rhabdomyoma, cortical tubers and subependymal nodules indicate tuberous sclerosis complex. TSC2 (tuberin), the gene more often mutated, forms a complex with hamartin that inactivates the GTPase Rheb, so mTORC1 stays off. Loss causes overgrowth of hamartomas, which explains why mTOR inhibitors such as everolimus shrink these tumours.

Takeaway: tuberous sclerosis: loss of hamartin/tuberin unleashes mTOR; mTOR inhibitors shrink the tumours.

whyNot.B: This is neurofibromin, the NF1 gene product.
whyNot.C: This is the function of the VHL protein, lost in von Hippel-Lindau disease.
whyNot.D: This describes merlin, the NF2 gene product.
whyNot.E: Activating GNAQ mutations cause Sturge-Weber syndrome.

items.objective: Describe the molecular function of the tuberous sclerosis gene products.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old girl has eight light-brown macules larger than 5 mm on her trunk, freckles in both axillae and two soft skin-coloured nodules on her back. Slit-lamp examination shows pigmented iris hamartomas. Her father has similar skin findings. The protein encoded by the mutated gene normally performs which of the following functions?

options.label: B
options.html: Arrests the cell cycle by binding E2F

options.label: D
options.html: Links membrane proteins to the actin cytoskeleton

items.explanationHtml:
Café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling, neurofibromas and Lisch nodules with an affected parent indicate neurofibromatosis type 1 (autosomal dominant, chromosome 17). Neurofibromin is a GTPase-activating protein that speeds conversion of active Ras-GTP to inactive Ras-GDP; loss of function leaves Ras signalling on.

Takeaway: NF1 neurofibromin switches off Ras; NF2 merlin is a different, cytoskeletal tumour suppressor.

whyNot.A: This is the function of the hamartin–tuberin complex in tuberous sclerosis.
whyNot.B: This is the retinoblastoma protein.
whyNot.C: Mismatch repair defects cause Lynch syndrome.
whyNot.D: This is merlin, the protein lost in NF2-related schwannomatosis.

items.objective: Identify the function of neurofibromin in neurofibromatosis type 1.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old man has headaches and unsteadiness. MRI shows a cystic cerebellar mass with an enhancing mural nodule. His haemoglobin is 18.9 g/dL (reference 13.5–17.5 g/dL). His mother died of renal cell carcinoma at 45, and he had a retinal vascular tumour treated with laser at 20. Loss of the gene product involved in this syndrome leads directly to which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Constitutive activation of the mTOR pathway

options.label: C
options.html: Failure of mismatch repair after DNA replication

options.label: D
options.html: Accumulation of hypoxia-inducible factor despite normal oxygen levels

options.label: E
options.html: Constitutive activation of the RET receptor tyrosine kinase

items.explanationHtml:
A cerebellar haemangioblastoma, a retinal haemangioblastoma and a family history of early renal cell carcinoma suggest von Hippel-Lindau disease (chromosome 3). The VHL protein targets hypoxia-inducible factor for proteasomal degradation. Without it, HIF accumulates and drives VEGF and erythropoietin production, which explains the vascular tumours and the polycythaemia.

Takeaway: VHL loss stabilises HIF: haemangioblastomas, clear cell renal carcinoma, pheochromocytoma and polycythaemia.

whyNot.A: mTOR activation is the mechanism in tuberous sclerosis.
whyNot.B: Persistent Ras activity is the mechanism in neurofibromatosis type 1.
whyNot.C: Mismatch repair failure is the mechanism of Lynch syndrome.
whyNot.E: RET activation causes MEN2, with medullary thyroid carcinoma and pheochromocytoma.

items.objective: Explain the molecular basis of von Hippel-Lindau disease.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy born at 28 weeks' gestation walks on his toes with his knees turned inward and his legs crossing when he is held up. His arms and hands work almost normally. He has hypertonia and brisk reflexes in both legs. His cognition is age-appropriate. MRI shows thinning of the white matter next to the lateral ventricles. Which of the following best explains why his legs are more affected than his arms?

options.label: A
options.html: The leg area of the motor cortex lies in the anterior cerebral artery territory

options.label: B
options.html: Corticospinal fibres to the legs pass closest to the lateral ventricles

options.label: C
options.html: Spinal cord motor neurons to the legs are more sensitive to hypoxia

options.label: D
options.html: Leg fibres are myelinated earlier than arm fibres and so are injured first

options.label: E
options.html: The basal ganglia preferentially control leg tone

items.explanationHtml:
In premature infants the periventricular white matter is a vulnerable watershed zone, and injury there is periventricular leukomalacia. The descending corticospinal fibres for the legs run medially, closest to the ventricles, so they are damaged most, producing spastic diplegia.

Takeaway: preterm periventricular leukomalacia causes spastic diplegia because leg fibres lie nearest the ventricles.

whyNot.A: The cortex is not the site of injury here; the damage is periventricular white matter.
whyNot.C: Anterior horn cells are not the site of injury, and their loss would cause flaccid, not spastic, weakness.
whyNot.D: Order of myelination does not explain the pattern; location next to the ventricles does.
whyNot.E: Basal ganglia injury causes dyskinetic, not spastic diplegic, cerebral palsy.

items.objective: Explain the leg-predominant pattern of spastic diplegia in preterm infants.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman comes for advice before trying to conceive. Her first pregnancy, 2 years ago, was terminated at 20 weeks because of anencephaly. She takes no medications and has no chronic illnesses. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation regarding folic acid?

options.label: A
options.html: 0.4 mg daily, starting once pregnancy is confirmed and continuing to delivery

options.label: B
options.html: 0.4 mg daily, starting at least 1 month before conception

options.label: C
options.html: 4 mg daily, starting at least 1 month before conception and continuing through the first trimester

options.label: D
options.html: 4 mg daily, starting at 12 weeks' gestation

options.label: E
options.html: No supplement, provided her diet contains folate-fortified grain products

items.explanationHtml:
After a pregnancy affected by a neural tube defect, the recurrence risk is several times higher, and a higher folic acid dose (4 mg daily) is recommended from at least 1 month before conception through the first trimester. The neural tube closes by about 4 weeks after fertilisation, so supplementation must begin before conception.

Takeaway: previous neural tube defect: 4 mg folic acid daily from at least 1 month before conception.

whyNot.A: Neural tube closure is complete by about day 28, often before pregnancy is recognised, and she needs a higher dose.
whyNot.B: This dose suits people without a previous affected pregnancy.
whyNot.D: Starting after the first trimester is too late to affect neural tube closure.
whyNot.E: Food fortification alone is insufficient after a previous affected pregnancy.

items.objective: Recommend high-dose periconceptional folic acid after a previous neural tube defect.

items.stemHtml: A boy is born at 39 weeks' gestation by caesarean delivery. He has a 5-cm open sac over the lumbosacral spine containing visible neural tissue, with a slight clear-fluid leak. He moves his hips but not his feet. Head circumference is at the 90th percentile. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Cover the sac with a sterile saline-moistened dressing, nurse him prone and arrange surgical closure

options.label: B
options.html: Apply a dry gauze dressing and place him supine for a full neurological examination

options.label: C
options.html: Insert a ventriculoperitoneal shunt today, before any repair of the back defect

options.label: D
options.html: Perform lumbar puncture to look for meningitis before any further management

options.label: E
options.html: Discharge home with a neurosurgical clinic review within the next 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
An open myelomeningocele needs protection of the exposed neural tissue: a sterile, saline-moistened, non-adherent dressing, prone or side-lying positioning and latex-free handling. Start antibiotics if the sac is leaking, and close the defect surgically within about 48–72 hours. Then watch for hydrocephalus.

Takeaway: newborn myelomeningocele: moist sterile dressing, prone position, latex precautions, closure within 72 hours.

whyNot.B: Dry dressings stick to and damage the neural placode, and supine positioning puts pressure on the sac.
whyNot.C: Closure of the back comes first; hydrocephalus is treated when it becomes significant.
whyNot.D: There is no indication for LP, and it would not be done through or near the defect.
whyNot.E: An open, leaking defect needs closure within about 48–72 hours to prevent infection.

items.objective: Provide immediate care for a newborn with an open myelomeningocele.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl with myelomeningocele and a ventriculoperitoneal shunt placed in infancy is brought to the emergency department because of headache and vomiting for 1 day. Today she is unusually sleepy. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). She is drowsy but rousable, and she cannot look upward fully. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravenous fluids and an antiemetic for presumed viral gastroenteritis

options.label: B
options.html: Lumbar puncture to measure the CSF opening pressure and send cultures

options.label: C
options.html: Outpatient MRI of the brain within the next 2 weeks

options.label: D
options.html: Urgent brain imaging and shunt series radiographs with neurosurgical consultation

options.label: E
options.html: Oral acetazolamide with clinical reassessment after 24 hours

items.explanationHtml:
Headache, vomiting, drowsiness and impaired upward gaze (pressure on the dorsal midbrain) in a child with a shunt mean acute shunt malfunction with raised intracranial pressure. Obtain urgent imaging (rapid MRI or CT) to compare ventricle size with prior scans, plus a shunt series to look for a break or disconnection, and involve neurosurgery straight away.

Takeaway: a child with a shunt and headache, vomiting or drowsiness has shunt failure until proven otherwise.

whyNot.A: Vomiting and drowsiness in a child with a shunt is shunt failure until proven otherwise.
whyNot.B: Lumbar puncture is unsafe with possible obstructive hydrocephalus.
whyNot.C: Shunt malfunction can lead to herniation within hours; imaging must be urgent.
whyNot.E: Medical therapy does not fix an obstructed shunt and delays definitive care.

items.objective: Recognise and evaluate ventriculoperitoneal shunt malfunction.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman has had occipital headaches for a year, brought on by coughing, sneezing or lifting and lasting a few minutes. For 3 months she has had tingling in her hands. Examination shows reduced pain and temperature sensation over the shoulders and upper arms with normal vibration sense. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: CT of the head without contrast

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain and cervical spine

options.label: D
options.html: Nerve conduction studies of the arms

items.explanationHtml:
Headache provoked by coughing or straining plus a cape-like loss of pain and temperature suggests a Chiari I malformation with a cervical syrinx. MRI of the brain and cervical spine shows the tonsillar descent and the syrinx. Symptomatic patients with a syrinx are referred for posterior fossa decompression.

Takeaway: cough headache with a cape-like sensory loss: MRI the brain and cervical spine for Chiari I and a syrinx.

whyNot.A: CT shows the posterior fossa and cord poorly and cannot show a syrinx reliably.
whyNot.C: LP is not diagnostic here and is risky with tonsillar herniation.
whyNot.D: The sensory loss is from a central cord lesion, which nerve conduction studies cannot show.
whyNot.E: Angiography looks for vascular lesions, which do not fit this picture.
whyNot.F: Cough-induced headache is not migraine and needs imaging to look for a structural cause.

items.objective: Choose MRI to evaluate a suspected Chiari I malformation with syringomyelia.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy with spastic diplegic cerebral palsy walks independently but on his toes because of tight calf muscles. His physical therapist reports that daily stretching and night splints have not improved his ankle range over 6 months. Passive dorsiflexion at the ankle reaches neutral with the knee bent. There is no fixed contracture. His spasticity is limited to the calves. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to improve his gait?

options.label: B
options.html: Implantation of an intrathecal baclofen pump

options.label: C
options.html: Selective dorsal rhizotomy of the lumbosacral roots

options.label: D
options.html: Surgical lengthening of both Achilles tendons

options.label: E
options.html: Botulinum toxin injections into the gastrocnemius muscles

items.explanationHtml:
For focal spasticity that limits function despite therapy and splinting, botulinum toxin injected into the overactive muscles reduces tone for several months by blocking acetylcholine release, and is combined with stretching, serial casting or orthoses. Surgery is kept for fixed contractures; systemic and intrathecal agents are for more generalised spasticity.

Takeaway: focal spasticity in cerebral palsy: botulinum toxin plus therapy; tendon surgery only for fixed contracture.

whyNot.A: Systemic drugs cause sedation or weakness throughout the body and are less suitable for focal spasticity.
whyNot.B: Intrathecal baclofen is for severe, generalised spasticity.
whyNot.C: Rhizotomy is reserved for carefully selected children with more widespread leg spasticity.
whyNot.D: Tendon surgery is for fixed contracture, which he does not have.

items.objective: Treat focal spasticity in a child with cerebral palsy.

items.stemHtml: A 5-month-old girl with tuberous sclerosis complex is brought to the clinic because, for 4 days, she has had clusters of sudden flexion of the neck, trunk and arms on waking. EEG shows hypsarrhythmia. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.label: E
options.html: Watchful waiting with repeat EEG in 1 month

items.explanationHtml:
Infantile spasms with hypsarrhythmia (West syndrome) need urgent treatment. When the cause is tuberous sclerosis, vigabatrin, an irreversible inhibitor of GABA transaminase, is first line and works especially well. Hormonal therapy is the usual first choice for most other causes. Vigabatrin can cause permanent peripheral visual field loss, so vision is monitored.

Takeaway: infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis: vigabatrin first; watch for visual field loss.

whyNot.B: Ethosuximide treats absence seizures only.
whyNot.C: Carbamazepine can worsen generalised seizures such as spasms and myoclonic seizures.
whyNot.D: Phenytoin is ineffective for infantile spasms.
whyNot.E: Infantile spasms are an emergency in development; delay worsens cognitive outcome.

items.objective: Choose first-line therapy for infantile spasms in tuberous sclerosis complex.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy was diagnosed with neurofibromatosis type 1 last year. He is developing normally and examination shows only café-au-lait macules and axillary freckling. His parents ask which surveillance he needs. Which of the following is most important to arrange yearly at his age?
items.explanationHtml:
Optic pathway gliomas occur in a minority of children with NF1, usually before age 7, and young children rarely report visual loss. A yearly ophthalmological examination (acuity, fields, fundi) through childhood detects them early. Surveillance also includes blood pressure checks, growth, development and spine examination.

Takeaway: children with NF1 need yearly eye examinations to detect optic pathway gliomas.

whyNot.A: Routine MRI in children without symptoms is not recommended; imaging is driven by signs or symptoms.
whyNot.B: Pheochromocytoma screening is directed by symptoms or high blood pressure, mainly in adults.
whyNot.D: Renal imaging is not routine in NF1; blood pressure checks are used to detect renal artery stenosis.
whyNot.E: Hearing loss from vestibular schwannomas is a feature of NF2-related schwannomatosis, not NF1.

items.objective: Plan surveillance for a child with neurofibromatosis type 1.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman at 30 weeks' gestation is admitted with preterm labour. Her cervix is 6 cm dilated and delivery is expected within hours. She has received betamethasone. Which of the following should be given now, chiefly to reduce the risk of cerebral palsy in the infant?
items.explanationHtml:
When preterm birth before about 32 weeks is imminent, antenatal magnesium sulfate lowers the risk of cerebral palsy in surviving infants, likely by stabilising neuronal membranes and blocking NMDA receptor-mediated excitotoxicity. It is given in addition to antenatal corticosteroids.

Takeaway: imminent delivery before 32 weeks: give magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection.

whyNot.A: Indomethacin is a tocolytic and does not provide neuroprotection; it is avoided late in active labour.
whyNot.B: Nifedipine is a tocolytic and has no proven neuroprotective effect.
whyNot.C: Progesterone was used to prevent recurrent preterm birth, not for neuroprotection during labour.
whyNot.E: Ampicillin prevents early-onset group B streptococcal disease, not cerebral palsy.

items.objective: Use magnesium sulfate for fetal neuroprotection in imminent preterm birth.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman has a first generalized seizure. MRI shows a 3-cm extra-axial mass attached to the dura over the left frontal convexity. It enhances uniformly and has a thin enhancing tail along the adjacent dura. After resection, microscopy shows spindle cells arranged in concentric whorls with scattered laminated calcified bodies. From which cell type did this tumour most likely arise?
items.explanationHtml:
A dural-based, extra-axial mass with a dural tail, whorls and psammoma bodies is a meningioma. Meningiomas arise from arachnoid cap cells, which sit in the arachnoid granulations and meninges.

Takeaway: meningioma = arachnoid cap cells; whorls and psammoma bodies.

whyNot.A: Astrocytic tumours grow within the brain (intra-axial) and lack whorls with psammoma bodies.
whyNot.C: Ependymomas arise from the ventricular lining and form perivascular pseudorosettes.
whyNot.D: Schwannomas arise on nerve roots and show Antoni A and B areas, not dural whorls.
whyNot.E: Oligodendrogliomas are intra-axial cortical tumours with round nuclei and perinuclear halos.

items.objective: Identify the cell of origin of a meningioma from its imaging and histology.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has 2 months of headaches and clumsiness of his right hand. On examination, he overshoots the target on right finger-to-nose testing. MRI shows a cystic mass in the right cerebellar hemisphere with an enhancing nodule in its wall. Microscopy of the resected nodule shows bipolar cells with long hair-like processes, eosinophilic corkscrew-shaped fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies. Which of the following best describes this tumour?

options.label: A
