options.html: A grade 4 tumour that requires craniospinal radiotherapy

options.label: B
options.html: A tumour arising from the floor of the fourth ventricle

options.label: D
options.html: A tumour usually cured by complete surgical removal

options.label: E
options.html: A tumour that commonly secretes erythropoietin

items.explanationHtml:
A cerebellar cyst with a mural nodule in a child, with piloid cells, Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies, is a pilocytic astrocytoma (WHO grade 1). It is well circumscribed, so complete resection is usually curative.

Takeaway: pilocytic astrocytoma is the most common childhood brain tumour and the most curable by surgery.

whyNot.A: Craniospinal radiotherapy is used for medulloblastoma, an embryonal grade 4 tumour of the vermis.
whyNot.B: Ependymomas arise from the floor of the fourth ventricle; this tumour is in the hemisphere.
whyNot.C: 1p/19q codeletion defines oligodendroglioma, an adult cortical tumour.
whyNot.E: Erythropoietin secretion and polycythemia are features of hemangioblastoma, an adult tumour.

items.objective: Recognise pilocytic astrocytoma and its favourable prognosis after resection.

items.stemHtml:
A 7-year-old girl is evaluated for headaches and slowed growth; her height has fallen from the 50th to the 10th percentile over 2 years. She often bumps into door frames. Visual field testing shows loss of both temporal fields. CT shows a partly calcified cystic mass. The figure shows a midline schematic of the brain. At which site is this tumour most likely located?

[[figure:s23e-fig0202]]
items.explanationHtml:
Growth failure, bitemporal hemianopia and a calcified cystic mass in a child point to craniopharyngioma, which arises from Rathke pouch remnants in the sellar and suprasellar region (site C). It compresses the optic chiasm from below and disrupts hypothalamic and pituitary function.

Takeaway: a calcified suprasellar cyst with bitemporal field loss and growth failure in a child is a craniopharyngioma.

whyNot.A: Site A is the convexity dura, the typical site of meningioma in adults.
whyNot.B: Site D is the pineal region, where germ cell tumours cause upgaze palsy rather than bitemporal field loss.
whyNot.C: Site F is the cerebellar vermis, the site of medulloblastoma, which causes ataxia and hydrocephalus.
whyNot.E: Site H is the pons, the site of diffuse midline glioma, which causes cranial nerve palsies and long-tract signs.

items.objective: Localise a craniopharyngioma to the suprasellar region from its clinical picture.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man has 4 months of unsteady gait. MRI shows a cystic mass with an enhancing nodule in the left cerebellar hemisphere. Fundoscopy shows a small red vascular lesion on the right retina. His hematocrit is 57% (reference range, 41–53%). His father died of kidney cancer at age 49. The protein encoded by the gene most likely mutated in this patient normally has which of the following functions?

options.label: A
options.html: Targeting hypoxia-inducible factor for proteasomal degradation

options.label: C
options.html: Linking membrane proteins to the actin cytoskeleton

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibiting the small GTPase Rheb as part of a complex with hamartin

options.label: E
options.html: Signalling as a receptor tyrosine kinase for GDNF-family ligands

items.explanationHtml:
Cerebellar and retinal hemangioblastomas, polycythemia and a family history of renal cancer indicate von Hippel–Lindau disease. The VHL protein is part of a ubiquitin ligase that marks hypoxia-inducible factor for destruction. Without it, HIF accumulates and drives VEGF and erythropoietin, producing vascular tumours and polycythemia.

Takeaway: VHL loss stabilises HIF, giving hemangioblastomas, clear cell renal carcinoma and erythrocytosis.

whyNot.B: Accelerating Ras GTP hydrolysis is the role of neurofibromin, lost in NF1.
whyNot.C: Linking membrane to cytoskeleton describes merlin, lost in NF2 (schwannomas, meningiomas).
whyNot.D: Tuberin inhibits Rheb; its loss causes tuberous sclerosis.
whyNot.E: RET is the GDNF-family receptor; activating mutations cause MEN2.

items.objective: Link hemangioblastoma to von Hippel–Lindau disease and the function of the VHL protein.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has 1 year of hearing loss in both ears and a cataract that was removed at age 16. MRI shows enhancing masses at both cerebellopontine angles, each arising from the vestibular nerve and widening the internal acoustic canal. Which of the following is most likely seen on microscopy of one of these masses?

options.label: A
options.html: Necrosis bordered by palisading tumour cells

options.label: B
options.html: Round nuclei with clear perinuclear halos

options.label: C
options.html: Rosenthal fibres in a biphasic glial tumour

options.label: D
options.html: Whorls of cells around laminated calcifications

options.label: E
options.html: Palisaded nuclei in cellular areas alternating with loose areas

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral vestibular schwannomas are diagnostic of NF2-related schwannomatosis (merlin, chromosome 22); juvenile cataract is another feature. Schwannomas show cellular Antoni A areas with nuclear palisades (Verocay bodies) and loose Antoni B areas, and are S-100 positive.

Takeaway: bilateral vestibular schwannomas = NF2; Antoni A/B pattern with Verocay bodies.

whyNot.A: Pseudopalisading necrosis is the hallmark of glioblastoma, an intra-axial tumour.
whyNot.B: Perinuclear halos describe oligodendroglioma, a cortical tumour.
whyNot.C: Rosenthal fibres in a biphasic glial tumour describe pilocytic astrocytoma.
whyNot.D: Whorls with psammoma bodies are meningioma; these masses arise from the vestibular nerve.

items.objective: Recognise the histology of schwannoma in a patient with NF2.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man has 6 months of headaches and decreased libido. He has bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 3.1-cm sellar mass that elevates the optic chiasm. Serum prolactin is 58 ng/mL (reference range, below 20 ng/mL). After resection, the tumour cells do not stain for prolactin or any other pituitary hormone. Which of the following best explains his raised prolactin?

options.label: B
options.html: Increased hypothalamic release of thyrotropin-releasing hormone

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of dopamine delivery to normal lactotrophs through a compressed stalk

items.explanationHtml:
Dopamine from the hypothalamus reaches the anterior pituitary through the portal vessels of the stalk and tonically inhibits prolactin release. A large nonfunctioning adenoma that compresses the stalk interrupts this inhibition, so normal lactotrophs release more prolactin (stalk effect). Levels are usually under about 100–150 ng/mL; macroprolactinomas of this size usually produce far higher levels.

Takeaway: mildly raised prolactin with a large sellar mass suggests stalk compression, not a prolactinoma.

whyNot.A: The tumour did not stain for prolactin, and a prolactin-secreting adenoma of this size would give a much higher level.
whyNot.B: Primary hypothyroidism raises TRH and prolactin, but nothing suggests it, and it does not explain the mass.
whyNot.D: Renal failure raises prolactin modestly, but there is no evidence of kidney disease.
whyNot.E: He has no source of excess estrogen, and lactotroph hyperplasia would not explain this tumour.

items.objective: Explain hyperprolactinemia from pituitary stalk compression by a nonfunctioning adenoma.

items.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy with many café-au-lait macules, axillary freckling and soft skin nodules has had a large, irregular subcutaneous mass along the course of his right sciatic nerve since childhood. Over the past 2 months the mass has grown quickly and become constantly painful, and he has new weakness of ankle dorsiflexion. Which of the following is the most likely explanation?
items.explanationHtml:
This patient has NF1 with a plexiform neurofibroma, a lesion specific to NF1. Rapid growth, new persistent pain and new neurological deficit suggest transformation into a malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour, the most important malignant complication of NF1.

Takeaway: rapid growth or new pain in a plexiform neurofibroma means MPNST until proven otherwise.

whyNot.B: Medullary thyroid carcinoma belongs to MEN2 (RET), not NF1, and does not arise on the sciatic nerve.
whyNot.C: Clear cell renal carcinoma is a feature of von Hippel–Lindau disease.
whyNot.D: Cardiac rhabdomyomas occur in tuberous sclerosis and are found in infancy.
whyNot.E: Hemangioblastomas arise in the cerebellum, brainstem, cord and retina, not in peripheral nerves.

items.objective: Recognise malignant transformation of a plexiform neurofibroma in NF1.

items.stemHtml: A 10-year-old boy has a suprasellar tumour removed. The cyst contains thick brownish fluid rich in cholesterol crystals, and the solid part shows nests of squamous epithelium with nodules of keratin and calcification. From which embryologic structure does this tumour most likely arise?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a craniopharyngioma, which develops from remnants of Rathke pouch, the outgrowth of oral ectoderm that forms the anterior pituitary. Cholesterol-rich fluid, squamous nests with keratin and calcification are typical.

Takeaway: craniopharyngioma comes from Rathke pouch (oral ectoderm), the precursor of the anterior pituitary.

whyNot.A: Neural crest gives rise to Schwann cells, melanocytes and the adrenal medulla, not to this tumour.
whyNot.B: Notochord remnants give rise to chordoma, usually at the clivus or sacrum.
whyNot.C: The neurohypophyseal bud forms the posterior pituitary, which is neural tissue, not squamous epithelium.
whyNot.D: The third pharyngeal pouch forms the thymus and inferior parathyroid glands.

items.objective: State the embryologic origin of craniopharyngioma.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has 6 weeks of worsening headaches and personality change. MRI shows an irregular ring-enhancing mass with a necrotic centre that extends across the corpus callosum into both frontal lobes. Which of the following microscopic findings is most likely in this tumour?

options.label: A
options.html: Necrosis bordered by palisading tumour cells and glomeruloid vessel proliferation

options.label: B
options.html: Bipolar piloid cells with Rosenthal fibres

options.label: C
options.html: Round nuclei with perinuclear halos and a fine branching capillary network

options.label: D
options.html: Small round blue cells forming Homer Wright rosettes

options.label: E
options.html: Spindle cells in whorls with psammoma bodies

items.explanationHtml:
A necrotic, ring-enhancing "butterfly" mass crossing the corpus callosum in an older adult is glioblastoma. Its hallmarks are necrosis with pseudopalisading tumour cells and microvascular (glomeruloid) proliferation.

Takeaway: glioblastoma = pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation, often crossing the corpus callosum.

whyNot.B: Piloid cells with Rosenthal fibres describe pilocytic astrocytoma, a circumscribed childhood tumour.
whyNot.C: Perinuclear halos with branching capillaries describe oligodendroglioma.
whyNot.D: Homer Wright rosettes of small blue cells describe medulloblastoma, a cerebellar tumour of children.
whyNot.E: Whorls and psammoma bodies describe meningioma, an extra-axial dural tumour.

items.objective: Recognise glioblastoma from its imaging and histology.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has a first seizure. MRI shows a partly calcified, poorly enhancing mass in the right frontal cortex. Microscopy shows uniform round nuclei with clear perinuclear halos. Sequencing shows a point mutation in isocitrate dehydrogenase 1 (IDH1), and FISH shows codeletion of chromosome arms 1p and 19q. The mutant enzyme produces a metabolite that promotes tumour growth mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Constitutive activation of the Ras–MAPK signalling pathway in glial cells

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of α-ketoglutarate–dependent DNA and histone demethylases

options.label: C
options.html: Stabilisation of β-catenin with activation of WNT target genes

options.label: D
options.html: Ligand-independent activation of the epidermal growth factor receptor

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of p53-mediated cell-cycle arrest and apoptosis after DNA damage

items.explanationHtml:
The diagnosis is oligodendroglioma, IDH-mutant and 1p/19q-codeleted. Mutant IDH converts α-ketoglutarate into 2-hydroxyglutarate, an oncometabolite that competitively inhibits α-ketoglutarate–dependent dioxygenases, including TET DNA demethylases and histone demethylases. The resulting hypermethylation blocks differentiation.

Takeaway: mutant IDH makes 2-hydroxyglutarate, which inhibits demethylases and causes a hypermethylated, undifferentiated state.

whyNot.A: Ras–MAPK activation drives pilocytic astrocytoma (BRAF) and NF1 tumours, not the IDH effect.
whyNot.C: β-catenin stabilisation drives adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma and WNT-group medulloblastoma.
whyNot.D: EGFR amplification is typical of IDH-wildtype glioblastoma.
whyNot.E: TP53 mutation accompanies IDH-mutant astrocytoma but is not how 2-hydroxyglutarate acts.

items.objective: Explain how mutant IDH promotes gliomagenesis through 2-hydroxyglutarate.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has 3 weeks of morning headaches, vomiting and a wide-based, unsteady gait. MRI shows a midline cerebellar mass that fills the fourth ventricle, with dilated lateral and third ventricles. Microscopy shows sheets of small cells with scant cytoplasm and hyperchromatic nuclei, some arranged around central tangles of fibrillary processes; the cells stain for synaptophysin. This tumour most likely spreads by which of the following routes?

options.label: B
options.html: Cerebrospinal fluid to the spinal leptomeninges

options.label: D
options.html: Direct invasion through the occipital bone

options.label: E
options.html: Along cranial nerves to the skull base

items.explanationHtml:
A midline cerebellar tumour of small round blue cells with Homer Wright rosettes in a child is medulloblastoma. It lies next to the fourth ventricle and seeds the CSF, producing "drop metastases" in the spinal subarachnoid space. Staging therefore includes MRI of the whole spine and CSF cytology.

Takeaway: medulloblastoma spreads through CSF; stage it with spine MRI and CSF cytology.

whyNot.A: Primary CNS tumours rarely spread through blood outside the nervous system.
whyNot.C: The brain has no conventional lymphatic drainage route for tumour spread to nodes.
whyNot.D: Direct invasion through bone is not the typical pattern of spread.
whyNot.E: Perineural spread is characteristic of some head and neck cancers, not medulloblastoma.

items.objective: Describe CSF dissemination of medulloblastoma.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old girl has vomiting, irritability and an enlarging head. MRI shows hydrocephalus and a mass arising from the floor of the fourth ventricle that extends through the foramen of Magendie. Microscopy shows tumour cells arranged around blood vessels, separated from them by a nucleus-free zone of fine processes, plus a few true rosettes around small lumens. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A fourth-ventricle floor tumour in a young child with perivascular pseudorosettes and true ependymal rosettes is an ependymoma. It obstructs CSF flow and causes hydrocephalus.

Takeaway: perivascular pseudorosettes from the floor of the fourth ventricle = ependymoma.

whyNot.A: Choroid plexus papilloma forms papillary fronds and in children is usually in a lateral ventricle.
whyNot.B: Hemangioblastoma is an adult cerebellar tumour of capillaries and foamy stromal cells.
whyNot.C: Medulloblastoma arises from the vermis (roof) and shows Homer Wright rosettes, not perivascular pseudorosettes.
whyNot.D: Pilocytic astrocytoma shows piloid cells and Rosenthal fibres, usually in a hemispheric cyst.

items.objective: Recognise ependymoma from its site and perivascular pseudorosettes.

items.stemHtml: A 36-year-old man with HIV infection who has not taken antiretroviral therapy for 3 years has 3 weeks of confusion. His CD4 count is 30/mm³. MRI shows a single 3-cm periventricular mass that enhances irregularly. Serum anti-Toxoplasma IgG is negative. Polymerase chain reaction of the cerebrospinal fluid is most likely to detect DNA of which virus?
items.explanationHtml:
A periventricular enhancing mass in advanced HIV with negative Toxoplasma serology suggests primary CNS lymphoma, a B-cell lymphoma driven by Epstein–Barr virus in immunosuppressed patients. EBV DNA in CSF supports the diagnosis.

Takeaway: in advanced HIV, primary CNS lymphoma is EBV-associated; CSF EBV PCR supports it.

whyNot.B: JC virus causes progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy: non-enhancing white matter lesions without mass effect.
whyNot.C: Cytomegalovirus causes ventriculoencephalitis and retinitis, not a solitary enhancing mass.
whyNot.D: HHV-8 causes Kaposi sarcoma and primary effusion lymphoma, not primary CNS lymphoma.
whyNot.E: HSV-1 causes temporal lobe encephalitis with fever, not a periventricular mass.

items.objective: Associate primary CNS lymphoma in AIDS with Epstein–Barr virus.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man undergoes resection of a glioblastoma and then receives radiotherapy with an oral drug that is continued for 6 months. The tumour's MGMT gene promoter is methylated, and his oncologist explains that this predicts a better response because the tumour cannot repair the drug-induced damage. This drug most likely acts by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: D
options.html: Addition of methyl groups to DNA guanine bases

items.explanationHtml:
The drug is temozolomide, an oral alkylating agent that crosses the blood–brain barrier and methylates guanine (at O6 and other positions). The DNA repair enzyme MGMT removes the O6-methyl group. Methylation of the MGMT promoter silences the enzyme, so damage persists and the tumour responds better.

Takeaway: temozolomide alkylates DNA; MGMT promoter methylation predicts benefit.

whyNot.A: Topoisomerase II inhibitors (etoposide) are not standard glioblastoma therapy and MGMT does not repair their damage.
whyNot.B: Microtubule inhibitors (vincristine) act on mitosis; MGMT is irrelevant to them.
whyNot.C: DHFR inhibition is how methotrexate works, used in primary CNS lymphoma.
whyNot.E: Bevacizumab binds VEGF-A; it is used for recurrence and does not depend on MGMT.

items.objective: Relate temozolomide's alkylating mechanism to MGMT promoter methylation.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl has 4 weeks of double vision and drooling. Examination shows a left abducens palsy, left facial weakness of both upper and lower face, and unsteady gait. MRI shows an expansile, poorly enhancing mass that infiltrates most of the pons. Molecular testing of this tumour is most likely to show an alteration in which of the following?
items.explanationHtml:
An infiltrating pontine tumour in a child with several cranial nerve palsies and ataxia is a diffuse midline glioma, H3 K27-altered. Alteration of histone H3 at lysine 27 defines it. It cannot be resected and carries a very poor prognosis.

Takeaway: diffuse midline glioma of the pons is defined by histone H3 K27 alteration.

whyNot.A: IDH mutations define adult diffuse gliomas, usually in the cerebral hemispheres.
whyNot.B: BRAF alterations are typical of pilocytic astrocytoma, a circumscribed tumour.
whyNot.D: SMARCB1 loss defines atypical teratoid/rhabdoid tumour of infants.
whyNot.E: β-catenin activation occurs in adamantinomatous craniopharyngioma and WNT-group medulloblastoma.

items.objective: Identify the molecular hallmark of diffuse midline glioma of the pons.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has 2 months of word-finding difficulty. MRI shows a non-enhancing, infiltrative lesion in the left temporal lobe. Biopsy shows a diffuse astrocytic tumour with moderate atypia but no necrosis and no microvascular proliferation. Molecular testing shows wild-type IDH1 and IDH2, a TERT promoter mutation, and gain of chromosome 7 with loss of chromosome 10. According to the current WHO classification, which of the following is the most accurate diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
In the 2021 WHO classification, an adult IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytic tumour with a TERT promoter mutation, EGFR amplification or +7/−10 is graded as glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, grade 4, even without necrosis or microvascular proliferation. These tumours behave like glioblastoma.

Takeaway: in adults, IDH-wildtype diffuse astrocytoma with TERT, EGFR or +7/−10 is glioblastoma, whatever the histology.

whyNot.A: This tumour is IDH-wildtype, so it cannot be an IDH-mutant astrocytoma.
whyNot.C: Oligodendroglioma requires both IDH mutation and 1p/19q codeletion.
whyNot.D: Pilocytic astrocytoma is a circumscribed tumour, usually of children, without these markers.
whyNot.E: Diffuse midline glioma needs a midline site and an H3 K27 alteration.

items.objective: Apply the molecular criteria for glioblastoma in the WHO CNS5 classification.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man who has smoked one pack of cigarettes daily for 45 years has a new seizure. MRI shows four round, enhancing lesions at the junction of gray and white matter in both cerebral hemispheres, each surrounded by extensive edema. Which of the following is the most likely primary tumour?
items.explanationHtml:
Multiple round enhancing lesions at the gray–white junction with disproportionate edema are metastases. Lung cancer is the most common source of brain metastases, and this patient has a heavy smoking history.

Takeaway: lung cancer is the leading source of brain metastases.

whyNot.A: Colorectal cancer can metastasise to the brain, but far less often than lung cancer.
whyNot.B: Prostate cancer favours bone, especially the spine, and rarely involves the brain parenchyma.
whyNot.D: Hepatocellular carcinoma rarely metastasises to the brain.
whyNot.E: Papillary thyroid carcinoma spreads mainly to cervical nodes and rarely to the brain.

items.objective: Name lung cancer as the most common source of brain metastases.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman with breast cancer has three brain metastases, each located where the cerebral cortex meets the underlying white matter. Which of the following best explains why metastases favour this location?

options.label: A
options.html: Seeding of tumour cells through the cerebrospinal fluid

options.label: B
options.html: Abrupt narrowing of arterioles that traps tumour emboli

options.label: C
options.html: Retrograde flow through valveless vertebral veins

options.label: D
options.html: Drainage of the region by meningeal lymphatic vessels

options.label: E
options.html: Absence of a blood–brain barrier at the junction

items.explanationHtml:
Most brain metastases arrive by arterial blood. Arterioles narrow abruptly as they pass from cortex into white matter, so tumour emboli lodge at the gray–white junction and in arterial border zones.

Takeaway: brain metastases lodge at the gray–white junction because arterioles narrow there.

whyNot.A: CSF seeding produces leptomeningeal disease, not parenchymal nodules at the gray–white junction.
whyNot.C: The vertebral venous plexus explains spinal and some posterior fossa metastases, not this distribution.
whyNot.D: Meningeal lymphatics drain outward and do not deliver tumour cells to the parenchyma.
whyNot.E: The blood–brain barrier is present at the gray–white junction.

items.objective: Explain the gray–white junction location of brain metastases.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman had an irregular, variably pigmented skin lesion removed from her back 3 years ago. She now has sudden headache and left-sided weakness. CT shows several brain lesions, two of which contain fresh hemorrhage. Which of the following is the most likely primary tumour?
items.explanationHtml:
Melanoma has one of the highest rates of brain metastasis of any cancer, and its metastases often bleed. Renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma and thyroid carcinoma also give hemorrhagic metastases.

Takeaway: hemorrhagic brain metastases suggest melanoma, renal cell carcinoma, choriocarcinoma or thyroid carcinoma.

whyNot.A: Basal cell carcinoma is locally invasive and almost never metastasises.
whyNot.B: Cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma spreads mainly to regional nodes; brain metastases are rare.
whyNot.C: Dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans recurs locally and rarely metastasises.
whyNot.D: Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumour of skin, mucosa and viscera; it rarely involves the brain.

items.objective: Recognise melanoma as a source of hemorrhagic brain metastases.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man has 2 months of low back pain that is worse at night. Radiographs show several dense, sclerotic lesions in the lumbar vertebral bodies. His serum prostate-specific antigen is markedly increased. Tumour cells most likely reached his spine by which of the following routes?

options.label: C
options.html: Perineural spread along the sacral nerves

items.explanationHtml:
Prostate cancer reaches the vertebral bodies through the valveless vertebral venous plexus (Batson plexus), which connects pelvic veins to the vertebral veins without valves. Its bone metastases are typically osteoblastic (sclerotic).

Takeaway: prostate cancer spreads to the spine through the valveless vertebral venous plexus and gives sclerotic lesions.

whyNot.A: Lymphatic spread goes to pelvic and para-aortic nodes, not directly into vertebral bodies.
whyNot.B: The portal system carries GI tumour cells to the liver.
whyNot.C: Perineural spread follows nerves and does not produce multiple vertebral body deposits.
whyNot.E: Prostate cancer does not enter the CSF to reach bone.

items.objective: Explain vertebral metastasis of prostate cancer through the vertebral venous plexus.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman has 6 weeks of rapidly worsening unsteadiness, slurred speech and double vision. She now cannot walk without help. Examination shows dysarthria, downbeat nystagmus and severe ataxia of all limbs and gait. MRI of the brain is normal. Serum contains antibodies that bind the cytoplasm of cerebellar Purkinje cells (anti-Yo). Which of the following is the most likely underlying cancer?
items.explanationHtml:
Subacute, severe pancerebellar dysfunction with a normal MRI is paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration. Anti-Yo (PCA-1) antibodies are tied to gynecologic (ovarian) and breast cancers. The syndrome often precedes the cancer diagnosis.

Takeaway: anti-Yo cerebellar degeneration → look for ovarian or breast cancer.

whyNot.A: Small cell lung cancer causes paraneoplastic syndromes through anti-Hu or calcium-channel antibodies, not anti-Yo.
whyNot.C: Thymoma is linked to myasthenia gravis and other autoimmune conditions.
whyNot.D: Testicular germ cell tumours are linked to anti-Ma2 limbic and brainstem encephalitis.
whyNot.E: Renal cell carcinoma causes endocrine paraneoplastic effects (erythrocytosis, hypercalcemia), not anti-Yo.

items.objective: Associate anti-Yo paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration with gynecologic and breast cancer.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man who smokes has 2 months of burning pain and numbness that began in his left hand and spread to all four limbs. He has severe loss of joint position sense and absent reflexes, with normal strength. Anti-Hu antibodies are found in serum, and CT shows a mediastinal mass. Despite five sessions of plasma exchange, his neurological deficits do not improve. Which of the following best explains this lack of response?

options.label: A
options.html: The antibodies block acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction

options.label: B
options.html: The neuronal injury is caused by cytotoxic T cells directed at an intracellular antigen

options.label: C
options.html: Complement-fixing antibodies strip myelin from peripheral nerves

options.label: D
options.html: The antibodies bind presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels

options.label: E
options.html: Tumour cells have directly invaded the dorsal root ganglia

items.explanationHtml:
Anti-Hu sensory neuronopathy accompanies small cell lung carcinoma. Hu is an intracellular neuronal protein, so the antibody is a marker. Dorsal root ganglion neurons are destroyed by cytotoxic T cells, and lost neurons do not regrow. Removing antibody by plasma exchange therefore helps little; treating the cancer is the priority.

Takeaway: antibodies against intracellular onconeural antigens are markers; T cells cause the damage, and immunotherapy helps little.

whyNot.A: Antibodies to acetylcholine receptors cause myasthenia gravis, with fatigable weakness, not sensory loss.
whyNot.C: Antibody-mediated demyelination (as in Guillain–Barré syndrome) usually responds to plasma exchange.
whyNot.D: Antibodies to voltage-gated calcium channels cause Lambert–Eaton syndrome, with weakness and autonomic features.
whyNot.E: Paraneoplastic neuronopathy is immune-mediated, not caused by tumour invasion.

items.objective: Explain why anti-Hu paraneoplastic syndromes respond poorly to antibody removal.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after 10 days of insomnia, agitation and paranoid ideas, followed by a generalized seizure. On examination, she has repetitive chewing and lip-smacking movements, a fluctuating level of consciousness, a heart rate that varies from 50/min to 140/min, and labile blood pressure. CSF shows 35 lymphocytes/mm³ (reference range, 0–5/mm³). Antibodies to the NR1 subunit of a glutamate receptor are found in the CSF. Which of the following tumours is most likely to be associated with this condition?
items.explanationHtml:
This is anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: psychiatric onset, seizures, orofacial dyskinesias, autonomic instability and reduced consciousness in a young woman. The associated tumour is an ovarian teratoma, which can contain neural tissue expressing NMDA receptors. The antibodies target a cell-surface receptor and cause the disease directly, so patients often recover with tumour removal and immunotherapy.

Takeaway: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis in a young woman → search for an ovarian teratoma.

whyNot.A: Breast cancer is associated with anti-Yo and anti-Ri syndromes, not anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
whyNot.B: Thymoma is linked to myasthenia gravis and other autoimmune syndromes.
whyNot.D: Small cell lung cancer is linked to anti-Hu and anti-GABA-B receptor encephalitis, mostly in older smokers.
whyNot.E: Neuroblastoma in young children is linked to opsoclonus–myoclonus, not this syndrome.

items.objective: Associate anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis with ovarian teratoma.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has 8 months of absent periods, milky nipple discharge and headaches. Pregnancy test is negative. Visual field testing shows bitemporal superior quadrant loss. Serum prolactin is 1,250 ng/mL (reference range, below 25 ng/mL). MRI shows a 2.4-cm pituitary macroadenoma that touches the optic chiasm. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Prolactin this high with a macroadenoma means a macroprolactinoma. A dopamine agonist, preferably cabergoline, is first-line treatment even when vision is affected. It usually normalises prolactin, shrinks the tumour and relieves chiasmal compression within days to weeks. Visual fields are re-checked closely.

Takeaway: prolactinomas of any size are treated first with a dopamine agonist.

whyNot.A: Surgery is reserved for intolerance or resistance to dopamine agonists, or for apoplexy with severe visual loss.
whyNot.C: Radiosurgery is a last resort for tumours that resist medical and surgical treatment.
whyNot.D: Octreotide treats growth hormone–secreting adenomas, not prolactinomas.
whyNot.E: Observation is inappropriate with a macroadenoma threatening vision and causing hypogonadism.

items.objective: Treat a macroprolactinoma with a dopamine agonist first, even with visual field loss.

items.stemHtml:
A 54-year-old man has 4 months of bumping into objects on both sides and decreased libido. He has bitemporal hemianopia. MRI shows a 3.2-cm sellar mass that elevates the optic chiasm.

TestResultReference range
Prolactin38 ng/mLbelow 20 ng/mL
IGF-1normal for age
Cortisol, 8 AM12 µg/dL (331 nmol/L)5–23 µg/dL
Free thyroxine (T4)0.7 ng/dL (9 pmol/L)0.8–1.8 ng/dL
TSH1.1 µU/mL0.5–5.0 µU/mL

Thyroid hormone replacement is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment of the mass?
items.explanationHtml:
A large sellar mass with only mildly raised prolactin is a nonfunctioning adenoma with stalk effect, and the low free T4 with a normal TSH shows central hypothyroidism. Chiasmal compression with visual loss is an indication for transsphenoidal resection.

Takeaway: a nonfunctioning macroadenoma causing visual loss needs transsphenoidal surgery.

whyNot.A: A dopamine agonist would lower the prolactin but would not shrink a nonfunctioning adenoma.
whyNot.B: Octreotide is used for growth hormone–secreting adenomas; IGF-1 is normal.
whyNot.D: Radiotherapy is used for residual or recurrent tumour and acts too slowly to relieve the chiasm.
whyNot.E: Observation is inappropriate when the tumour is already causing visual loss.

items.objective: Choose surgery for a nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma compressing the chiasm.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item undergoes transsphenoidal resection of a nonfunctioning pituitary adenoma. On the first postoperative day, his urine output is 350 mL/h and he is very thirsty. Serum sodium is 148 mEq/L (reference range, 136–145 mEq/L), and urine osmolality is 110 mOsm/kg. He is alert and drinking. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Dilute polyuria with a rising sodium after pituitary surgery is central diabetes insipidus from disturbance of vasopressin release. Treat with desmopressin and free access to water, with close monitoring of sodium. Postoperative diabetes insipidus is often transient.

Takeaway: after pituitary surgery, dilute polyuria with high sodium is central diabetes insipidus: give desmopressin.

whyNot.A: Fluid restriction would worsen hypernatremia in diabetes insipidus.
whyNot.B: Hypertonic saline treats hyponatremia; this patient is hypernatremic.
whyNot.C: Demeclocycline induces nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and is used for SIADH.
whyNot.D: Thiazides are used in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; central diabetes insipidus responds to desmopressin.

items.objective: Recognise and treat central diabetes insipidus after pituitary surgery.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man with a known nonfunctioning pituitary macroadenoma under observation has sudden severe headache, vomiting and double vision. He is drowsy. Blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg and pulse is 112/min. His right eye is deviated down and out, with ptosis. CT shows hemorrhage within an enlarged sellar mass. Serum sodium is 131 mEq/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step?
items.explanationHtml:
This is pituitary apoplexy: hemorrhage into an adenoma with headache, ophthalmoplegia and acute loss of ACTH, causing adrenal crisis (hypotension, hyponatremia). The first step is stress-dose intravenous hydrocortisone with fluids. Urgent neurosurgical review then decides on decompression, especially with visual loss or falling consciousness.

Takeaway: pituitary apoplexy: give IV hydrocortisone first, then consider decompression.

whyNot.A: Giving thyroid hormone before glucocorticoid can precipitate or worsen adrenal crisis.
whyNot.B: Lumbar puncture adds nothing once CT shows hemorrhage into a sellar mass.
whyNot.C: Nimodipine prevents vasospasm in aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, not apoplexy.
whyNot.E: Cabergoline treats prolactinomas and has no role in this emergency.

items.objective: Give stress-dose glucocorticoid first in pituitary apoplexy.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old woman has mild ringing in her left ear. Audiometry shows a small high-frequency sensorineural hearing loss on the left with good speech discrimination. MRI shows an 8-mm enhancing mass confined to the left internal acoustic canal. She has no imbalance or facial weakness. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: C
options.html: MRI and audiometry repeated at intervals

items.explanationHtml:
A small intracanalicular vestibular schwannoma with few symptoms in an older patient is usually managed by observation with serial MRI and audiometry. Many never grow. Radiosurgery or surgery is offered if the tumour grows or symptoms progress.

Takeaway: small, minimally symptomatic vestibular schwannomas are watched with serial MRI.

whyNot.A: Translabyrinthine surgery sacrifices residual hearing and is not needed for a small, stable tumour.
whyNot.B: Radiosurgery is reserved for growth; treating now exposes her to risk without proven benefit.
whyNot.D: Bevacizumab is used for progressive schwannomas in NF2, not a small sporadic tumour.
whyNot.E: Whole-brain radiotherapy has no role in a benign nerve sheath tumour.

items.objective: Choose observation with serial imaging for a small, minimally symptomatic vestibular schwannoma.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old woman has 2 focal seizures that began with jerking of the left foot, and 3 months of progressive weakness of the left leg. MRI shows a 4-cm extra-axial, homogeneously enhancing mass attached to the falx next to the right paracentral lobule, with surrounding edema. She is otherwise healthy. Levetiracetam has controlled the seizures. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment of the mass?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a symptomatic parasagittal meningioma causing seizures and a deficit. Surgical resection is the treatment of choice for a symptomatic, accessible meningioma in a fit patient. Radiotherapy is added for residual or higher-grade tumour.

Takeaway: symptomatic, accessible meningioma → resect.

whyNot.B: Temozolomide is a glioma drug with no established role in meningioma.
whyNot.C: Whole-brain radiotherapy is for multiple metastases, not a single benign tumour.
whyNot.D: Observation is for small asymptomatic meningiomas; this one causes seizures and weakness.
whyNot.E: Bevacizumab is not standard treatment for meningioma.

items.objective: Resect a symptomatic accessible meningioma.

items.stemHtml: A 4-year-old boy with neurofibromatosis type 1 comes for a health supervision visit. He has many café-au-lait macules and axillary freckles. His development, growth and blood pressure are normal, and he has no symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate yearly surveillance for him?
items.explanationHtml:
Young children with NF1 are at risk of optic pathway glioma, which can silently impair vision. A yearly ophthalmologic examination through childhood is recommended. Routine brain MRI in a child without symptoms is not, and blood pressure is checked at each visit.

Takeaway: NF1 in childhood: yearly eye examinations to detect optic pathway glioma.

whyNot.A: Audiometric surveillance is part of NF2 care (vestibular schwannomas), not NF1.
whyNot.B: Routine MRI in asymptomatic children with NF1 is not recommended; image if symptoms or eye findings appear.
whyNot.C: Pheochromocytoma is sought in NF1 when hypertension or symptoms appear, not by yearly testing in a young child.
whyNot.E: Renal imaging is part of von Hippel–Lindau and tuberous sclerosis surveillance.

items.objective: Recommend yearly eye examinations for children with NF1.

items.stemHtml: An 8-year-old girl has 6 weeks of morning headaches and recent clumsiness of her left hand. She has left-sided dysmetria and mild papilledema. MRI shows a 4-cm cyst in the left cerebellar hemisphere with an enhancing nodule in its wall and mild hydrocephalus. There is no other lesion in the brain or spine. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
A cerebellar cyst with a mural nodule in a child is most likely a pilocytic astrocytoma. Complete resection of the nodule is usually curative, and removing the mass often relieves the hydrocephalus without a permanent shunt.

Takeaway: pilocytic astrocytoma: complete resection is usually curative.

whyNot.B: Craniospinal radiotherapy is used for medulloblastoma and carries major late effects in children.
whyNot.C: Temozolomide is a glioma drug for higher-grade tumours, not first-line for this tumour.
whyNot.D: A shunt treats hydrocephalus but leaves the growing tumour in place.
whyNot.E: Watching a symptomatic tumour with hydrocephalus is unsafe.

items.objective: Treat pilocytic astrocytoma with complete surgical resection.

items.stemHtml: A 60-year-old man undergoes maximal safe resection of a right temporal mass. Pathology shows glioblastoma, IDH-wildtype, with a methylated MGMT promoter. He has recovered well and is fully independent. Which of the following is the most appropriate next treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: MRI every 3 months without further treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Focal radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide

items.explanationHtml:
Standard care for glioblastoma in a fit patient after maximal safe resection is focal radiotherapy with daily temozolomide, followed by adjuvant temozolomide. MGMT promoter methylation predicts greater benefit. Tumour-treating fields can be added.

Takeaway: glioblastoma: resection, then radiotherapy with concurrent and adjuvant temozolomide.

whyNot.A: High-dose methotrexate is the basis of primary CNS lymphoma treatment.
whyNot.B: Observation after resection leads to rapid regrowth; glioblastoma always needs adjuvant therapy.
whyNot.C: Bevacizumab is used for recurrent disease and does not improve overall survival as first-line therapy.
whyNot.D: Whole-brain radiotherapy is for multiple metastases; glioblastoma is treated with focal fields plus temozolomide.

items.objective: Choose chemoradiation with temozolomide after resection of glioblastoma.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman has 5 weeks of confusion and apathy. She is alert, oriented to person only, and has no focal weakness. She is HIV-negative. MRI shows a homogeneously enhancing 3-cm mass next to the frontal horn of the right lateral ventricle with mild edema and no midline shift. Slit-lamp examination shows cells in the vitreous of both eyes. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A deep periventricular, homogeneously enhancing mass with vitreous cells in an older immunocompetent patient suggests primary CNS lymphoma. Make the diagnosis with stereotactic biopsy, and avoid corticosteroids beforehand if the patient is stable, because they can make the lymphoma vanish and give a nondiagnostic biopsy.

Takeaway: suspected primary CNS lymphoma: biopsy before steroids.

whyNot.A: Steroids before biopsy can shrink lymphoma and leave a nondiagnostic sample; she has no herniation to justify them.
whyNot.C: Resection gives no survival benefit in lymphoma and risks deficits; the tumour responds to chemotherapy.
whyNot.D: Treating without tissue is inappropriate; whole-brain radiotherapy is no longer first-line.
whyNot.E: Empirical toxoplasmosis treatment is for advanced HIV with positive serology, not an HIV-negative patient.

items.objective: Biopsy suspected primary CNS lymphoma before giving corticosteroids.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy undergoes resection of a midline cerebellar mass that was causing hydrocephalus. Pathology shows medulloblastoma. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional evaluation to stage this tumour?

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the entire spine and lumbar CSF cytology

items.explanationHtml:
Medulloblastoma spreads through the CSF, so staging needs MRI of the whole spine (ideally before surgery or about 2 weeks after) and CSF cytology, plus a postoperative brain MRI for residual tumour. Results set the radiotherapy and chemotherapy intensity.

Takeaway: stage medulloblastoma with spine MRI and CSF cytology.

whyNot.A: Bone marrow spread is very rare at diagnosis and is not routine staging.
whyNot.B: Spread outside the CNS is rare, so body CT is not part of routine staging.
whyNot.D: Bone scintigraphy is not routine because bone metastases are rare at diagnosis.
whyNot.E: AFP and β-hCG are markers for germ cell tumours of the pineal or suprasellar region.

items.objective: Stage medulloblastoma with whole-spine MRI and CSF cytology.

items.stemHtml:
A 61-year-old man is in week 2 of focal radiotherapy with daily temozolomide after resection of a glioblastoma. He is taking dexamethasone 4 mg daily for edema. He feels well. Laboratory results today:

TestResultReference range
Leukocytes3,600/mm³4,500–11,000/mm³
Neutrophils2,600/mm³
Lymphocytes380/mm³
Hemoglobin13.4 g/dL13.5–17.5 g/dL
Platelets168,000/mm³150,000–400,000/mm³

Which of the following should be added to his treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Concurrent temozolomide and radiotherapy cause marked lymphopenia, and he also takes a corticosteroid. Together these put him at risk of Pneumocystis pneumonia, so trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole prophylaxis is given during the concurrent phase.

Takeaway: give Pneumocystis prophylaxis during concurrent temozolomide–radiotherapy.

whyNot.A: Antifungal prophylaxis against Candida is not routine in this setting.
whyNot.B: His neutrophil count is adequate; filgrastim does not correct lymphopenia.
whyNot.C: CMV prophylaxis is for transplant recipients at high risk, not glioblastoma chemoradiation.
whyNot.E: Isoniazid is for latent tuberculosis; nothing suggests TB exposure or a positive test.

items.objective: Add Pneumocystis prophylaxis for lymphopenia during temozolomide chemoradiation.

items.stemHtml: A 9-year-old boy has 3 weeks of headaches on waking, morning vomiting and a new wide-based, unsteady gait. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilledema. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain with and without gadolinium

options.label: D
options.html: Referral for an outpatient ophthalmology assessment

options.label: E
options.html: A headache diary and a trial of sumatriptan

items.explanationHtml:
Morning headache with vomiting, ataxia and papilledema in a child suggests a posterior fossa tumour with raised intracranial pressure. The next step is MRI of the brain with contrast.

Takeaway: a child with morning headache, ataxia and papilledema needs brain MRI before anything else.

whyNot.A: Lumbar puncture with possible posterior fossa mass effect risks tonsillar herniation and must wait for imaging.
whyNot.C: EEG is for seizures and does not detect a mass.
whyNot.D: Papilledema with neurological signs needs urgent imaging, not an outpatient referral.
whyNot.E: Red-flag features rule out treating this as primary headache.

items.objective: Image the brain first in a child with signs of a posterior fossa mass.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman completed 6 weeks of focal radiotherapy with daily temozolomide for glioblastoma 6 weeks ago. She feels well, takes no corticosteroid and her examination is unchanged. A planned MRI shows larger enhancement around the resection cavity, all within the radiation field, with no new distant lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Continue adjuvant temozolomide and repeat MRI in 4–8 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
New enhancement within the radiation field during the first 12 weeks after chemoradiation, in a stable patient, is often pseudoprogression: a treatment effect, more common with MGMT-methylated tumours. Continue the planned temozolomide and repeat MRI. Advanced imaging or surgery is considered if enhancement keeps growing or symptoms appear.

Takeaway: early post-chemoradiation enhancement in a stable patient: suspect pseudoprogression and keep treating.

whyNot.B: Switching therapy assumes true progression, which cannot be called this early without more evidence.
whyNot.C: Surgery is not needed in a well patient when enhancement may be treatment effect.
whyNot.D: Hospice is premature; she is well, and the finding may be pseudoprogression.
whyNot.E: Further radiation so soon carries high toxicity and is not indicated.

items.objective: Recognise pseudoprogression after glioblastoma chemoradiation and continue therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has a seizure that begins with jerking of his right hand and becomes bilateral tonic-clonic. MRI shows a left frontal ring-enhancing mass, and resection confirms glioblastoma. He will start radiotherapy with temozolomide and dexamethasone. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term antiseizure medication?
items.explanationHtml:
He has had a seizure, so he needs an antiseizure medication. Levetiracetam is preferred in brain tumours: it is effective for focal seizures, needs no level monitoring and does not induce hepatic enzymes, so it does not lower dexamethasone or chemotherapy levels.

Takeaway: in patients with brain tumours and seizures, prefer a non–enzyme-inducing drug such as levetiracetam.

whyNot.A: Carbamazepine induces CYP enzymes and lowers dexamethasone and many anticancer drug levels; it also suppresses marrow.
whyNot.B: Phenytoin is an enzyme inducer with complex kinetics and interactions with dexamethasone.
whyNot.C: Phenobarbital is sedating and a strong enzyme inducer.
whyNot.E: He has already had a seizure, so treatment is indicated; prophylaxis is withheld only in patients who have never had one.

items.objective: Choose levetiracetam for seizures in a patient with a brain tumour.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has 2 weeks of worsening mid-back pain that wakes him at night and is worse lying flat. Since yesterday, his legs feel weak and he has had trouble starting urination. Both hip flexors are 4/5, and pinprick is reduced below the umbilicus. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Plain radiographs of the thoracic and lumbar spine today

options.label: C
options.html: Intravenous dexamethasone and an emergency MRI of the whole spine

options.label: D
options.html: Lumbar puncture with CSF cytology and protein

options.label: E
options.html: An NSAID now and an outpatient MRI within 2 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Back pain, leg weakness, a sensory level near T10 and urinary hesitancy in a patient with cancer mean metastatic spinal cord compression. Give dexamethasone at once and get an emergency MRI of the whole spine, because other levels are often involved. Surgery and/or radiotherapy follow.

Takeaway: cancer + back pain + neurological deficit: dexamethasone now and emergency whole-spine MRI.

whyNot.A: Plain radiographs miss epidural disease and delay the diagnosis.
whyNot.B: A bone scan shows bone metastases but not the cord or epidural space.
whyNot.D: Lumbar puncture does not diagnose compression and can worsen a spinal block.
whyNot.E: Delay risks permanent paraplegia; neurological function at treatment predicts outcome.

items.objective: Manage suspected metastatic spinal cord compression as an emergency.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old woman who has smoked for 40 years has a focal seizure with jerking of her left arm. She has no known cancer. Examination shows mild weakness of the left hand. MRI shows a single 2.5-cm ring-enhancing lesion at the gray–white junction of the right frontal lobe with surrounding edema. Levetiracetam and dexamethasone are started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in evaluation?

options.label: A
options.html: Stereotactic biopsy of the brain lesion

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis with contrast

items.explanationHtml:
A single ring-enhancing lesion at the gray–white junction in a smoker is likely a metastasis. CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis often finds the primary and other sites. That sets prognosis, decides where to biopsy and guides how to treat the brain lesion.

Takeaway: with a probable brain metastasis and no known cancer, search for the primary with body CT first.

whyNot.A: Biopsy of the brain may be needed, but body CT first may find a safer biopsy site and changes the plan.
whyNot.C: Lumbar puncture risks herniation with a mass and edema and rarely helps here.
whyNot.D: Tumour markers are neither sensitive nor specific for finding an unknown primary.
whyNot.E: Treatment should not start before the diagnosis and extent of disease are known.

items.objective: Search for the primary with CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis when a brain metastasis is suspected.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item has CT showing a 3-cm spiculated mass in the right upper lobe with no other lesions outside the brain. She is fully active and her lung cancer is judged treatable. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment of the brain lesion?

options.label: B
options.html: Observation with a repeat brain MRI in 3 months

options.label: C
options.html: Systemic platinum-based chemotherapy as the only treatment

options.label: D
options.html: Whole-brain radiotherapy as the only treatment

options.label: E
options.html: Surgical resection followed by radiosurgery to the cavity

items.explanationHtml:
For a single, accessible, symptomatic metastasis with mass effect in a fit patient with treatable disease, resection relieves symptoms, provides tissue and improves local control. Stereotactic radiosurgery to the cavity then lowers the local recurrence rate while sparing cognition compared with whole-brain radiotherapy.

Takeaway: single accessible symptomatic brain metastasis in a fit patient: resect, then radiosurgery to the cavity.

whyNot.A: Steroids relieve edema but do not treat the tumour.
whyNot.B: Observation leaves a symptomatic, growing lesion untreated.
whyNot.C: Chemotherapy alone controls a large symptomatic metastasis poorly.
whyNot.D: Whole-brain radiotherapy alone gives worse local control and more cognitive decline than focal treatment.

items.objective: Treat a single accessible symptomatic brain metastasis with resection plus cavity radiosurgery.

items.stemHtml: A 53-year-old woman with breast cancer whose systemic disease is well controlled has a staging MRI that shows three brain metastases, the largest 1.4 cm. She has no neurological symptoms and is fully active. Which of the following is the most appropriate management of the brain lesions?

options.label: C
options.html: Surgical resection of all three lesions

options.label: E
options.html: Levetiracetam and repeat MRI in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
A limited number of small brain metastases in a patient with good performance status and controlled extracranial disease is best treated with stereotactic radiosurgery. It controls the treated lesions well and preserves cognition better than whole-brain radiotherapy, with MRI surveillance for new lesions.

Takeaway: a few small brain metastases: radiosurgery, not whole-brain radiotherapy.

whyNot.B: Whole-brain radiotherapy causes more cognitive decline and is reserved for many lesions.
whyNot.C: Surgery is for large, symptomatic or single lesions, not three small asymptomatic ones.
whyNot.D: Steroids are for symptomatic edema and do not treat the tumours.
whyNot.E: Prophylactic antiseizure drugs are not indicated, and untreated metastases will grow.

items.objective: Choose radiosurgery for a few small brain metastases.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer has 3 weeks of headache, double vision and numbness of the left chin, and 1 week of pain shooting down both legs. She has a right abducens palsy, numbness in the territory of the left mental nerve, and absent ankle reflexes. A noncontrast head CT is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: Electroencephalography and a serum CA 15-3 level

options.label: B
options.html: Nerve conduction studies of the facial and leg nerves

options.label: C
options.html: A repeat noncontrast head CT scan in 1 month

options.label: D
options.html: Gadolinium MRI of the brain and whole spine, then CSF cytology

options.label: E
options.html: Whole-body FDG-PET as the only further test

items.explanationHtml:
Several cranial nerve palsies with radicular pain in a patient with cancer suggest leptomeningeal metastasis. Obtain MRI of the brain and entire spine with gadolinium to show leptomeningeal and nerve-root enhancement. Follow with lumbar puncture for CSF cytology, repeated with a large volume if the first is negative.

Takeaway: multilevel cranial and spinal root deficits in cancer: gadolinium MRI of neuraxis, then CSF cytology.

whyNot.A: EEG and serum tumour markers do not detect leptomeningeal disease.
whyNot.B: Nerve conduction studies cannot show the cause of deficits at several cranial and spinal levels.
whyNot.C: Noncontrast CT is insensitive, and waiting a month lets deficits accumulate.
whyNot.E: PET is poor at showing leptomeningeal disease and does not replace MRI and CSF.

items.objective: Diagnose leptomeningeal metastasis with neuraxis MRI and CSF cytology.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with newly diagnosed non-small cell lung cancer has a staging MRI that shows two brain metastases with mild edema. He has never had a seizure. He is started on dexamethasone for headache and referred for radiosurgery. Which of the following is the most appropriate approach to seizure prevention?
items.explanationHtml:
Patients with brain metastases who have never had a seizure do not benefit from prophylactic antiseizure medication. They are exposed only to side effects and interactions. Start treatment if a seizure occurs.

Takeaway: no prophylactic antiseizure drugs for brain tumours without seizures.

whyNot.A: Short-term prophylaxis may be considered around craniotomy, but not around radiosurgery in a seizure-free patient.
whyNot.B: Phenytoin prophylaxis adds toxicity and interactions without benefit.
whyNot.D: Routine EEG monitoring does not prevent seizures and is not indicated.
whyNot.E: Valproate prophylaxis is not indicated and can cause thrombocytopenia and liver toxicity.

items.objective: Avoid antiseizure prophylaxis in brain metastases without seizures.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after 2 weeks of anxiety, insomnia and bizarre behaviour, followed by a seizure. She has fluctuating alertness, repetitive orofacial movements and episodes of tachycardia with sweating. CSF shows lymphocytic pleocytosis and normal glucose, and antibodies to the NMDA receptor are detected in the CSF. Intravenous methylprednisolone is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Haloperidol and transfer to a psychiatric unit

options.label: C
options.html: CT of the chest to look for thymoma

items.explanationHtml:
This is anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis. Young women often have an ovarian teratoma, so image the pelvis (MRI or transvaginal ultrasonography). Removing a teratoma together with first-line immunotherapy (corticosteroids, IVIG or plasma exchange) speeds recovery. Rituximab is the second-line option.

Takeaway: anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis: look for and remove an ovarian teratoma, and give immunotherapy.

whyNot.A: This is an autoimmune encephalitis, not a primary psychosis; antipsychotics may worsen rigidity and autonomic instability.
whyNot.C: Thymoma is associated with myasthenia gravis, not anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
whyNot.D: Breast cancer is not the associated tumour, and mammography is not indicated at 23.
whyNot.E: Nothing suggests a hematologic cancer.

items.objective: Search for an ovarian teratoma in anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man with newly diagnosed multiple myeloma has 10 days of mid-back pain and 2 days of mild leg weakness. Dexamethasone is given. MRI shows epidural tumour compressing the cord at T8, arising from a vertebral body with preserved height and alignment. Spine surgeons judge the spine stable. Which of the following is the most appropriate definitive treatment of the compression?

options.label: A
options.html: External-beam radiotherapy to the involved segment

options.label: E
options.html: Bed rest and analgesia with MRI in 4 weeks

items.explanationHtml:
Myeloma is highly radiosensitive. In a stable spine with mild deficits, radiotherapy plus dexamethasone (and then systemic myeloma therapy) is the definitive treatment of compression. Surgery is chosen for spinal instability, bony fragments compressing the cord, radioresistant tumours or worsening despite radiotherapy.

Takeaway: radiosensitive tumour + stable spine: treat cord compression with radiotherapy.

whyNot.B: Laminectomy alone removes posterior elements that support a spine weakened by an anterior vertebral body tumour, and gives worse outcomes.
whyNot.C: Vertebroplasty treats painful fractures, not epidural tumour compressing the cord.
whyNot.D: Bisphosphonates reduce skeletal events but do not relieve cord compression.
whyNot.E: Delay risks permanent paralysis.

items.objective: Choose radiotherapy for cord compression from a radiosensitive tumour in a stable spine.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old right-handed man is brought to the emergency department 50 minutes after he suddenly slumped at the dinner table. He cannot speak or follow commands. His right face and arm are flaccid, and his right leg is less weak. His eyes are deviated to the left. Refer to the figure of the arteries at the base of the brain. An occlusion at which numbered site best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Global aphasia, right face-and-arm-predominant weakness and gaze deviation toward the left hemisphere indicate a large left middle cerebral artery infarct. An occlusion of the middle cerebral stem (site 1) cuts off both the cortical branches (language, face and arm cortex, frontal eye field) and the deep lenticulostriate branches.

Takeaway: face and arm worse than leg, aphasia and gaze toward the lesion mean the dominant middle cerebral artery.

whyNot.B: Site 2 is the anterior cerebral artery; its infarct weakens the opposite leg more than the arm and spares language.
whyNot.C: Site 3 is the posterior cerebral artery, which causes an opposite homonymous hemianopia without major weakness.
whyNot.D: Site 4 is a single lenticulostriate branch; a lacune causes pure motor weakness without aphasia or gaze deviation.
whyNot.E: Site 5 is the basilar artery; occlusion causes bilateral brainstem signs, coma or a locked-in state, not a cortical aphasia.

items.objective: Localise a dominant-hemisphere middle cerebral stem occlusion from aphasia, face-arm weakness and gaze deviation.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman with atrial fibrillation who stopped taking her anticoagulant has sudden weakness of the right leg. Two days later she is incontinent of urine and speaks little unless prompted. Strength is 2/5 in the right leg and 4+/5 in the right arm; the face is normal. Sensation is reduced over the right foot and leg. Refer to the figure of the arteries at the base of the brain. An embolus lodged at which numbered site best explains her findings?
items.explanationHtml:
The anterior cerebral artery supplies the medial surface of the frontal and parietal lobes, where the leg area of the motor and sensory cortex lies. Medial frontal damage also causes urinary incontinence and abulia (reduced initiative and speech). Site 2 lies beyond the anterior communicating artery, so collateral flow from the other side cannot reach the territory.

Takeaway: leg weakness worse than arm, with incontinence and abulia, means an anterior cerebral artery infarct.

whyNot.A: Site 1 (middle cerebral stem) weakens the face and arm more than the leg and would cause aphasia in a left lesion.
whyNot.C: Site 3 (posterior cerebral) causes a visual field defect, not leg weakness.
whyNot.D: Site 4 (lenticulostriate) causes an equal face, arm and leg pure motor deficit.
whyNot.E: Site 5 (basilar) causes bilateral or crossed brainstem signs and altered consciousness.

items.objective: Recognise the anterior cerebral artery syndrome: contralateral leg weakness, incontinence and abulia.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man notices that he keeps bumping into objects on his right side. Examination shows a right homonymous hemianopia; central vision is preserved in both right hemifields. He can write a sentence to dictation but cannot read it back. Strength, sensation and speech are normal. Refer to the figure of the arteries at the base of the brain. An occlusion at which numbered site best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
A right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing points to the left occipital lobe, the territory of the left posterior cerebral artery (site 3). The occipital pole keeps some collateral flow from the middle cerebral artery, which preserves central vision. If the infarct also involves the splenium of the corpus callosum, visual information from the intact right occipital lobe cannot reach the left-hemisphere language areas: the patient can write but cannot read (alexia without agraphia).

Takeaway: homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing, and alexia without agraphia, localise to the dominant posterior cerebral artery.

whyNot.A: A middle cerebral stem occlusion would add aphasia, face-arm weakness and sensory loss; reading and writing would both fail.
whyNot.B: An anterior cerebral artery occlusion produces leg weakness and abulia, not a field defect.
whyNot.D: A lenticulostriate lacune produces a pure motor or sensory deficit with no field loss.
whyNot.E: Basilar occlusion produces brainstem signs; bilateral posterior cerebral involvement would cause cortical blindness, not a one-sided field defect with alexia.

items.objective: Localise homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing and alexia without agraphia to the left posterior cerebral artery.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with long-standing poorly controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes wakes up with weakness of the left side of his face, arm and leg, all to a similar degree. He has no sensory loss, visual field defect, neglect or speech disturbance. MRI shows a 9-mm infarct. Refer to the figure of the arteries at the base of the brain. Occlusion of a vessel at which numbered site best explains this presentation?
items.explanationHtml:
Pure motor hemiparesis affecting face, arm and leg equally with no cortical signs is a lacunar syndrome. Corticospinal and corticobulbar fibres are packed tightly in the posterior limb of the internal capsule, so a small infarct there weakens the whole side. The supplying vessels are the lenticulostriate arteries (site 4), penetrating end-arteries damaged by hypertension and diabetes (lipohyalinosis). The figure marks the left side, but the vessel type is the same on the right, where this patient's lesion lies.

Takeaway: pure motor hemiparesis without cortical signs is a lacune from a penetrating artery such as a lenticulostriate branch.

whyNot.A: A middle cerebral stem occlusion produces a large cortical infarct with sensory loss, neglect or aphasia and face-arm predominance.
whyNot.B: An anterior cerebral occlusion affects the leg far more than the face and arm.
whyNot.C: A posterior cerebral occlusion causes a field defect rather than hemiparesis.
whyNot.E: A basilar occlusion produces bilateral signs, cranial nerve palsies or altered consciousness.

items.objective: Link pure motor lacunar stroke to occlusion of a lenticulostriate penetrating artery.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman develops sudden vertigo, vomiting and hiccups. She has a hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing. Her left eyelid droops and the left pupil is smaller than the right. She cannot feel a pin on the left side of her face or on the right side of her trunk and limbs. Finger-to-nose testing is clumsy on the left. Strength is normal. Refer to the figure of the arteries at the base of the brain. An occlusion at which numbered site best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
This is the lateral medullary syndrome. The left lateral medulla contains the spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract (same-side facial pain and temperature loss), the already-crossed spinothalamic tract (opposite body), descending sympathetic fibres (Horner syndrome), the nucleus ambiguus (hoarseness and dysphagia), vestibular nuclei (vertigo, nystagmus) and the inferior cerebellar peduncle (ataxia). It is supplied by the vertebral artery and its posterior inferior cerebellar branch; vertebral occlusion at the origin of that branch (site 6) is a common cause.

Takeaway: crossed pain-temperature loss with Horner syndrome, hoarseness and ataxia means a lateral medullary infarct from the vertebral artery or PICA.

whyNot.A: Site 2 (anterior cerebral) causes leg weakness and abulia, not brainstem signs.
whyNot.B: Site 3 (posterior cerebral) causes a visual field defect and possibly thalamic sensory loss without crossed signs.
whyNot.C: Site 4 (lenticulostriate) causes a lacunar syndrome without vertigo, Horner syndrome or dysphagia.
whyNot.D: Site 5 (basilar) usually causes bilateral pontine signs with weakness or coma; the medulla is supplied by the vertebral arteries below it.

items.objective: Localise the lateral medullary syndrome to the vertebral artery or posterior inferior cerebellar artery.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man has an infarct confined to region 1 shown in the figure of the medulla (on the left side). Which of the following combinations of findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Tongue deviates to the right; right arm and leg weakness; reduced vibration sense on the right

options.label: B
options.html: Tongue deviates to the left; right arm and leg weakness; reduced vibration sense on the right

options.label: C
options.html: Tongue deviates to the left; left arm and leg weakness; reduced pain sense on the left body

options.label: D
options.html: Hoarse voice; reduced pain sense on the left face; reduced pain sense on the right body

options.label: E
options.html: Tongue midline; right arm and leg weakness; reduced pain sense on the right body

items.explanationHtml:
Region 1 contains the left pyramid, left medial lemniscus and left hypoglossal nucleus or fibres (the medial medullary syndrome). The left genioglossus is weak, so the tongue is pushed toward the weak (left) side on protrusion. The pyramid lies above the motor decussation, so the limb weakness is on the right. The medial lemniscus has already crossed (internal arcuate fibres), so vibration and position sense are lost on the right. The usual vessel is the anterior spinal artery or a paramedian branch of the vertebral artery.

Takeaway: medial medullary infarct: tongue toward the lesion, opposite hemiparesis and opposite loss of vibration and position sense.

whyNot.A: The tongue deviates toward a hypoglossal lesion, not away from it.
whyNot.C: The pyramids decussate below this level, so limb weakness is on the opposite (right) side; pain pathways are lateral and spared.
whyNot.D: Hoarseness and crossed pain-temperature loss describe the lateral medullary syndrome (region 2), not region 1.
whyNot.E: Region 1 includes the hypoglossal nucleus or fascicles, so the tongue is not midline, and the spinothalamic tract (pain) lies laterally.

items.objective: Predict the findings of a medial medullary infarct from the tracts and nucleus in the medial medulla.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman with normal blood pressure has had three hemorrhages over 4 years: in the right occipital lobe, the left frontal lobe and now the left parietal lobe. Her family reports gradual memory decline. MRI shows many small cortical microbleeds. She dies of the latest hemorrhage. Microscopic examination of the cortical and leptomeningeal arterioles is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Hyaline thickening of penetrating arterioles with tiny wall dilatations

options.label: B
options.html: A saccular outpouching lacking an internal elastic lamina and media

options.label: C
options.html: Tangled thick- and thin-walled vessels with no intervening capillary bed

options.label: D
options.html: Transmural granulomatous inflammation with giant cells

options.label: E
options.html: Extracellular material in vessel walls that is apple-green birefringent with Congo red

items.explanationHtml:
Recurrent lobar hemorrhages in an older normotensive person with cognitive decline and cortical microbleeds suggest cerebral amyloid angiopathy. Beta-amyloid is deposited in the walls of cortical and leptomeningeal vessels, making them brittle. Like other amyloid, it shows apple-green birefringence under polarised light after Congo red staining.

Takeaway: recurrent lobar hemorrhage in an older normotensive patient points to amyloid angiopathy.

whyNot.A: Hyaline arteriolosclerosis with microaneurysms is the hypertensive lesion, which bleeds in deep sites such as the putamen and thalamus.
whyNot.B: A saccular (berry) aneurysm at the circle of Willis causes subarachnoid hemorrhage rather than repeated lobar hematomas.
whyNot.C: An arteriovenous malformation causes hemorrhage in younger patients and is a single lesion, not a diffuse vasculopathy.
whyNot.D: Granulomatous angiitis of the CNS causes headache, encephalopathy and infarcts more often than recurrent lobar bleeding, and is uncommon.

items.objective: Identify cerebral amyloid angiopathy as the cause of recurrent lobar hemorrhage in older adults.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease develops a sudden severe headache while lifting a box. On examination her right upper eyelid droops, and the right eye rests down and out. The right pupil is 7 mm and does not react to light. An aneurysm at which of the following sites is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
A painful oculomotor palsy with a dilated pupil and a sudden headache suggests an expanding or ruptured aneurysm at the posterior communicating artery junction. The oculomotor nerve runs right beside this artery, and the pupilloconstrictor (parasympathetic) fibres lie on the outer surface of the nerve, so compression dilates the pupil early. Polycystic kidney disease increases the risk of saccular aneurysms.

Takeaway: a third nerve palsy with a dilated pupil and headache means a posterior communicating artery aneurysm until proven otherwise.

whyNot.A: The anterior communicating artery is the most common aneurysm site overall, but it lies far from the oculomotor nerve; it can compress the optic chiasm.
whyNot.B: Middle cerebral bifurcation aneurysms lie in the Sylvian fissure and cause hemispheric signs rather than an oculomotor palsy.
whyNot.C: A basilar tip aneurysm can affect both oculomotor nerves near the midbrain, but a one-sided palsy beside the internal carotid is far more typical of a posterior communicating aneurysm.
whyNot.E: A posterior inferior cerebellar aneurysm lies near the lower cranial nerves and medulla.

items.objective: Link a pupil-involving oculomotor palsy with sudden headache to a posterior communicating artery aneurysm.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old man has a large left middle cerebral artery infarct and dies 18 hours after the onset of symptoms. Microscopic examination of the infarcted cortex is most likely to show which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: A cystic cavity lined by reactive astrocytes

options.label: C
options.html: Dense neutrophilic infiltration with abscess formation

options.label: D
options.html: Shrunken neurons with hypereosinophilic cytoplasm and pyknotic nuclei

items.explanationHtml:
The first reliable light-microscopic change in an ischemic brain is the red neuron, seen about 12–24 hours after the insult: a shrunken cell body, intensely eosinophilic cytoplasm and a small, dark (pyknotic) nucleus. Neutrophils arrive over the next days, macrophages follow, and a glial-lined cyst forms over months.

Takeaway: red neurons appear 12–24 hours after ischemic injury.

whyNot.A: A cyst bounded by glial scar is the end stage of liquefactive necrosis, weeks to months later.
whyNot.B: Lipid-laden macrophages that clear myelin debris dominate from about 3 days to weeks.
whyNot.C: Neutrophils enter from about the first to the third day and do not form abscesses in a sterile infarct.
whyNot.E: Neurofibrillary tangles are a feature of neurodegenerative tauopathies such as Alzheimer disease, not of acute ischemia.

items.objective: Recall the timeline of microscopic changes after a brain infarct.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old man with hypertension is found unresponsive. CT shows a small hemorrhage confined to the tegmentum of the upper pons and lower midbrain on both sides of the midline. The cerebral hemispheres are normal. Damage to which of the following structures best explains his loss of consciousness?
items.explanationHtml:
Arousal depends on the ascending reticular activating system: neurons in the tegmentum of the upper pons and midbrain project through the thalamus to the cortex. A small bilateral lesion here can cause coma, whereas a large one-sided hemispheric lesion does not, unless it compresses the brainstem.

Takeaway: coma requires dysfunction of the upper brainstem reticular formation or of both hemispheres.

whyNot.B: The corticospinal tracts run in the ventral basis pontis; damage causes weakness, not unconsciousness.
whyNot.C: The medial longitudinal fasciculus coordinates conjugate horizontal gaze; a lesion causes internuclear ophthalmoplegia.
whyNot.D: Superior cerebellar peduncle damage causes ataxia and tremor.
whyNot.E: Spinothalamic damage causes loss of pain and temperature sensation.

items.objective: Explain coma from bilateral damage to the ascending reticular activating system in the upper brainstem.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man had vertigo and double vision for 2 days that then rapidly progressed. Now he lies motionless with his eyes open. He cannot move his limbs, face or tongue, or make a sound. When asked, he looks up and blinks twice to answer yes, and he blinks once to answer no, correctly. Refer to the figure of the arteries at the base of the brain. Occlusion at which numbered site best explains his condition?
items.explanationHtml:
He is locked in: fully aware but quadriplegic and mute, with only vertical eye movement and blinking preserved. The lesion is a bilateral infarct of the ventral pons, which destroys both corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts while sparing the tegmentum (arousal) and the midbrain centres for vertical gaze. The cause is usually occlusion of the basilar artery (site 5), often preceded by fluctuating brainstem symptoms.

Takeaway: awake, quadriplegic and mute with vertical eye movements preserved means a ventral pontine infarct from basilar occlusion.

whyNot.A: An anterior cerebral occlusion weakens one leg; it does not abolish movement of all four limbs and the face.
whyNot.B: A posterior cerebral occlusion affects vision, thalamus and memory, not bulbar and limb movement on both sides.
whyNot.C: A single lenticulostriate lacune weakens one side only.
whyNot.E: A vertebral occlusion at the posterior inferior cerebellar origin causes the lateral medullary syndrome, with preserved limb strength.
