items.objective: Recognise locked-in syndrome and link it to basilar artery occlusion and ventral pontine infarction.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old man is resuscitated after 14 minutes of cardiac arrest. He never regains consciousness and dies 6 days later. Autopsy shows the brain is diffusely swollen. In which of the following regions are neurons most likely to show the most severe loss?

options.label: D
options.html: Anterior horn of the lumbar spinal cord

items.explanationHtml:
Global hypoxia-ischemia selectively kills the most vulnerable neurons: the pyramidal cells of hippocampal sector CA1, cerebellar Purkinje cells and neocortical pyramidal neurons in layers 3, 5 and 6. These cells have high metabolic demand and dense glutamate receptors, making them sensitive to excitotoxic injury.

Takeaway: after cardiac arrest, hippocampal CA1 neurons, Purkinje cells and deep cortical layers die first.

whyNot.B: Dorsal root ganglion neurons lie outside the CNS and are relatively resistant to brief global ischemia.
whyNot.C: Hypothalamic neurosecretory neurons are comparatively resistant; that is one reason hormone secretion can continue in severe brain injury.
whyNot.D: Spinal anterior horn cells are much less vulnerable than hippocampal and cerebellar neurons.
whyNot.E: The olfactory bulb is not a recognised site of selective vulnerability.

items.objective: Identify the neurons most vulnerable to global hypoxic-ischemic injury.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old woman has a prolonged episode of severe hypotension during cardiac surgery. After she wakes, she cannot lift either arm above her shoulders or flex either hip against gravity. Hand grip, facial movement and ankle strength are normal, and she has no aphasia. Ischemia in which of the following regions best explains her findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Posterior limbs of both internal capsules

options.label: B
options.html: Calcarine cortex of both occipital lobes

options.label: C
options.html: Central grey matter of the cervical spinal cord

options.label: D
options.html: Basis pontis on both sides of the midline

options.label: E
options.html: Anterior–middle cerebral border zones on both sides

items.explanationHtml:
Global hypoperfusion damages watershed zones, the most distal fields between two arterial territories. The border zone between the anterior and middle cerebral territories runs over the part of the motor strip that controls the shoulder and hip. Bilateral involvement weakens the proximal arms and legs while the hand and face, which lie deeper in the middle cerebral territory, are spared.

Takeaway: proximal arm and thigh weakness after profound hypotension means bilateral anterior–middle cerebral watershed infarcts.

whyNot.A: Bilateral internal capsule lesions would weaken the face, hands and legs equally.
whyNot.B: Bilateral occipital (posterior cerebral) border-zone or territorial infarcts cause cortical blindness, not proximal weakness.
whyNot.C: A cervical central cord lesion weakens the hands more than the legs, the opposite of this pattern.
whyNot.D: Bilateral pontine infarcts produce quadriplegia with facial and bulbar weakness.

items.objective: Recognise bilateral watershed infarction after global hypoperfusion.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old man is being evaluated for death by neurologic criteria after a severe traumatic brain injury. Prerequisites are met and all brainstem reflexes are absent. During the apnea test he is disconnected from the ventilator while oxygen is delivered by catheter. After 9 minutes arterial PCO2 is 68 mm Hg and pH is 7.19, and he has made no breathing movements. A breathing response in this test would normally be triggered by a change detected by which of the following?

options.label: A
options.html: Carotid body glomus cells sensing a fall in arterial PO<sub>2</sub>

options.label: B
options.html: Pulmonary stretch receptors sensing a fall in lung volume

options.label: C
options.html: Medullary chemoreceptors sensing a rise in CSF hydrogen ions

options.label: D
options.html: Aortic arch baroreceptors sensing a fall in blood pressure

options.label: E
options.html: Juxtacapillary receptors sensing pulmonary interstitial fluid

items.explanationHtml:
Carbon dioxide diffuses across the blood–brain barrier and lowers CSF pH. Central chemoreceptors near the ventral surface of the medulla sense this rise in hydrogen ion concentration and drive the medullary respiratory centres. The apnea test lets PCO2 rise to a level that would powerfully stimulate breathing (at least 60 mm Hg and at least 20 mm Hg above baseline) while oxygen is supplied, so the absence of any breath shows the medulla no longer works.

Takeaway: the apnea test probes the medullary response to a CO₂-driven fall in CSF pH.

whyNot.A: Oxygen is delivered during the test precisely so that hypoxemia is avoided; peripheral hypoxic drive is not what is tested.
whyNot.B: Pulmonary stretch receptors mediate the Hering–Breuer reflex that ends inspiration; they do not generate the drive to breathe in response to CO₂.
whyNot.D: Baroreceptors regulate heart rate and vascular tone, not ventilation; hypotension is avoided during the test.
whyNot.E: Juxtacapillary receptors cause rapid shallow breathing in pulmonary edema; they are not the CO₂ sensor.

items.objective: Explain the physiological basis of the apnea test: central chemoreceptor sensing of CSF hydrogen ions.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man with untreated hypertension suddenly becomes unresponsive. He has pinpoint pupils that react weakly to light, absent horizontal eye movements, quadriplegia and a temperature of 39.4 °C (102.9 °F). Hemorrhage at which of the following sites best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
A pontine hemorrhage causes sudden coma (tegmental reticular formation), quadriplegia (corticospinal tracts in the basis pontis), loss of horizontal gaze (abducens nuclei and paramedian pontine reticular formation) and pinpoint pupils because descending sympathetic fibres are interrupted while parasympathetic pupilloconstriction is preserved. Hyperthermia is common. Hypertensive hemorrhages favour the putamen, thalamus, pons and cerebellum.

Takeaway: coma with pinpoint pupils and quadriplegia localises to the pons.

whyNot.A: A putaminal hemorrhage causes opposite hemiparesis and gaze deviation toward the lesion, with normal-sized pupils early.
whyNot.B: A thalamic hemorrhage causes opposite sensory loss and hemiparesis, often with the eyes deviated down; pupils are small but the picture is not quadriplegia.
whyNot.D: A cerebellar hemorrhage causes vomiting, ataxia and inability to walk; coma comes later from brainstem compression.
whyNot.E: An occipital hemorrhage causes a visual field defect and headache, not coma with quadriplegia.

items.objective: Localise coma with pinpoint pupils and quadriplegia to a pontine hemorrhage.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman had a cardiac arrest 4 months ago. She now opens her eyes spontaneously each morning and closes them at night. She breathes on her own, coughs, yawns and withdraws a limb from pain. On repeated assessment she never follows a command, tracks an object or responds to her name. Which of the following best describes her state?
items.explanationHtml:
She has sleep–wake cycles and brainstem functions but no sign of awareness on repeated testing: this is unresponsive wakefulness, also called the vegetative state. It reflects severe diffuse cortical or thalamic injury with a functioning brainstem.

Takeaway: eyes open with sleep–wake cycles but no awareness defines unresponsive wakefulness.

whyNot.A: In coma the eyes stay closed and there are no sleep–wake cycles.
whyNot.B: Death by neurologic criteria requires absent brainstem reflexes and no breathing; she breathes and coughs.
whyNot.C: A locked-in patient is fully aware and communicates with eye movements or blinks.
whyNot.D: A minimally conscious state requires reproducible, if inconsistent, signs of awareness such as following a command or visual tracking.

items.objective: Distinguish unresponsive wakefulness from coma, locked-in syndrome, minimally conscious state and brain death.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is struck on the side of the head by a baseball. He is briefly unconscious and then talks normally for 2 hours before becoming drowsy, with a dilated right pupil. CT shows a biconvex hyperdense collection over the right temporal lobe that does not cross the suture lines, and a fracture of the squamous temporal bone. Which vessel is the most likely source of bleeding?
items.explanationHtml:
A lens-shaped collection limited by sutures with a temporal bone fracture and a lucid interval is an epidural hematoma. The middle meningeal artery runs in a groove on the inner surface of the thin squamous temporal bone near the pterion and is torn by the fracture. Arterial bleeding strips the dura off the skull and expands quickly, causing uncal herniation.

Takeaway: a biconvex hematoma after temporal bone fracture means epidural bleeding from the middle meningeal artery.

whyNot.A: Bridging vein tears cause a subdural hematoma, which is crescent-shaped and crosses suture lines.
whyNot.B: Sinus injury can cause an epidural or subdural collection near the midline, but the classic temporal epidural source is arterial.
whyNot.C: Lenticulostriate rupture causes a deep intracerebral (putaminal) hemorrhage, not an extra-axial collection.
whyNot.E: Anterior cerebral artery injury would bleed into the interhemispheric fissure or brain, not between dura and skull.

items.objective: Identify the middle meningeal artery as the source of a temporal epidural hematoma.

items.stemHtml: An 82-year-old woman who takes warfarin for atrial fibrillation has had headaches and increasing confusion for 3 weeks. Her daughter remembers that she bumped her head on a cabinet about a month ago. CT shows a crescent-shaped hypodense collection over the left hemisphere that crosses the coronal suture. Tearing of which structure most likely caused this lesion?

options.label: B
options.html: Saccular aneurysm of the circle of Willis

options.label: D
options.html: Penetrating arterioles of the basal ganglia

options.label: E
options.html: Bridging veins between the cortex and a dural sinus

items.explanationHtml:
A crescent-shaped collection that crosses suture lines lies in the subdural space. With age the brain shrinks, stretching the bridging veins that run from the cortex to the dural sinuses, so minor trauma can tear them. Anticoagulation adds to the risk. Low-pressure venous bleeding accumulates slowly; the blood becomes hypodense on CT over weeks, which defines a chronic subdural hematoma.

Takeaway: a crescentic collection crossing sutures in an older or anticoagulated patient is a subdural hematoma from torn bridging veins.

whyNot.A: Middle meningeal artery bleeding causes an epidural hematoma that is lens-shaped and limited by sutures.
whyNot.B: A ruptured saccular aneurysm bleeds into the subarachnoid space, causing a sudden severe headache rather than weeks of confusion.
whyNot.C: Choroid plexus bleeding causes intraventricular hemorrhage.
whyNot.D: Penetrating arteriolar rupture causes a deep intracerebral hemorrhage.

items.objective: Link chronic subdural hematoma to torn bridging veins in atrophic or anticoagulated older adults.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with an expanding right-sided acute subdural hematoma becomes less responsive. Refer to the figure of herniation types. The herniation shown by arrow 2 is most likely to compress which of the following structures first, causing a dilated, unreactive right pupil?
items.explanationHtml:
Arrow 2 shows uncal (lateral transtentorial) herniation: the medial temporal lobe slides over the free edge of the tentorium beside the midbrain. It compresses the oculomotor nerve on the same side. The parasympathetic pupilloconstrictor fibres run on the surface of the nerve, so the first sign is a fixed dilated pupil; ptosis and a down-and-out eye follow.

Takeaway: uncal herniation compresses the same-side oculomotor nerve, and a blown pupil is often the first sign.

whyNot.A: Optic tract compression would cause a homonymous field defect, not a fixed dilated pupil.
whyNot.C: The abducens nerve can be stretched by raised pressure (a false localising sign), causing failure of abduction, not mydriasis.
whyNot.D: The trochlear nerve causes vertical diplopia when injured and has no role in pupil size.
whyNot.E: Loss of sympathetic input from the superior cervical ganglion would make the pupil small (Horner syndrome).

items.objective: Explain why uncal herniation produces an ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has a large right-sided subdural hematoma and the herniation shown by arrow 2 in the figure of herniation types. His right pupil is dilated and fixed, and he has new weakness of his right arm and leg. Which of the following best explains weakness on the same side as the hematoma?

options.label: A
options.html: Compression of the right cerebral peduncle by the herniating uncus

options.label: B
options.html: Compression of the left cerebral peduncle against the edge of the tentorium

options.label: C
options.html: Infarction of the right occipital lobe from posterior cerebral artery compression

options.label: D
options.html: Compression of the anterior cerebral artery under the falx

options.label: E
options.html: Compression of the medullary pyramids in the foramen magnum

items.explanationHtml:
The mass pushes the midbrain toward the opposite side, so the left cerebral peduncle is pressed against the sharp tentorial edge (Kernohan notch). The left corticospinal tract has not yet crossed, so the right limbs weaken. Weakness on the same side as the mass is a false localising sign; the dilated pupil remains a reliable guide to the side of the lesion.

Takeaway: in uncal herniation, the opposite peduncle hitting the tentorium can cause weakness on the same side as the mass.

whyNot.A: Compression of the right peduncle would weaken the left limbs, because corticospinal fibres cross in the medulla.
whyNot.C: Posterior cerebral compression causes an occipital infarct with a visual field defect, not limb weakness.
whyNot.D: Subfalcine herniation compresses the anterior cerebral artery, which would weaken the opposite (left) leg.
whyNot.E: Tonsillar herniation compresses the medulla and causes respiratory and cardiac arrest, not a one-sided hemiparesis.

items.objective: Explain the Kernohan notch phenomenon as a false localising sign in uncal herniation.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman has a large right frontal glioblastoma with marked edema. Refer to the figure of herniation types. If the herniation shown by arrow 1 compresses the adjacent artery, which of the following new deficits is most likely?

options.label: E
options.html: Bilateral arm weakness with spared legs

items.explanationHtml:
Arrow 1 is subfalcine herniation: the cingulate gyrus is pushed under the free edge of the falx. The anterior cerebral artery runs along the medial surface beside it and can be compressed, infarcting the medial frontal and parietal cortex. The right leg area of the motor strip controls the left leg.

Takeaway: subfalcine herniation compresses the anterior cerebral artery and weakens the opposite leg.

whyNot.B: A homonymous hemianopia follows posterior cerebral artery compression in uncal herniation, not subfalcine herniation.
whyNot.C: Same-side ptosis comes from oculomotor nerve compression in uncal herniation.
whyNot.D: Hoarseness reflects vagal or nucleus ambiguus injury in the medulla.
whyNot.E: Weakness of both arms with spared legs suggests a central cervical cord lesion or watershed injury, not subfalcine herniation.

items.objective: Link subfalcine herniation to anterior cerebral artery compression and contralateral leg weakness.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man in the intensive care unit after a severe head injury has a mean arterial pressure of 80 mm Hg and an intracranial pressure of 30 mm Hg. Central venous pressure is 8 mm Hg. Which of the following is his cerebral perfusion pressure?
items.explanationHtml:
Cerebral perfusion pressure = mean arterial pressure − intracranial pressure (when ICP exceeds venous pressure, as here): 80 − 30 = 50 mm Hg. That is below the usual target in severe traumatic brain injury (roughly 60–70 mm Hg), so cerebral ischemia is a risk.

Takeaway: CPP equals MAP minus ICP.

whyNot.A: 22 mm Hg is the difference between intracranial and central venous pressure, not a perfusion pressure.
whyNot.B: 42 mm Hg subtracts both the intracranial and the central venous pressures; only the higher downstream pressure (here ICP) is subtracted.
whyNot.D: 72 mm Hg subtracts the central venous pressure instead of the intracranial pressure.
whyNot.E: 110 mm Hg adds the intracranial pressure instead of subtracting it.

items.objective: Calculate cerebral perfusion pressure from mean arterial pressure and intracranial pressure.

items.stemHtml: A 6-month-old boy recovered from bacterial meningitis 2 months ago. His head circumference has crossed two percentile lines, and his anterior fontanelle is full. MRI shows symmetric enlargement of the lateral, third and fourth ventricles, with no mass and an open aqueduct. Impaired function of which of the following structures is the most likely cause?

options.label: E
options.html: Ependymal lining of the central canal

items.explanationHtml:
Enlargement of all four ventricles with open pathways means CSF reaches the subarachnoid space but is not absorbed: a communicating hydrocephalus. Meningitis and subarachnoid hemorrhage leave fibrosis and scarring of the arachnoid granulations, through which CSF drains into the venous sinuses.

Takeaway: all ventricles enlarged after meningitis means communicating hydrocephalus from scarred arachnoid granulations.

whyNot.A: Choroid plexus overproduction (as in a papilloma) is rare and is not a consequence of meningitis.
whyNot.B: Aqueductal obstruction would enlarge the lateral and third ventricles but not the fourth; the aqueduct is open.
whyNot.D: Blockage at the foramina of Monro enlarges only the lateral ventricles.
whyNot.E: The central canal of the spinal cord does not take part in CSF absorption.

items.objective: Distinguish communicating from obstructive hydrocephalus by which ventricles enlarge.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman with a BMI of 36 kg/m² has had daily headaches and brief episodes of blurred vision for 2 months. She started minocycline for acne 3 months ago. She has bilateral papilledema. MRI with MR venography is normal. Lumbar puncture shows an opening pressure of 340 mm H2O (normal 70–180) and normal CSF composition. A drug is started to reduce CSF production. Inhibition of which enzyme accounts for its effect?
items.explanationHtml:
She has idiopathic intracranial hypertension, probably provoked by a tetracycline. Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase in the choroid plexus epithelium; less bicarbonate and sodium are secreted, so less water follows and CSF production falls. The drug should be stopped and weight loss encouraged.

Takeaway: acetazolamide lowers CSF production by inhibiting choroid plexus carbonic anhydrase.

whyNot.A: Na<sup>+</sup>/K<sup>+</sup>-ATPase inhibition (digoxin) is not used to lower CSF production.
whyNot.C: Cyclooxygenase inhibitors relieve headache pain but do not lower CSF pressure.
whyNot.D: Monoamine oxidase inhibitors are antidepressants with no role here.
whyNot.E: Xanthine oxidase inhibitors (allopurinol) lower uric acid.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of acetazolamide in idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman is in deep coma after a high-speed car crash in which her car spun several times. Initial CT shows only a few tiny hemorrhages at the grey–white junction and in the corpus callosum, with no mass lesion. She dies 2 days later. Microscopy of the white matter shows many swollen, rounded axon ends that stain for beta-amyloid precursor protein. Which of the following mechanisms best explains her injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Rupture of bridging veins by linear deceleration

options.label: B
options.html: Shearing of axons by rotational acceleration and deceleration

options.label: C
options.html: Compression of the brainstem by a rapidly expanding hematoma

options.label: D
options.html: Excitotoxic death of neurons from global hypoperfusion

options.label: E
options.html: Inflammatory demyelination triggered by blood products

items.explanationHtml:
This is diffuse axonal injury. Rotational forces shear axons where tissues of different density meet (grey–white junction), in the corpus callosum and in the dorsolateral brainstem. Damaged axons cannot transport proteins, so the proteins accumulate in axonal swellings that stain for beta-amyloid precursor protein within hours. CT can look deceptively normal despite deep coma.

Takeaway: deep coma with nearly normal CT after a rotational injury suggests diffuse axonal injury.

whyNot.A: Bridging vein rupture causes a subdural hematoma, which would be visible as a mass on CT.
whyNot.C: No mass lesion was seen, so compression by a hematoma does not explain the coma.
whyNot.D: Hypoperfusion damages vulnerable neurons and border zones, not axons in a shear distribution.
whyNot.E: Demyelination does not develop within 2 days and does not produce axonal swellings.

items.objective: Recognise diffuse axonal injury and its mechanism and histology.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after his wife saw him suddenly drop his coffee cup and start speaking nonsense. She says he was normal 1 hour 40 minutes ago. He has hypertension and takes amlodipine. Blood pressure is 176/98 mm Hg, pulse is 92/min and irregular, and fingerstick glucose is 128 mg/dL. He has fluent but meaningless speech, does not follow commands, and has a right facial droop and right arm drift. Noncontrast head CT shows no hemorrhage and no established infarct. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Lower blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg before any other treatment

options.label: E
options.html: MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging before deciding on treatment

items.explanationHtml:
He has a disabling acute ischemic stroke (aphasia and weakness) within 4.5 hours of last known well, no hemorrhage on CT and a blood pressure below 185/110 mm Hg. He should receive intravenous thrombolysis (alteplase or tenecteplase) now. CT angiography for a large-vessel occlusion is done at the same visit but must not delay the thrombolytic.

Takeaway: a disabling ischemic stroke within 4.5 hours, with no hemorrhage and blood pressure below 185/110, gets IV thrombolysis without delay.

whyNot.A: Aspirin is for patients who are not receiving thrombolysis, and it is withheld for 24 hours after a thrombolytic.
whyNot.B: Heparin does not improve outcome in acute ischemic stroke and raises bleeding risk.
whyNot.C: Only a pressure above 185/110 mm Hg must be lowered before thrombolysis; aggressive lowering may harm the penumbra.
whyNot.E: MRI is not needed when CT has excluded hemorrhage within the window; it delays treatment.

items.objective: Give intravenous thrombolysis to an eligible patient with acute ischemic stroke inside 4.5 hours.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item receives intravenous tenecteplase. CT angiography performed immediately afterwards shows occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at its stem (M1 segment). His deficits are unchanged. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Stop the thrombolytic effect with cryoprecipitate

items.explanationHtml:
An occlusion of the middle cerebral stem is a large-vessel occlusion of the anterior circulation. Endovascular thrombectomy within 6 hours of last known well clearly improves functional outcome, and it is added to thrombolysis rather than replacing it. Transfer to a thrombectomy-capable centre should not wait to see whether the thrombolytic works.

Takeaway: large-vessel anterior-circulation occlusion means thrombectomy, even after IV thrombolysis.

whyNot.A: Cryoprecipitate is used to reverse a thrombolytic only if a symptomatic hemorrhage occurs.
whyNot.B: Anticoagulation in the first 24 hours after thrombolysis increases hemorrhage and does not open the vessel.
whyNot.D: The occlusion is intracranial; endarterectomy treats symptomatic extracranial carotid stenosis and is not an emergency reperfusion therapy.
whyNot.E: Waiting forfeits salvageable brain; the time-dependent benefit of thrombectomy is large.

items.objective: Add endovascular thrombectomy for an anterior-circulation large-vessel occlusion.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous items has the clot removed, and his aphasia improves. Follow-up MRI at 24 hours shows a moderate left middle cerebral infarct with no hemorrhage. Telemetry confirms persistent atrial fibrillation. His creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL (0.6–1.2 mg/dL) and he has no history of valve disease. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term antithrombotic plan?

options.label: A
options.html: Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, then aspirin alone

options.label: B
options.html: Warfarin with a target INR of 2.0–3.0, as warfarin is preferred after stroke

options.label: C
options.html: Left atrial appendage occlusion instead of drug therapy

options.label: D
options.html: A direct oral anticoagulant such as apixaban, started within days

options.label: E
options.html: No antithrombotic therapy for 3 months, then reassessment

items.explanationHtml:
A cardioembolic stroke from nonvalvular atrial fibrillation calls for long-term oral anticoagulation. A direct oral anticoagulant is preferred over warfarin: it is at least as effective with less intracranial hemorrhage. Starting it within days of a small-to-moderate infarct is reasonable once hemorrhage has been excluded.

Takeaway: stroke with nonvalvular atrial fibrillation: a direct oral anticoagulant, started within days.

whyNot.A: Dual antiplatelet therapy is for minor noncardioembolic stroke or high-risk TIA; it is inferior to anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation.
whyNot.B: Warfarin is reserved for mechanical valves or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis; otherwise direct oral anticoagulants are preferred.
whyNot.C: Left atrial appendage occlusion is an option only when long-term anticoagulation cannot be taken.
whyNot.E: The early risk of recurrent embolism is substantial; delaying for months is not appropriate after a moderate infarct.

items.objective: Choose a direct oral anticoagulant for secondary prevention after cardioembolic stroke in nonvalvular atrial fibrillation.

items.stemHtml:
A 64-year-old woman comes to the emergency department 5 hours after a 25-minute episode of right hand and arm weakness with slurred speech, now fully resolved. She has type 2 diabetes. Findings are shown below.

AssessmentResult
Blood pressure152/90 mm Hg
Neurological examinationNormal
ECG and 12 hours of telemetrySinus rhythm
MRI brain with diffusion-weighted imagingNo acute infarct
CT angiography head and neckLeft internal carotid stenosis about 30%; intracranial vessels normal
Hemoglobin A1c7.8% (below 5.7%)
LDL cholesterol142 mg/dL [3.7 mmol/L] (below 130 mg/dL)

In addition to a high-intensity statin, which of the following is the most appropriate antithrombotic therapy?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a high-risk TIA: age 60 or over, blood pressure 140/90 or higher, unilateral weakness, duration of at least 10 minutes and diabetes. With no cardioembolic source, short-term dual antiplatelet therapy (aspirin plus clopidogrel) started within 24 hours lowers the early risk of stroke more than aspirin alone. It is stopped after about 3 weeks because longer use mainly adds bleeding.

Takeaway: high-risk TIA or minor stroke without a cardiac source: aspirin plus clopidogrel for about 3 weeks, then one antiplatelet drug.

whyNot.A: Aspirin alone is less effective in the high-risk early period after a TIA.
whyNot.C: Anticoagulation is for a cardioembolic source such as atrial fibrillation, which telemetry did not show.
whyNot.D: Indefinite dual antiplatelet therapy increases major bleeding without extra long-term benefit.
whyNot.E: Endarterectomy is for symptomatic stenosis of 70–99% (sometimes 50–69%); 30% stenosis is managed medically.

items.objective: Use short-term dual antiplatelet therapy after a high-risk TIA without a cardioembolic source.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man has two episodes in 1 week of painless loss of vision in his right eye, "like a curtain coming down," each lasting 3 minutes. He has hypertension and smokes. Examination is normal. Carotid duplex ultrasound, confirmed by CT angiography, shows an 80% stenosis of the right internal carotid artery and a 40% stenosis on the left. He is started on aspirin and a high-intensity statin. Which of the following is the most appropriate additional management?
items.explanationHtml:
Transient monocular blindness (amaurosis fugax) is a TIA in the territory of the right internal carotid, which supplies the ophthalmic artery. A symptomatic stenosis of 70–99% should be treated with carotid endarterectomy, ideally within 2 weeks, when the risk of stroke is highest and the benefit greatest.

Takeaway: symptomatic carotid stenosis of 70–99% means early endarterectomy, together with best medical therapy.

whyNot.B: The left stenosis is asymptomatic and below 50%; surgery there is not indicated.
whyNot.C: Surveillance alone leaves him at high early risk of a disabling stroke.
whyNot.D: Anticoagulation does not reduce stroke risk from carotid atherosclerosis better than antiplatelet therapy and adds bleeding.
whyNot.E: The left side is asymptomatic and only 40% narrowed.

items.objective: Refer symptomatic 70–99% carotid stenosis for early carotid endarterectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman who takes warfarin for a prior deep venous thrombosis develops sudden left-sided weakness and headache. Blood pressure is 168/94 mm Hg. CT shows a 25-mL right thalamic hemorrhage without intraventricular extension. INR is 3.4 (0.8–1.1). Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment to reverse her anticoagulation?

options.label: A
options.html: Fresh frozen plasma plus oral vitamin K

options.label: B
options.html: Oral vitamin K alone, repeated daily

options.label: C
options.html: Protamine sulfate plus IV vitamin K

options.label: D
options.html: Prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K

items.explanationHtml:
Warfarin-associated intracerebral hemorrhage tends to expand, so reversal must be fast. Four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate replaces factors II, VII, IX and X within minutes in a small volume. Intravenous vitamin K is given at the same time because the concentrate's effect wears off before the liver can make new factors. Systolic pressure should be lowered toward about 140 mm Hg.

Takeaway: warfarin-related brain hemorrhage: four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate plus IV vitamin K.

whyNot.A: Plasma corrects the INR slowly and needs large volumes; it is a fallback when prothrombin complex concentrate is unavailable.
whyNot.B: Oral vitamin K takes many hours to work and is too slow alone.
whyNot.C: Protamine reverses unfractionated heparin (and partly low-molecular-weight heparin), not warfarin.
whyNot.E: Idarucizumab is a specific antidote for dabigatran, which she does not take.

items.objective: Reverse warfarin in intracerebral hemorrhage with four-factor prothrombin complex concentrate and IV vitamin K.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman comes to the emergency department because of a severe headache that started suddenly 10 hours ago while she was at the gym and peaked within seconds. She vomited twice. She has no history of headaches. Temperature is 37.1 °C (98.8 °F) and blood pressure is 148/88 mm Hg. She has mild neck stiffness; the neurological examination is otherwise normal. Noncontrast CT of the head is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Discharge with a triptan and outpatient follow-up

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
A thunderclap headache is subarachnoid hemorrhage until proven otherwise. CT is highly sensitive in the first 6 hours but becomes less so afterwards. At 10 hours a normal CT does not exclude bleeding, so a lumbar puncture is needed to look for xanthochromia and red cells that do not clear between tubes. (CT angiography is an accepted alternative in some centres.)

Takeaway: thunderclap headache with a normal CT after 6 hours: do a lumbar puncture.

whyNot.A: Triptans are for migraine; they are contraindicated until a vascular cause is excluded, and discharge risks a fatal rebleed.
whyNot.B: Waiting a week risks a rebleed and delays securing an aneurysm.
whyNot.D: She is afebrile with an abrupt onset; meningitis is unlikely, and the hemorrhage question remains unanswered.
whyNot.E: Repeating CT later lowers sensitivity further; it does not replace CSF analysis.

items.objective: Perform lumbar puncture after a normal CT in suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage presenting after 6 hours.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old man has a sudden severe headache and is found to have a subarachnoid hemorrhage on CT. CT angiography shows a 6-mm anterior communicating artery aneurysm, which is coiled the next morning. He is alert with no focal deficit. Blood pressure is 138/82 mm Hg. Which of the following drugs, started now, improves his neurological outcome?
items.explanationHtml:
Oral nimodipine, a calcium channel blocker, given for 21 days after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, reduces delayed cerebral ischemia and improves outcome. Its benefit does not come from reversing large-vessel vasospasm on angiography and may reflect neuroprotection or effects on small vessels.

Takeaway: every patient with aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage gets oral nimodipine for 21 days.

whyNot.B: Nicardipine controls blood pressure before the aneurysm is secured but has not been shown to improve outcome in the way nimodipine does.
whyNot.C: Glucocorticoids do not improve outcome after subarachnoid hemorrhage.
whyNot.D: Prolonged antifibrinolytic therapy reduces rebleeding but increases ischemic complications without improving outcome; the aneurysm is already secured.
whyNot.E: Fludrocortisone may be used for hyponatremia from salt wasting but is not a routine outcome-improving therapy.

items.objective: Give oral nimodipine after aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage to reduce delayed cerebral ischemia.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman, 2 weeks after delivering her second child, has had a worsening headache for 4 days and a generalised seizure this morning. She is drowsy but follows commands and has mild right arm weakness. There is bilateral papilledema. CT shows a small left parietal hemorrhage. MR venography shows thrombosis of the superior sagittal sinus and left transverse sinus. Platelets are 240,000/mm³ (150,000–400,000/mm³). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: A
options.html: Withhold anticoagulation because of the hemorrhage

items.explanationHtml:
She has cerebral venous thrombosis, with the postpartum state as the risk factor. The hemorrhage is a venous infarct caused by the blocked outflow. Anticoagulation with heparin (low-molecular-weight or unfractionated) is the treatment even when there is hemorrhage: it stops the clot propagating and allows recanalisation. An antiseizure drug is also indicated after a seizure, and oral anticoagulation continues for months.

Takeaway: cerebral venous thrombosis is anticoagulated with heparin even if there is a hemorrhagic venous infarct.

whyNot.A: Withholding anticoagulation allows the thrombus to propagate; the hemorrhage results from venous congestion, not from an arterial bleed.
whyNot.B: Aspirin is not adequate treatment for venous sinus thrombosis.
whyNot.C: Systemic thrombolysis is not first-line; endovascular therapy is considered only if the patient worsens despite anticoagulation.
whyNot.D: Acetazolamide may lower intracranial pressure but does not treat the thrombosis.

items.objective: Anticoagulate cerebral venous thrombosis even in the presence of hemorrhagic venous infarction.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man has had left-sided neck and face pain for 3 days since a chiropractic neck manipulation. This morning his right hand became clumsy for 20 minutes. His left eyelid droops slightly and the left pupil is smaller than the right, with normal sweating. Strength is now normal. CT angiography shows a tapered narrowing of the left internal carotid artery starting 2 cm above the bifurcation, consistent with dissection; MRI shows no infarct. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
A painful partial Horner syndrome (ptosis and miosis with sweating preserved, because facial sweat fibres travel with the external carotid) plus a TIA in the same carotid territory indicates an internal carotid dissection. Emboli from the intimal flap cause most strokes, so antithrombotic therapy is given; antiplatelet and anticoagulant drugs have similar efficacy, and antiplatelet therapy is a standard choice.

Takeaway: cervical artery dissection: antithrombotic therapy; stenting only for failure of medical treatment.

whyNot.A: Stenting is reserved for recurrent ischemia despite medical therapy or for critical hemodynamic compromise.
whyNot.B: Glucocorticoids have no role in arterial dissection.
whyNot.C: The risk of embolic stroke is highest early after dissection, so antithrombotic therapy is needed.
whyNot.D: Endarterectomy is a treatment for atherosclerotic stenosis at the bifurcation, not for a dissection above it.

items.objective: Treat cervical artery dissection with antithrombotic therapy.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man with type 1 diabetes is found unresponsive in bed by his wife. He uses insulin glargine and insulin lispro and does not drink alcohol. He is breathing regularly at 16/min, with blood pressure 142/84 mm Hg and pulse 104/min. He is sweaty and moves all four limbs to pain; pupils are 4 mm and reactive. Fingerstick glucose is 32 mg/dL. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Severe hypoglycemia explains his coma, sweating and tachycardia. Treat it at once with intravenous dextrose (or glucagon if there is no intravenous access). Recheck glucose and monitor, because long-acting insulin can cause recurrent hypoglycemia. Imaging is needed only if he does not wake after glucose is corrected or has focal signs.

Takeaway: check the fingerstick glucose in every comatose patient and give dextrose for hypoglycemia before anything else.

whyNot.A: CT is needed only if he does not recover after glucose correction or has focal signs.
whyNot.C: Naloxone is for suspected opioid toxicity, with small pupils and slow breathing, which he does not have.
whyNot.D: EEG is for unexplained coma or suspected nonconvulsive status epilepticus, not when a reversible cause is obvious.
whyNot.E: He has no fever or meningism; the low glucose explains the coma.

items.objective: Treat hypoglycemic coma immediately with intravenous dextrose.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after friends found him unresponsive at a party. Respirations are 5/min and shallow; oxygen saturation is 84% on room air. Pulse is 58/min and blood pressure 104/62 mm Hg. His pupils are 1 mm. Fingerstick glucose is 96 mg/dL. Bag-mask ventilation is started. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Coma with respiratory depression and pinpoint pupils is the opioid toxidrome. Support breathing and give naloxone, an opioid receptor antagonist, titrated to adequate breathing rather than full arousal. Observe him, because naloxone wears off sooner than many opioids, especially long-acting and high-potency synthetic ones.

Takeaway: coma, slow breathing and pinpoint pupils: ventilate and give naloxone.

whyNot.A: Flumazenil reverses benzodiazepines but can precipitate seizures, especially in mixed overdoses; it is not the antidote for this picture.
whyNot.B: Physostigmine reverses anticholinergic toxicity, which causes dilated pupils, fever and agitation.
whyNot.D: Thiamine is given with glucose in suspected Wernicke encephalopathy, not for opioid toxicity.
whyNot.E: Oral charcoal in an unprotected airway risks aspiration and does not treat the respiratory depression.

items.objective: Recognise the opioid toxidrome and treat with naloxone.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man is resuscitated from an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest due to ventricular fibrillation; return of spontaneous circulation took 22 minutes. He remains comatose on a ventilator, with sedation stopped this morning. Temperature control is in place to prevent fever. On day 2 after the arrest, his pupils react to light, and he extends his arms to painful stimuli. His family asks whether he will wake up. Which of the following is the most appropriate response?

options.label: A
options.html: Advise withdrawal of life support because the motor response predicts a poor outcome

options.label: B
options.html: Order serum neuron-specific enolase and base the prognosis on that result

options.label: C
options.html: Explain that prognosis cannot be judged reliably yet and will be assessed at 72 hours or later using several tests

options.label: D
options.html: Arrange an apnea test to determine death by neurologic criteria

options.label: E
options.html: Tell the family that full recovery is likely because the pupils react

items.explanationHtml:
Early after cardiac arrest, sedatives, temperature management and evolving injury make the examination unreliable. Guidelines advise waiting at least about 72 hours after the arrest (and after sedation has cleared) and using a combination of findings (pupillary and corneal reflexes, motor response, EEG, somatosensory evoked potentials, neuron-specific enolase and MRI) before predicting a poor outcome. Telling the family this honestly avoids self-fulfilling withdrawal of care.

Takeaway: neurological prognosis after cardiac arrest is multimodal and is not made before about 72 hours.

whyNot.A: Extensor posturing on day 2 is not reliable enough on its own to predict a poor outcome.
whyNot.B: No single biomarker determines prognosis; neuron-specific enolase is one part of a multimodal assessment.
whyNot.D: Reactive pupils and motor responses show brainstem function, so he does not meet criteria for brain death.
whyNot.E: Reactive pupils are necessary for a good outcome but do not predict full recovery.

items.objective: Defer and use multimodal assessment for neurological prognosis after cardiac arrest.

items.stemHtml: A 46-year-old woman had a massive intracerebral hemorrhage 2 days ago. She has received no sedatives for 36 hours. She is unresponsive to all stimuli, with fixed pupils and absent corneal, gag and cough reflexes. Core temperature is 34.6 °C (94.3 °F), blood pressure is 118/70 mm Hg on norepinephrine, and serum sodium is 142 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L). The team plans to evaluate her for death by neurologic criteria. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Obtain a nuclear cerebral blood flow study in place of the examination

options.label: C
options.html: Warm her to a core temperature of at least 36 °C before the evaluation

options.label: D
options.html: Wait 7 days and repeat the examination

options.label: E
options.html: Obtain written consent from the family before the evaluation

items.explanationHtml:
Before brain death can be determined, confounders must be corrected. Hypothermia suppresses brainstem reflexes and lowers carbon dioxide production, so the current consensus requires a core temperature of at least 36 °C before the examination and apnea test. Her other prerequisites (no sedatives, adequate blood pressure, normal sodium) are met.

Takeaway: correct hypothermia and other confounders before determining death by neurologic criteria.

whyNot.A: Testing while hypothermic can give a falsely positive result and does not meet the prerequisites.
whyNot.B: Ancillary blood-flow tests are used when the examination or apnea test cannot be completed, not to bypass a correctable confounder.
whyNot.D: A fixed 7-day wait is not required once the prerequisites are met.
whyNot.E: Determining death is a medical decision; consent is not required, although the family must be informed.

items.objective: Correct hypothermia before an evaluation for death by neurologic criteria.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man with a fatal traumatic brain injury is evaluated for death by neurologic criteria. All prerequisites are met: core temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), blood pressure is adequate and no sedatives have been given for 48 hours. He has no response to pain in the face or limbs, fixed pupils, and absent corneal, oculocephalic, cold caloric, gag and cough reflexes. When the nail bed of his right great toe is pressed, the right hip, knee and ankle flex. During the apnea test arterial PCO2 rises from 40 to 66 mm Hg and pH falls to 7.20, with no breathing movements. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.label: A
options.html: He meets the criteria for death by neurologic criteria

options.label: B
options.html: An ancillary blood-flow study is required because of the leg movement

options.label: C
options.html: The apnea test is invalid because PCO<sub>2</sub> did not reach 70 mm Hg

options.label: D
options.html: The examination must be repeated after 24 hours before any conclusion

options.label: E
options.html: Death cannot be declared until the family agrees

items.explanationHtml:
The examination shows coma, absent brainstem reflexes and apnea with PCO2 at least 60 mm Hg and at least 20 mm Hg above baseline. The leg flexion to toe pressure is a spinal reflex (triple flexion), mediated below the brain, and is compatible with brain death. He meets the criteria, and the time of death is the time the evaluation is completed.

Takeaway: spinal reflexes such as triple flexion are compatible with brain death; they do not mandate an ancillary test.

whyNot.B: Ancillary tests are needed only when part of the examination or apnea test cannot be completed or interpreted; a spinal reflex does not invalidate the examination.
whyNot.C: The threshold is a PCO<sub>2</sub> of at least 60 mm Hg and a rise of at least 20 mm Hg; both are met.
whyNot.D: When the prerequisites are met and the evaluation is complete, a fixed 24-hour repeat is not required in adults.
whyNot.E: Determining death does not require family consent, though the team must communicate with them sensitively.

items.objective: Interpret a complete brain death evaluation and recognise spinal reflexes as compatible with it.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman is admitted with vertigo and slurred speech that progressed over 6 hours. Now she does not move her limbs or face and makes no sounds; the nurse documents her as "unresponsive." Her eyes are open. When asked to look up she does so, and she blinks once for yes and twice for no, answering questions about her family correctly. Horizontal eye movements are absent. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
She is aware and communicates by vertical eye movements and blinking, with loss of horizontal gaze, limb, face and speech movement: the locked-in syndrome from a ventral pontine infarct, usually a basilar artery occlusion. She needs emergency vascular imaging for possible thrombectomy, and staff must speak to her as a fully aware person.

Takeaway: always test vertical eye movement and blinking to command before calling a patient unresponsive.

whyNot.A: In akinetic mutism (medial frontal or diencephalic lesions) patients are awake but show little drive; they do not have absent horizontal gaze with selective vertical eye signalling.
whyNot.C: Unresponsive wakefulness means no awareness; she answers questions correctly.
whyNot.D: Psychogenic unresponsiveness does not cause loss of horizontal gaze and is a diagnosis made only after organic causes are excluded.
whyNot.E: Nonconvulsive status impairs awareness; she is fully aware.

items.objective: Recognise locked-in syndrome from a basilar occlusion in a patient labelled unresponsive.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man remains comatose 3 days after a cardiac arrest. Sedation was stopped 48 hours ago. With the head of the bed at 30°, 50 mL of ice water is instilled into his right ear canal. Both eyes slowly and steadily move toward the right and stay there for about a minute, with no rapid corrective movements. Which of the following best interprets this finding?

options.label: A
options.html: The brainstem vestibulo-ocular pathways are intact and the cerebral hemispheres are dysfunctional

options.label: B
options.html: The findings meet a criterion for death by neurologic criteria

options.label: C
options.html: The patient is awake and feigning unresponsiveness

options.label: D
options.html: There is a lesion of the right medial longitudinal fasciculus

options.label: E
options.html: There is destruction of the right vestibular nerve

items.explanationHtml:
Cold water in one ear reduces firing of that side's vestibular afferents, which drives a slow (tonic) movement of both eyes toward the cold ear through intact brainstem pathways. In an awake person the cortex generates a corrective fast phase away from the cold ear (nystagmus). Tonic deviation without a fast phase therefore means the brainstem works but the hemispheres do not, as in coma from diffuse hypoxic injury.

Takeaway: cold calorics in coma: tonic deviation toward the cold ear means an intact brainstem; no movement means brainstem loss.

whyNot.B: Brain death requires no eye movement at all on caloric testing.
whyNot.C: An awake patient would show nystagmus with a fast phase away from the cold ear.
whyNot.D: A right medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion would stop the right eye from adducting, so the eyes would not move together.
whyNot.E: A destroyed right vestibular nerve would produce no response to cold water in the right ear.

items.objective: Interpret the cold caloric response in a comatose patient.

items.stemHtml: A 21-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after being struck in the left temple during a fight. He was briefly unconscious, then talked to the paramedics. Over the next hour he became drowsy. His Glasgow Coma Scale score is now 9, and his left pupil is larger than the right. CT shows a 40-mL biconvex hyperdense collection over the left temporal lobe with 7 mm of midline shift. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Burr-hole drainage at the bedside after 24 hours of observation

options.label: D
options.html: Mannitol alone with a repeat CT in 6 hours

items.explanationHtml:
A large epidural hematoma with midline shift, a falling coma score and a dilated pupil is a surgical emergency. Arterial bleeding expands rapidly, and outcome depends on the time to craniotomy and evacuation. Hyperosmolar therapy and head elevation can be used briefly while the operating room is prepared, but they do not replace surgery.

Takeaway: a symptomatic epidural hematoma with mass effect needs immediate craniotomy.

whyNot.B: Delay is dangerous with an expanding arterial hematoma; burr-hole drainage is used for liquefied chronic subdural collections.
whyNot.C: Lumbar puncture with a supratentorial mass lesion can precipitate fatal herniation.
whyNot.D: Mannitol is only a temporising measure; waiting 6 hours risks herniation and death.
whyNot.E: Glucocorticoids do not help and are harmful in traumatic brain injury.

items.objective: Treat an epidural hematoma with mass effect by emergency craniotomy.

items.stemHtml: A 79-year-old man has had 3 weeks of worsening headache, slowed thinking and two falls. He takes aspirin for coronary disease. He is oriented to person only and has a mild right pronator drift. CT shows a 22-mm crescentic, low-density collection over the left convexity, with 6 mm of midline shift. Platelet count and INR are normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Start haloperidol for delirium and observe

options.label: C
options.html: Start therapeutic anticoagulation for possible venous thrombosis

items.explanationHtml:
A chronic subdural hematoma (crescentic, hypodense, weeks of decline after possible minor trauma) that causes symptoms and midline shift should be drained surgically, usually through burr holes, because the blood has liquefied. Aspirin should be held around surgery. Small collections without symptoms can be observed.

Takeaway: a symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma with mass effect is drained, usually through burr holes.

whyNot.A: His confusion has a structural cause; sedating antipsychotics do not treat it and may worsen falls.
whyNot.B: Lumbar puncture is dangerous with midline shift and adds nothing.
whyNot.C: Anticoagulation would enlarge the hematoma; nothing suggests venous thrombosis.
whyNot.E: Waiting is appropriate only for small collections without symptoms.

items.objective: Drain a symptomatic chronic subdural hematoma with mass effect.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old woman slips on ice and hits the back of her head. She did not lose consciousness and has a mild headache. She takes apixaban for atrial fibrillation. Glasgow Coma Scale score is 15, and the neurological examination is normal. She has a small occipital scalp bruise. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the brain within 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: Give andexanet alfa and then discharge

items.explanationHtml:
Anticoagulation greatly raises the risk of intracranial bleeding after even a minor head injury, and the examination can be normal at first. Patients taking anticoagulants need a noncontrast head CT, and her age is a further risk factor. Reversal is only for confirmed bleeding.

Takeaway: an anticoagulated patient with a head injury needs a head CT even with a normal examination.

whyNot.A: Discharge without imaging is unsafe in an older anticoagulated patient.
whyNot.B: Skull radiographs do not show intracranial bleeding and are not used to triage head injury.
whyNot.D: MRI is slower and less available in the emergency setting; CT is the test for acute hemorrhage.
whyNot.E: Reversal is given only when significant bleeding is found; giving it without a diagnosis exposes her to thrombosis.

items.objective: Image the head with CT after minor head trauma in an anticoagulated patient.

items.stemHtml: A 16-year-old soccer player collides heads with an opponent. He did not lose consciousness but seemed dazed for a few minutes, had a headache and asked the same question twice. On the sideline 20 minutes later he says he feels fine. His neurological examination is normal. His coach asks whether he can go back into the game. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: A
options.html: He may return to the game now because his symptoms have resolved

options.label: B
options.html: He should not return to play today and should follow a graded return-to-sport plan

options.label: C
options.html: He needs noncontrast CT of the head before any decision

options.label: D
options.html: He should stay in bed in a dark room for 2 weeks

options.label: E
options.html: He may return after 1 hour if a repeat examination is normal

items.explanationHtml:
He had a concussion: confusion and repetitive questioning after a head impact, even without loss of consciousness. An athlete with a suspected concussion is removed from play and does not return the same day. After a short period of relative rest he resumes light activity and school, then follows a stepwise return to sport once he is symptom-free, with medical clearance before contact.

Takeaway: no same-day return to play after a concussion; return is graded and stepwise.

whyNot.A: Symptoms can return or worsen later, and a second impact before recovery can cause severe harm.
whyNot.C: CT is needed only for red flags such as focal deficits, worsening headache, repeated vomiting or falling consciousness.
whyNot.D: Prolonged strict rest does not speed recovery and can prolong symptoms.
whyNot.E: Same-day return is not allowed regardless of how quickly symptoms resolve.

items.objective: Manage sport-related concussion with removal from play and a graded return.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old man with a severe traumatic brain injury from a motorcycle crash is intubated in the intensive care unit. CT shows diffuse swelling without a surgical lesion. An external ventricular drain is in place. Despite the head of the bed at 30°, adequate sedation and analgesia, and normal temperature, ICP is 28 mm Hg. Mean arterial pressure is 86 mm Hg, PaCO2 is 38 mm Hg and serum sodium is 140 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Sustained hyperventilation to a PaCO<sub>2</sub> of 25 mm Hg

options.label: C
options.html: Lower the mean arterial pressure to 65 mm Hg

options.label: D
options.html: Drain CSF and give a bolus of hypertonic saline

items.explanationHtml:
ICP above about 22 mm Hg despite first-tier measures is treated by draining CSF through the ventricular drain and giving hyperosmolar therapy (hypertonic saline or mannitol), which draws water out of brain tissue. Mean arterial pressure must be kept up to maintain perfusion pressure. Refractory cases may need decompressive craniectomy or barbiturates.

Takeaway: first-line treatment of raised ICP after the basics: CSF drainage and hyperosmolar therapy.

whyNot.A: Glucocorticoids increase mortality in traumatic brain injury.
whyNot.B: Prolonged deep hyperventilation causes cerebral vasoconstriction and ischemia; it is only a short bridge for herniation.
whyNot.C: Lowering blood pressure would reduce cerebral perfusion pressure (86 − 28 = 58 mm Hg already) and risk ischemia.
whyNot.E: Prophylactic hypothermia has not improved outcome in traumatic brain injury; normothermia is the goal.

items.objective: Escalate raised ICP treatment with CSF drainage and hyperosmolar therapy in traumatic brain injury.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old woman has had daily headaches for 3 months, worse in the morning, with a whooshing noise in her ears in time with her pulse. Several times a day her vision greys out for a few seconds when she stands up. She has gained 12 kg in the past year; BMI is 38 kg/m². Blood pressure is 124/78 mm Hg. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling. Her left eye does not abduct fully. The rest of the examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain with MR venography

items.explanationHtml:
Headache, pulsatile tinnitus, transient visual obscurations, papilledema and an abducens palsy indicate raised intracranial pressure. Idiopathic intracranial hypertension is likely in a young woman with obesity and recent weight gain, but a mass, hydrocephalus and venous sinus thrombosis must first be excluded with MRI and MR venography. Imaging also confirms that a lumbar puncture is safe.

Takeaway: papilledema needs brain imaging with venography before a lumbar puncture.

whyNot.A: Lumbar puncture comes after imaging has excluded a mass lesion or venous thrombosis.
whyNot.C: Acetazolamide is the treatment once the diagnosis is confirmed; starting it now skips essential exclusions.
whyNot.D: Triptans treat migraine and do not address papilledema or raised pressure.
whyNot.E: EEG has no role in the evaluation of papilledema.

items.objective: Image with MRI and MR venography before lumbar puncture in suspected idiopathic intracranial hypertension.

items.stemHtml: The patient in the previous item has normal MRI and MR venography apart from an empty sella and flattened posterior globes. Lumbar puncture in the lateral decubitus position shows an opening pressure of 360 mm H2O (normal 70–180 mm H2O), with normal cell count, protein and glucose. Formal visual field testing shows mild enlargement of both blind spots. Visual acuity is 20/20 in both eyes. In addition to a weight-loss program, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
The diagnosis is idiopathic intracranial hypertension: raised opening pressure with normal CSF composition and imaging. With mild visual involvement, first-line treatment is weight loss plus acetazolamide, with regular visual field monitoring. Surgery (optic nerve sheath fenestration, CSF shunting or venous sinus stenting) is reserved for severe or progressive visual loss.

Takeaway: idiopathic intracranial hypertension with mild visual change: weight loss plus acetazolamide and visual field monitoring.

whyNot.B: Glucocorticoids cause weight gain and rebound and are not a standard treatment.
whyNot.C: Shunting is for severe, rapidly progressive visual loss or failure of medical therapy.
whyNot.D: Serial lumbar punctures give only brief relief and are not a sustainable treatment.
whyNot.E: Propranolol may help migraine but does not lower intracranial pressure.

items.objective: Start weight loss and acetazolamide in idiopathic intracranial hypertension with mild visual involvement.

items.stemHtml: A 76-year-old man has had increasing difficulty walking for 1 year: his steps are short and his feet seem stuck to the floor. For 6 months he has had urinary urgency with occasional incontinence, and his wife says he is slower to answer questions. Strength, sensation and reflexes are normal; there is no tremor or rigidity. CT shows enlarged lateral and third ventricles out of proportion to the cortical sulci. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
A gait disorder, urinary incontinence and cognitive slowing with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy suggest normal pressure hydrocephalus. A high-volume lumbar puncture (tap test) or temporary lumbar drain with a timed gait assessment before and after predicts who will benefit from a ventriculoperitoneal shunt, the definitive treatment.

Takeaway: suspected normal pressure hydrocephalus: tap test first, then shunt the responders.

whyNot.A: Cholinesterase inhibitors are for Alzheimer and Lewy body dementias; the gait disorder points to normal pressure hydrocephalus.
whyNot.B: There is no tremor or rigidity; levodopa is not expected to help this gait pattern.
whyNot.D: A shunt carries risks (infection, overdrainage and subdural hematoma), so responders are first identified with a tap test.
whyNot.E: Lumbar stenosis causes leg pain with walking, not urinary incontinence with cognitive slowing and ventriculomegaly.

items.objective: Use a high-volume lumbar puncture to select patients with normal pressure hydrocephalus for shunting.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man was admitted 6 hours ago with an acute right-sided subdural hematoma, 9 mm thick, and was being observed. He is now hard to rouse. Blood pressure is 196/104 mm Hg (previously 142/80), pulse is 48/min and respirations are irregular. The right pupil is 7 mm and unreactive. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Intravenous labetalol to bring the blood pressure below 140/90 mm Hg

options.label: C
options.html: Hyperosmolar therapy, head elevation and emergency surgical evacuation

options.label: D
options.html: Lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure

items.explanationHtml:
Hypertension, bradycardia and irregular breathing (the Cushing reflex) with a new fixed dilated pupil mean uncal herniation from the expanding hematoma. Protect the airway, elevate the head, give hypertonic saline or mannitol, use brief hyperventilation if needed, and take him for emergency evacuation.

Takeaway: Cushing reflex with a blown pupil means herniation: osmotherapy and emergency decompression, not antihypertensives.

whyNot.A: The hypertension is a compensatory response that maintains cerebral perfusion; lowering it causes ischemia.
whyNot.B: The bradycardia is a brainstem reflex to raised pressure; atropine does not treat the cause.
whyNot.D: Lumbar puncture with a supratentorial mass and herniation can be fatal.
whyNot.E: Nimodipine is for aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage, not for herniation from a hematoma.

items.objective: Recognise the Cushing reflex and uncal herniation, and treat with osmotherapy and emergency surgery.

items.stemHtml:
A 34-year-old woman is in the intensive care unit 3 days after a severe traumatic brain injury with a basal skull fracture. Over the past 8 hours her urine output has been 400–500 mL/h. She receives maintenance intravenous fluids only and no diuretics or mannitol. Laboratory results are shown below.

TestResultReference range
Serum sodium154 mEq/L136–145 mEq/L
Serum glucose118 mg/dL70–100 mg/dL (fasting)
Serum osmolality318 mOsm/kg275–295 mOsm/kg
Urine osmolality110 mOsm/kg–
Urine specific gravity1.0021.003–1.030

Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Large volumes of dilute urine with a rising serum sodium and osmolality, without an osmotic agent or hyperglycemia, indicate central diabetes insipidus: the injury has damaged the hypothalamus or pituitary stalk and cut off vasopressin release. Treat with desmopressin and replace the free-water deficit, monitoring sodium closely so it falls gradually.

Takeaway: polyuria with dilute urine and hypernatremia after brain injury is central diabetes insipidus; give desmopressin.

whyNot.A: Fluid restriction would worsen the hypernatremia in a patient losing free water.
whyNot.B: Thiazides are used in nephrogenic diabetes insipidus; this is central and responds to desmopressin.
whyNot.C: Hypertonic saline would raise an already high sodium.
whyNot.E: Furosemide adds to water and salt loss and does not correct the vasopressin deficiency.

items.objective: Diagnose and treat central diabetes insipidus after traumatic brain injury.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man has an MRI of the cervical spine after a fall. It shows a small, sharply bounded contusion confined to the region labelled A in the figure, at the C4 level. Which of the following deficits is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Loss of vibration and joint position sense in the right arm

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of vibration and joint position sense in the left arm

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of pain and temperature sensation in the left leg

options.label: D
options.html: Spastic weakness of the right arm and leg

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of vibration and joint position sense in the right leg only

items.explanationHtml:
Site A is the right fasciculus cuneatus, the lateral part of the dorsal column. It carries vibration, position sense and fine touch from the upper limb and upper trunk on the same side; the fibres do not cross until the medulla. At C4 every arm fibre has already entered the tract.

Takeaway: the cuneatus carries same-side arm proprioception; the gracilis carries the leg.

whyNot.B: Dorsal column fibres ascend uncrossed, so a right-sided lesion affects the right side.
whyNot.C: Pain and temperature travel in the spinothalamic tract (site C), not in the dorsal columns.
whyNot.D: Spastic weakness needs damage to the lateral corticospinal tract (site B).
whyNot.E: Leg fibres run in the more medial fasciculus gracilis, which is not part of site A.

items.objective: Predict the deficit from a lesion of the fasciculus cuneatus.

items.stemHtml: Refer to the figure. A small tumour at the C6 level destroys only the region labelled C. Which of the following is the most likely sensory finding?

options.label: A
options.html: Loss of pain and temperature on the right side below C6

options.label: B
options.html: Loss of pain and temperature on the left side beginning one or two segments below the lesion

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of pain and temperature in a cape over both shoulders and arms

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of light touch and vibration on the left side below the lesion

options.label: E
options.html: Loss of all sensation on the right side at the C6 dermatome only

items.explanationHtml:
Site C is the right spinothalamic tract. Its second-order axons crossed in the anterior white commissure, so it carries pain and temperature from the left side of the body. Because fibres ascend one or two segments before crossing, the sensory level on the left sits a little below the lesion.

Takeaway: a spinothalamic lesion causes opposite-side pain and temperature loss starting slightly below the lesion.

whyNot.A: The tract carries fibres that have already crossed, so the deficit is on the opposite (left) side.
whyNot.C: A bilateral cape-like loss comes from the crossing fibres in the anterior white commissure (site D).
whyNot.D: Light touch and vibration are carried mainly by the dorsal columns, which are intact.
whyNot.E: Segmental loss at one level on the same side comes from the dorsal horn or root, not the ascending tract.

items.objective: Localise a lesion of the lateral spinothalamic tract and predict the side and level of sensory loss.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has painless burns on both hands from cooking. For a year she has had neck pain. Examination shows loss of pain and temperature sensation over both shoulders and the outer arms, with normal light touch, vibration and joint position sense. Strength is normal. MRI shows downward displacement of the cerebellar tonsils and a fluid-filled cavity in the cervical cord. Damage in which of the labelled regions of the figure best explains her sensory findings?
items.explanationHtml:
A syrinx expands from around the central canal and first interrupts the pain and temperature fibres crossing in the anterior white commissure (site D) at the affected segments. That gives bilateral, cape-like loss of pain and temperature with preserved dorsal column sensation (dissociated sensory loss). Chiari I malformation is the usual association.

Takeaway: dissociated, bilateral cape-like sensory loss localises to the anterior white commissure (syringomyelia).

whyNot.A: A dorsal column lesion would affect vibration and position sense, which are normal.
whyNot.B: A corticospinal lesion causes spastic weakness, not sensory loss.
whyNot.C: A one-sided spinothalamic lesion causes loss on the opposite side below the lesion, not a bilateral cape.
whyNot.E: The ventral horn is motor; its involvement would cause hand wasting and weakness, which she lacks.

items.objective: Recognise syringomyelia as a lesion of the anterior white commissure causing dissociated sensory loss.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old man is stabbed in the back on the right side. A week later, examination shows a spastic, weak right leg with an upgoing right plantar response. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Lost vibration sense in the left leg and lost pain sense in the right leg

options.label: B
options.html: Lost vibration sense and lost pain sense in both legs

options.label: C
options.html: Lost vibration sense in the right leg and lost pain sense in the left leg

options.label: D
options.html: Lost pain sense in the right leg with normal vibration sense in both legs

options.label: E
options.html: Lost vibration sense in both legs with normal pain sense in both legs

items.explanationHtml:
This is a cord hemisection (Brown-Séquard syndrome) on the right. The right lateral corticospinal tract and right dorsal column carry uncrossed signals, so the right leg is weak and has lost vibration and position sense. The right spinothalamic tract carries pain and temperature from the left side, which is therefore affected.

Takeaway: after a hemisection, weakness and proprioceptive loss are on the side of the lesion and pain loss on the other side.

whyNot.A: This reverses the sides of both sensory deficits.
whyNot.B: Bilateral loss of both modalities implies a complete cord lesion, not a one-sided one.
whyNot.D: Pain sensation is lost on the side opposite the lesion, and the right dorsal column is also cut.
whyNot.E: Spinothalamic fibres from the left side cross into the injured right half, so pain sense cannot be normal in both legs.

items.objective: Predict the deficits of a spinal cord hemisection.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man wakes after open repair of a thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm unable to move his legs. He cannot feel a pinprick or cold below the umbilicus and has urinary retention. Which of the following functions is most likely preserved in his legs?

options.label: E
options.html: Joint position sense in the toes

items.explanationHtml:
Interrupting the segmental feeders of the anterior spinal artery (for example, the great radicular artery) infarcts the anterior two-thirds of the cord: corticospinal tracts, spinothalamic tracts, ventral horns and descending autonomic pathways. The dorsal columns are supplied by the paired posterior spinal arteries, so vibration and position sense survive.

Takeaway: anterior spinal artery infarction spares the dorsal columns.

whyNot.A: Pinprick is carried by the spinothalamic tracts in the anterior cord, which are infarcted.
whyNot.B: Temperature also travels in the infarcted spinothalamic tracts.
whyNot.C: The lateral corticospinal tracts lie within the anterior spinal artery territory.
whyNot.D: Descending autonomic fibres that control the bladder are damaged, as his retention shows.

items.objective: Identify the functions spared by anterior spinal artery infarction.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old man has had tingling in his feet and hands and an unsteady gait for 2 months. He has inhaled nitrous oxide from whipped-cream chargers almost daily for a year. He sways and falls when he closes his eyes while standing. Vibration and joint position sense are lost in both feet. Knee reflexes are brisk, ankle reflexes are absent and both plantar responses are extensor. Serum vitamin B12 is within the reference range. Which of the following combinations of structures is most likely damaged?

options.label: A
options.html: Dorsal root ganglia and spinothalamic tracts only

options.label: B
options.html: Spinothalamic tracts and ventral horn cells

options.label: C
options.html: Ventral horn cells and lateral corticospinal tracts only

options.label: D
options.html: Dorsal columns, lateral corticospinal tracts and peripheral nerves

options.label: E
options.html: Spinocerebellar tracts and cerebellar vermis only

items.explanationHtml:
Nitrous oxide oxidises the cobalt of cobalamin and inactivates it, producing a functional B12 deficiency even when the measured serum level is normal (methylmalonic acid and homocysteine are high). The result is subacute combined degeneration: dorsal column loss (sensory ataxia, positive Romberg sign), lateral corticospinal tract damage (brisk knees, extensor plantars) and an accompanying neuropathy (absent ankle jerks).

Takeaway: subacute combined degeneration hits the dorsal columns, corticospinal tracts and peripheral nerves; nitrous oxide can cause it with a normal B12 level.

whyNot.A: The dominant deficits are proprioceptive; pain and temperature pathways are not the main target.
whyNot.B: Spinothalamic and ventral horn damage would cause pain and temperature loss and wasting, not sensory ataxia.
whyNot.C: This pattern (upper plus lower motor neuron) suggests motor neuron disease, which spares sensation.
whyNot.E: Cerebellar ataxia does not worsen markedly with eye closure and does not explain upgoing toes.

items.objective: Recognise the tract pattern of subacute combined degeneration and its link to nitrous oxide misuse.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old man has brief, stabbing pains in his legs and a wide-based gait that is worse in the dark. Both pupils are small and irregular; they constrict when he looks at a near object but not in response to light. Knee and ankle reflexes are absent, and the Romberg sign is positive. Damage to which of the following structures best explains his gait disorder?

options.label: A
options.html: Anterior horn cells of the lumbar cord

items.explanationHtml:
This is tabes dorsalis, a late form of neurosyphilis. Inflammation of the dorsal roots and the dorsal columns removes proprioceptive input, causing sensory ataxia with a positive Romberg sign, lost reflexes and lightning pains. The pupils that accommodate but do not react to light are Argyll Robertson pupils.

Takeaway: tabes dorsalis destroys the dorsal roots and columns: sensory ataxia, areflexia, lightning pains.

whyNot.A: Anterior horn disease causes weakness and wasting with fasciculations, not sensory ataxia.
whyNot.B: Corticospinal damage causes spasticity and brisk reflexes, the opposite of his findings.
whyNot.C: Cerebellar ataxia is not markedly worsened by eye closure and does not abolish reflexes.
whyNot.D: Spinothalamic damage removes pain and temperature, not position sense.

items.objective: Recognise tabes dorsalis as a lesion of the dorsal roots and dorsal columns.

items.stemHtml: A lumbar puncture is performed with the needle entering the subarachnoid space at the L4–L5 interspace in a 40-year-old woman. At this level, which of the following structures lies free within the subarachnoid space around the needle tip?

options.label: B
options.html: Lumbar enlargement of the spinal cord

items.explanationHtml:
In adults the cord ends at about L1–L2. Below that, the subarachnoid space (lumbar cistern) contains the cauda equina, roots that float in CSF and are pushed aside by the needle, plus the filum terminale. This is why lumbar puncture is done at L3–L4 or L4–L5.

Takeaway: below L2 the subarachnoid space contains roots, not cord.

whyNot.A: The conus ends at about L1–L2 in adults, above the needle.
whyNot.B: The lumbar enlargement lies at about the T9–T12 vertebral levels, well above the needle.
whyNot.C: Dorsal root ganglia sit in the intervertebral foramina, outside the dural sac.
whyNot.E: The denticulate ligaments anchor the cord itself and end at about the level where the cord ends.

items.objective: Explain the anatomical basis for the level of lumbar puncture.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with a complete spinal cord injury at T3 from a car crash 2 years ago has a pounding headache. He is flushed and sweating above the nipple line. Blood pressure is 204/112 mm Hg and pulse is 46/min. His urinary catheter is kinked. Which of the following best explains his bradycardia?

options.label: A
options.html: Direct injury to the vagal nuclei in the medulla

options.label: B
options.html: Baroreceptor-triggered increase in vagal output to the heart

options.label: C
options.html: Loss of sympathetic fibres to the heart from the injury itself

options.label: D
options.html: Hyperkalaemia from muscle breakdown below the lesion

options.label: E
options.html: Release of adrenaline from the adrenal medulla

items.explanationHtml:
In autonomic dysreflexia, a stimulus below the lesion (here, a distended bladder) drives unchecked sympathetic outflow from the isolated cord, constricting splanchnic vessels and raising blood pressure.
