The intact baroreflex responds through the brainstem: vagal output slows the heart and vasodilation occurs above the lesion. The descending signals that would damp the reflex cannot pass the injury.

Takeaway: autonomic dysreflexia pairs reflex hypertension with baroreflex-mediated bradycardia.

whyNot.A: The brainstem is intact; his vagal reflexes are working normally.
whyNot.C: Loss of cardiac sympathetic tone cannot explain a sudden episode of bradycardia during a hypertensive surge.
whyNot.D: Nothing suggests muscle breakdown, and hyperkalaemia would not cause hypertension and flushing.
whyNot.E: Adrenaline would raise the heart rate, not slow it.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of bradycardia in autonomic dysreflexia.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman has a sudden severe headache. Her left eyelid droops, and when it is lifted, the left eye rests down and out. The left pupil is 7 mm and does not react to light. CT angiography shows an aneurysm at the junction of the left internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries. Why is the pupil involved?

options.label: A
options.html: The parasympathetic pupillary fibres lie on the outer surface of the nerve

options.label: B
options.html: The aneurysm compresses the sympathetic plexus on the carotid artery

options.label: C
options.html: The Edinger–Westphal nucleus has been infarcted

options.label: D
options.html: The ciliary ganglion lies next to the posterior communicating artery

options.label: E
options.html: Ischaemia affects the central core of the oculomotor nerve

items.explanationHtml:
The pupillomotor parasympathetic fibres run in the superficial part of the oculomotor nerve. An external mass such as an aneurysm presses on them early, giving a fixed dilated pupil along with ptosis and the down-and-out eye.

Takeaway: compressive third nerve palsies involve the pupil because the parasympathetic fibres lie on the outside of the nerve.

whyNot.B: Sympathetic damage would make the pupil small, not dilated.
whyNot.C: The aneurysm is outside the midbrain; it compresses the nerve, not the nucleus.
whyNot.D: The ciliary ganglion lies in the orbit, far from the posterior communicating artery.
whyNot.E: Ischaemia of the core is the mechanism of pupil-sparing palsy, as in diabetes.

items.objective: Explain why compressive oculomotor palsies affect the pupil.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes has had aching pain above his right eye for 2 days and now double vision. His right eyelid droops, and the eye cannot move up, down or in. Both pupils are 3 mm and react briskly to light. Which of the following is the most likely mechanism of his nerve injury?

options.label: A
options.html: Compression of the nerve by a herniating uncus

options.label: B
options.html: Demyelination of the oculomotor fascicle in the midbrain

options.label: D
options.html: Ischaemia of the inner fibres from small-vessel disease of the nerve

options.label: E
options.html: Compression of the nerve by a posterior communicating artery aneurysm

items.explanationHtml:
A pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in a patient with diabetes is typically microvascular. Disease of the small vessels that supply the nerve infarcts its central fibres; the superficial pupillary fibres are spared. Pain is common, and recovery over about 3 months is the rule.

Takeaway: ischaemic third nerve palsy usually spares the pupil.

whyNot.A: Uncal herniation compresses the nerve from outside and dilates the pupil early, in a drowsy patient.
whyNot.B: Demyelination in the midbrain is unusual and would often produce other brainstem signs.
whyNot.C: Cavernous sinus thrombosis typically causes fever, proptosis and several cranial nerve deficits.
whyNot.E: An aneurysm compresses the superficial pupillary fibres, so the pupil would usually be dilated.

items.objective: Identify microvascular ischaemia as the cause of a pupil-sparing third nerve palsy in diabetes.

items.stemHtml: Three weeks after a bicycle accident, a 19-year-old man reports vertical double vision when walking down stairs or reading. He holds his head tilted to the left. When he tilts his head to the right, the right eye drifts upward and the double vision worsens. Weakness of which of the following muscles is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
The superior oblique depresses the eye when it is adducted and intorts it. A right fourth nerve palsy makes the right eye ride high, worse on looking down and to the left and on tilting the head to the right. Patients tilt their head toward the opposite shoulder to reduce the need for intorsion. The long, thin trochlear nerve is easily injured by head trauma.

Takeaway: a fourth nerve palsy causes vertical diplopia on looking down and a head tilt away from the weak eye.

whyNot.A: A left superior oblique palsy would make the left eye ride high and the head tilt to the right.
whyNot.B: Inferior oblique weakness reduces elevation in adduction; the eye would not drift upward.
whyNot.D: Inferior rectus weakness causes a high eye but worst on looking down and out, without the head-tilt pattern.
whyNot.E: A left superior rectus palsy would leave the left eye low, not the right eye high.

items.objective: Identify a trochlear nerve palsy from the pattern of vertical diplopia and head tilt.

items.stemHtml: A small haemorrhage destroys the left trochlear nucleus in the midbrain of a 60-year-old woman and no other structure. Which of the following muscles will be weak?
items.explanationHtml:
The trochlear nerve is the only cranial nerve whose fibres cross completely before leaving the brainstem; they decussate in the superior medullary velum and exit dorsally. The left nucleus therefore supplies the right superior oblique.

Takeaway: a trochlear nucleus lesion weakens the opposite superior oblique.

whyNot.A: The left superior oblique is supplied by the right trochlear nucleus.
whyNot.C: The lateral rectus is supplied by the abducens nerve from the pons.
whyNot.D: The inferior oblique is supplied by the oculomotor nerve.
whyNot.E: Each nucleus supplies only one muscle, on the opposite side.

items.objective: Apply the crossing of the trochlear nerve to localise a nuclear lesion.

items.stemHtml: A 28-year-old woman with obesity has had daily headaches for 2 months and now has horizontal double vision when looking at distant objects, worse when she looks to the left. Fundoscopy shows bilateral optic disc swelling. MRI of the brain shows no mass. Which nerve is most likely affected?
items.explanationHtml:
Raised intracranial pressure, here from idiopathic intracranial hypertension, can stretch the abducens nerve along its long course over the clivus, a false localising sign. Diplopia worse on looking left means the left lateral rectus is weak.

Takeaway: abducens palsy can be a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure.

whyNot.B: A right abducens palsy would cause diplopia worse on looking to the right.
whyNot.C: Oculomotor palsy causes ptosis and failure of adduction, elevation and depression.
whyNot.D: Trochlear palsy causes vertical, not horizontal, diplopia.
whyNot.E: A medial longitudinal fasciculus lesion impairs adduction of the eye on the same side during side gaze.

items.objective: Recognise abducens palsy as a false localising sign of raised intracranial pressure.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man has had a hoarse voice and difficulty swallowing liquids for 1 month. When he says "ah", the uvula and soft palate move toward the left. His gag reflex is reduced on the right. Tongue movements are normal. Which of the following nerves is most likely damaged?
items.explanationHtml:
The palate and uvula are pulled away from the paralysed side by the intact muscles of the other side. A deviation to the left with hoarseness and dysphagia means a lesion of the right vagus, the motor supply of the palate, pharynx and larynx.

Takeaway: the uvula deviates away from the side of a vagus nerve lesion.

whyNot.A: A left vagus lesion would pull the uvula to the right.
whyNot.B: The glossopharyngeal nerve is mainly the sensory limb of the gag; it does not move the palate or cause hoarseness.
whyNot.C: Tongue movements are normal, and the hypoglossal nerve does not supply the palate.
whyNot.E: The accessory nerve supplies the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius, not the palate or larynx.

items.objective: Localise a vagus nerve lesion from palatal deviation.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old woman has slurred speech. When she protrudes her tongue it deviates to the right, and the right half of the tongue is thin with visible fasciculations. Which of the following is the most likely site of the lesion?

options.label: C
options.html: Right corticobulbar tract in the internal capsule

items.explanationHtml:
Wasting and fasciculations are lower motor neuron signs. The intact left genioglossus pushes the tongue toward the weak right side, so the lesion is in the right hypoglossal nucleus or nerve.

Takeaway: the tongue deviates toward the side of a hypoglossal lesion; wasting with fasciculations means lower motor neuron.

whyNot.A: A cortical lesion is upper motor neuron and does not cause wasting or fasciculations.
whyNot.B: A left hypoglossal lesion would push the tongue to the left.
whyNot.C: An upper motor neuron lesion would not cause wasting or fasciculations.
whyNot.E: The glossopharyngeal nerve does not move the tongue.

items.objective: Localise a lower motor neuron hypoglossal lesion.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman has a slowly enlarging aneurysm of the right internal carotid artery within the cavernous sinus. Which of the following cranial nerves is usually affected first?

options.label: C
options.html: Right ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve

options.label: D
options.html: Right mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve

items.explanationHtml:
The oculomotor, trochlear, ophthalmic and maxillary nerves run in the lateral wall of the cavernous sinus, but the abducens nerve runs through the sinus itself, right beside the carotid artery. An expanding cavernous carotid aneurysm therefore tends to cause an abducens palsy first.

Takeaway: the abducens nerve lies free in the cavernous sinus next to the internal carotid artery.

whyNot.A: The oculomotor nerve is in the lateral wall and is affected later.
whyNot.B: The trochlear nerve is also in the lateral wall, further from the artery.
whyNot.C: The ophthalmic division lies in the lateral wall and is usually involved after the abducens nerve.
whyNot.D: The mandibular division leaves through the foramen ovale and does not pass through the cavernous sinus.

items.objective: Relate the anatomy of the cavernous sinus to the order of cranial nerve involvement.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman has pulsatile tinnitus in the left ear. Examination shows a reduced gag reflex on the left, a hoarse voice and loss of taste on the posterior third of the tongue on the left. Imaging shows a vascular tumour at the left jugular foramen. Which of the following additional findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Weakness of shoulder shrugging on the left

options.label: B
options.html: Deviation of the protruded tongue to the left

options.label: C
options.html: Weakness of the left side of the forehead

options.label: D
options.html: Loss of taste on the anterior two-thirds of the tongue on the left

options.label: E
options.html: Deviation of the jaw to the left on opening

items.explanationHtml:
The glossopharyngeal, vagus and accessory nerves leave the skull together through the jugular foramen, so a paraganglioma there typically affects all three. The accessory nerve supplies the trapezius, so shoulder shrugging weakens on the same side.

Takeaway: the jugular foramen syndrome affects cranial nerves IX, X and XI together.

whyNot.B: The hypoglossal nerve leaves through its own canal; it may be involved only by a larger tumour.
whyNot.C: The facial nerve runs through the internal acoustic meatus, not the jugular foramen.
whyNot.D: Taste from the anterior tongue travels in the chorda tympani branch of the facial nerve.
whyNot.E: The jaw is moved by the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve, which leaves through the foramen ovale.

items.objective: List the cranial nerves that pass through the jugular foramen.

items.stemHtml: A 3.9-kg (8.6-lb) boy is delivered vaginally after a difficult shoulder delivery that needed firm lateral traction on the head. His right arm hangs at his side, internally rotated, with the elbow extended and the forearm pronated. He grasps normally with the right hand. Refer to the figure. Injury at which labelled site best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Forceful separation of the head from the shoulder stretches the C5–C6 roots and upper trunk (Erb palsy). The deltoid, the external rotators and the elbow flexors and supinators are weak, so the arm hangs adducted and internally rotated with the elbow extended. Hand function (C8–T1) is preserved.

Takeaway: Erb palsy is an upper trunk (C5–C6) injury from lateral traction on the head.

whyNot.B: A lower trunk injury weakens the hand intrinsics and spares shoulder and elbow movement.
whyNot.C: A posterior cord lesion causes weak shoulder abduction and wrist drop, but elbow flexion and supination are preserved.
whyNot.D: Long thoracic nerve injury causes scapular winging, not a limp arm.
whyNot.E: An ulnar nerve lesion affects the hand intrinsics, which are normal here.

items.objective: Localise neonatal Erb palsy to the upper trunk of the brachial plexus.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old man grabbed a tree branch to stop a fall from a ladder and hung by his left arm. He now has weakness of all the small muscles of the left hand, numbness along the medial forearm and hand, and a drooping left eyelid with a small left pupil. Using the figure, which labelled site of injury best accounts for his findings?
items.explanationHtml:
Forced upward traction on the arm stretches the C8–T1 roots and lower trunk (Klumpke palsy). All hand intrinsics are weak and the medial forearm is numb. Damage to the T1 root also interrupts the preganglionic sympathetic fibres to the head, giving a Horner syndrome.

Takeaway: upward traction injures the lower trunk; Horner syndrome signals T1 involvement.

whyNot.A: Upper trunk injury affects the shoulder and elbow, not the hand.
whyNot.C: A posterior cord lesion causes deltoid and extensor weakness without Horner syndrome.
whyNot.D: The long thoracic nerve supplies only serratus anterior.
whyNot.E: An ulnar nerve lesion spares the median-supplied thenar muscles, the medial forearm sensation and the sympathetic outflow.

items.objective: Localise a Klumpke palsy with Horner syndrome to the lower trunk.

items.stemHtml: Refer to the figure. A 51-year-old woman has a mastectomy with axillary lymph node dissection. Afterward, the nerve labelled D is found to have been injured. Which of the following findings is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Weakness of the first 15 degrees of shoulder abduction

options.label: B
options.html: Numbness of the skin over the lateral shoulder

options.label: C
options.html: Winging of the scapula when she pushes against a wall

options.label: D
options.html: Inability to extend the wrist and fingers

options.label: E
options.html: Weakness of elbow flexion and forearm supination

items.explanationHtml:
Site D is the long thoracic nerve (C5–C7), which runs on the surface of serratus anterior along the chest wall and is at risk in axillary surgery. Serratus anterior holds the scapula against the chest and rotates it upward, so its loss causes medial winging and difficulty raising the arm above the head.

Takeaway: long thoracic nerve injury causes winging of the scapula.

whyNot.A: The first 15 degrees of abduction are driven by supraspinatus (suprascapular nerve).
whyNot.B: Lateral shoulder numbness follows axillary nerve injury.
whyNot.D: Wrist drop follows radial nerve injury.
whyNot.E: Weak elbow flexion and supination follow musculocutaneous nerve injury.

items.objective: Predict the deficit after long thoracic nerve injury.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man has a closed spiral fracture of the middle third of the right humeral shaft after a fall. Which of the following findings is most likely?

options.label: C
options.html: Numbness of the palmar little finger

items.explanationHtml:
The radial nerve winds around the humerus in the spiral groove and is stretched or bruised by midshaft fractures. It supplies the wrist and finger extensors, so the patient has wrist and finger drop and numbness over the back of the first web space. The branches to triceps arise above the groove, so elbow extension is usually preserved.

Takeaway: midshaft humerus fracture → radial nerve injury → wrist drop with triceps spared.

whyNot.A: Shoulder abduction depends on the axillary and suprascapular nerves.
whyNot.B: Triceps is supplied by radial branches that leave above the spiral groove.
whyNot.C: The palmar little finger is ulnar territory.
whyNot.D: Thumb opposition depends on the median nerve.

items.objective: Predict the deficit from radial nerve injury at the spiral groove.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old girl fell onto her outstretched hand and has a displaced supracondylar fracture of the humerus. After reduction, she cannot bend the tip of her thumb or the tip of her index finger, so she cannot form a circle with them. Sensation in the hand is normal. Weakness of which of the following muscles is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Abductor pollicis brevis and opponens pollicis

options.label: B
options.html: Adductor pollicis and first dorsal interosseous

options.label: C
options.html: Extensor pollicis longus and extensor indicis

options.label: E
options.html: Flexor pollicis longus and flexor digitorum profundus to the index finger

items.explanationHtml:
The anterior interosseous nerve, a purely motor branch of the median nerve given off near the elbow, supplies flexor pollicis longus, the index (and middle) parts of flexor digitorum profundus and pronator quadratus. Its injury removes flexion at the tip joints of the thumb and index finger, so the thumb–index circle collapses, with no sensory loss.

Takeaway: anterior interosseous nerve palsy: weak distal flexion of the thumb and index finger, no sensory loss.

whyNot.A: The thenar muscles are supplied by the recurrent branch of the median nerve in the hand.
whyNot.B: These muscles are supplied by the deep branch of the ulnar nerve.
whyNot.C: These extensors are supplied by the radial nerve and do not flex the fingertips.
whyNot.D: The lumbricals flex the knuckles and extend the finger joints; they do not flex the fingertips.

items.objective: Identify anterior interosseous nerve palsy after a supracondylar fracture.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old man who cycles long distances has had numbness of the palmar surface of the little finger and weakness of his hand for 2 months. He cannot spread his fingers apart. Sensation over the back of the medial hand is normal. Flexion of the tip of the little finger is strong. Which of the following is the most likely site of nerve compression?

options.label: B
options.html: Medial cord of the brachial plexus

options.label: C
options.html: Ulnar canal (Guyon canal) at the wrist

items.explanationHtml:
The ulnar nerve gives off its dorsal cutaneous branch in the forearm and its branch to flexor digitorum profundus near the elbow. Compression in Guyon canal, for example from handlebar pressure, spares both: the back of the hand feels normal and the fingertip flexes, while the interossei and palmar sensation are lost.

Takeaway: sparing of dorsal hand sensation and long finger flexion localises an ulnar lesion to the wrist.

whyNot.A: An elbow lesion would also numb the back of the medial hand and weaken the little finger's long flexor.
whyNot.B: A medial cord lesion would add median-supplied hand muscle weakness and forearm sensory loss.
whyNot.D: The carpal tunnel contains the median nerve, not the ulnar nerve.
whyNot.E: A C8 radiculopathy would affect dorsal hand sensation and long finger flexors and often causes neck or arm pain.

items.objective: Localise an ulnar nerve lesion to Guyon canal from the branches spared.

items.stemHtml: A 30-year-old soccer player has a fracture of the neck of the left fibula. Which of the following deficits is most likely?

options.label: A
options.html: Weak ankle plantar flexion and inversion

options.label: E
options.html: Numbness of the sole of the foot

items.explanationHtml:
The common fibular nerve winds around the fibular neck, where it is easily injured. Its deep branch supplies the ankle and toe dorsiflexors and its superficial branch the evertors, so the patient has foot drop with weak eversion and numbness of the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.

Takeaway: fibular neck injury → common fibular nerve → foot drop and weak eversion.

whyNot.A: Plantar flexion and inversion depend on the tibial nerve.
whyNot.C: Knee extension depends on the femoral nerve.
whyNot.D: Hip adduction depends on the obturator nerve.
whyNot.E: The sole is supplied by branches of the tibial nerve.

items.objective: Predict the deficit after a fibular neck fracture.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man taking warfarin for atrial fibrillation develops severe right groin pain. Two days later he cannot straighten his right knee against gravity. The right patellar reflex is absent, and he has numbness over the anterior thigh and the medial side of the lower leg. INR is 5.8 (reference 0.8–1.1). CT shows a large haematoma in the right iliopsoas muscle. Which nerve is most likely compressed?
items.explanationHtml:
The femoral nerve runs between the psoas and iliacus muscles and is easily compressed by an iliopsoas haematoma. It supplies the quadriceps (knee extension, patellar reflex) and, through the saphenous nerve, the skin of the medial leg.

Takeaway: an iliopsoas haematoma compresses the femoral nerve: weak quadriceps, lost knee jerk, numb medial leg.

whyNot.A: The obturator nerve supplies the hip adductors and medial thigh skin, not the quadriceps.
whyNot.B: The sciatic nerve supplies the hamstrings and everything below the knee except the saphenous territory.
whyNot.C: The lateral femoral cutaneous nerve is purely sensory, to the lateral thigh.
whyNot.E: An L5 root lesion causes foot drop and does not abolish the patellar reflex.

items.objective: Identify femoral neuropathy from an iliopsoas haematoma.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 15 years has burning and numbness in both feet that now reaches her mid-shins. Her fingertips have just started to tingle. Ankle reflexes are absent. Which of the following best explains why her symptoms began in the feet?

options.label: A
options.html: Lower blood glucose concentrations in the hands

options.label: B
options.html: Greater density of sensory receptors in the feet

options.label: C
options.html: Earlier failure of the longest axons

options.label: D
options.html: Selective autoimmune attack on lumbosacral dorsal root ganglia

options.label: E
options.html: Compression of nerves by the weight of the body

items.explanationHtml:
Diabetic polyneuropathy is a length-dependent axonopathy. Metabolic injury from chronic hyperglycaemia (polyol pathway, advanced glycation end products, oxidative stress and microvascular disease) disrupts axonal transport and supply, and the longest axons, to the toes, fail first. Symptoms reach the fingers when the leg symptoms reach about the knees, giving a stocking-and-glove pattern.

Takeaway: distal symmetric polyneuropathy starts in the feet because the longest axons fail first.

whyNot.A: Blood glucose concentration does not differ meaningfully between hands and feet.
whyNot.B: Fingertips have a higher receptor density than the feet, yet are affected later.
whyNot.D: Diabetic polyneuropathy is a metabolic, not an autoimmune, axonopathy.
whyNot.E: Weight-bearing compression does not produce a symmetric, ascending sensory loss.

items.objective: Explain the length-dependent pattern of diabetic polyneuropathy.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman has bouts of stabbing, electric pain in her right cheek and upper lip lasting a few seconds, set off by brushing her teeth. Neurological examination is normal. A drug is started that reduces repetitive neuronal firing by prolonging the inactivated state of a channel. Which channel does this drug act on?
items.explanationHtml:
The first-line drug for trigeminal neuralgia is carbamazepine. It binds voltage-gated sodium channels in the inactivated state and slows their recovery, which suppresses the high-frequency, paroxysmal discharges of the demyelinated trigeminal root.

Takeaway: carbamazepine treats trigeminal neuralgia by stabilising inactivated sodium channels.

whyNot.B: Benzodiazepines and barbiturates act on GABA<sub>A</sub> receptors; they are not first-line for this pain.
whyNot.C: Ethosuximide blocks T-type calcium channels and is used for absence seizures.
whyNot.D: Ketamine and memantine block NMDA receptors; neither is the standard drug here.
whyNot.E: Sulfonylureas act on ATP-sensitive potassium channels in beta cells.

items.objective: Identify the mechanism of carbamazepine in trigeminal neuralgia.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man started carbamazepine 2 months ago for trigeminal neuralgia. He is brought in because he has become confused. He is euvolaemic. Serum sodium is 121 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L), serum osmolality 254 mOsm/kg (275–295 mOsm/kg), and urine osmolality is inappropriately high. Which of the following best explains his laboratory findings?

options.label: A
options.html: Increased antidiuretic hormone effect on the collecting duct

options.label: B
options.html: Impaired aldosterone synthesis in the adrenal cortex

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibition of the sodium–chloride cotransporter in the distal tubule

options.label: D
options.html: Excessive free-water intake from drug-induced thirst

items.explanationHtml:
Carbamazepine (and more often oxcarbazepine) causes hyponatraemia with the features of inappropriate antidiuresis: euvolaemia, low serum osmolality and concentrated urine. It increases antidiuretic hormone release and the sensitivity of the collecting duct to it, so free water is retained.

Takeaway: carbamazepine and oxcarbazepine cause SIADH-like hyponatraemia; monitor sodium.

whyNot.B: Aldosterone deficiency would cause hyperkalaemia and volume depletion and is not a carbamazepine effect.
whyNot.C: Thiazide diuretics, not carbamazepine, inhibit the distal sodium–chloride cotransporter.
whyNot.D: Primary polydipsia produces maximally dilute urine, not inappropriately concentrated urine.
whyNot.E: Hyperglycaemia would raise serum osmolality, not lower it.

items.objective: Explain carbamazepine-associated hyponatraemia.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man whose parents emigrated from southern China is to start carbamazepine for trigeminal neuralgia. Testing for which of the following before treatment reduces his risk of a severe drug reaction?
items.explanationHtml:
HLA-B*15:02, common in people with ancestry from much of East and Southeast Asia, greatly increases the risk of Stevens–Johnson syndrome and toxic epidermal necrolysis with carbamazepine. Carriers should receive another drug.

Takeaway: screen for HLA-B*15:02 before carbamazepine in at-risk ancestries.

whyNot.A: HLA-B*57:01 predicts hypersensitivity to abacavir.
whyNot.B: HLA-B*58:01 predicts severe cutaneous reactions to allopurinol.
whyNot.C: HLA-B27 is associated with spondyloarthritis, not drug reactions.
whyNot.D: CYP2C19 poor metabolisers activate clopidogrel poorly; this does not predict carbamazepine skin reactions.

items.objective: Identify the pharmacogenetic test required before carbamazepine.

items.stemHtml: A 77-year-old woman has burning pain and extreme sensitivity to clothing over a band on the left side of her chest, 4 months after a shingles rash there healed. She is started on a drug that binds the α2δ subunit of presynaptic voltage-gated calcium channels. Which of the following effects of this drug most directly reduces her pain?

options.label: C
options.html: Blockade of serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake

options.label: D
options.html: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase in the skin

items.explanationHtml:
Gabapentin and pregabalin bind the α2δ subunit of voltage-gated calcium channels, reducing their trafficking and the calcium entry that triggers release of glutamate, substance P and other transmitters. This damps the sensitised pain pathway in postherpetic neuralgia.

Takeaway: gabapentinoids act on the α2δ subunit to reduce excitatory transmitter release.

whyNot.A: Opioids act on μ receptors; gabapentinoids do not.
whyNot.C: SNRIs and tricyclics block monoamine reuptake.
whyNot.D: NSAIDs inhibit cyclooxygenase and work poorly for neuropathic pain.
whyNot.E: Benzodiazepines increase GABA<sub>A</sub> channel opening frequency; despite its name, gabapentin does not act on GABA receptors.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of gabapentinoids in neuropathic pain.

items.stemHtml: Three months after an ischaemic stroke, a 68-year-old man has constant, burning pain on the left side of his body, where he has had numbness since the stroke. Light touch of the left arm is unpleasantly painful. Strength is normal. A lesion in which of the following locations most likely caused this syndrome?

options.label: A
options.html: Ventral posterolateral nucleus of the right thalamus

options.label: B
options.html: Lateral geniculate nucleus of the right thalamus

options.label: C
options.html: Anterior limb of the right internal capsule

options.label: D
options.html: Left dorsal column nuclei in the medulla

items.explanationHtml:
Infarction of the ventral posterolateral (and posteromedial) nuclei of the thalamus first causes opposite-side sensory loss. Weeks to months later, maladaptive reorganisation produces burning pain and allodynia in the numb area: central post-stroke (thalamic) pain, or Dejerine–Roussy syndrome.

Takeaway: delayed burning pain in the numb half of the body after a stroke points to the VPL thalamus.

whyNot.B: The lateral geniculate nucleus relays vision; its lesion causes a visual field defect.
whyNot.C: The anterior limb carries frontopontine and thalamocortical fibres; sensory fibres run in the posterior limb.
whyNot.D: A medullary lesion of the dorsal column nuclei would affect the same (left) side and would not abolish pain sensation.
whyNot.E: A motor cortex lesion causes weakness, which he does not have.

items.objective: Localise central post-stroke pain to the sensory thalamus.

items.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man with painful diabetic neuropathy has a high-concentration capsaicin patch applied to both feet. After the burning during application, his pain is reduced for several weeks. Which of the following best explains the lasting effect?

options.label: A
options.html: Blockade of voltage-gated sodium channels in the skin

options.label: B
options.html: Activation of descending serotonergic pathways from the brainstem

options.label: C
options.html: Antagonism of substance P at NK1 receptors in the dorsal horn

options.label: D
options.html: Activation of TRPV1 channels causing reversible defunctionalisation of nociceptor terminals

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of prostaglandin synthesis in the dermis

items.explanationHtml:
Capsaicin is a TRPV1 agonist. A high dose opens the channel strongly, and the resulting calcium overload and mitochondrial dysfunction cause the epidermal nociceptor terminals to retract and stop working for weeks, until they regrow.

Takeaway: high-dose capsaicin defunctionalises nociceptors through TRPV1 activation.

whyNot.A: Sodium channel blockade is the mechanism of lidocaine, not capsaicin.
whyNot.B: Capsaicin acts peripherally on the nerve endings, not on brainstem pathways.
whyNot.C: Capsaicin depletes substance P from terminals but does not block its receptor.
whyNot.E: Inhibiting prostaglandin synthesis is the action of NSAIDs.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism of topical capsaicin.

items.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman touches a hot pan. She feels an immediate sharp, well-localised pain, followed about a second later by a dull, burning, poorly localised pain. Which of the following fibre types carries the second, burning pain?
items.explanationHtml:
Unmyelinated C fibres conduct slowly (about 0.5–2 m/s) and carry the delayed, burning, poorly localised "second pain". Thinly myelinated A-delta fibres carry the fast, sharp "first pain".

Takeaway: first pain travels in A-delta fibres; slow burning pain travels in C fibres.

whyNot.A: A-alpha fibres are large myelinated fibres for muscle spindles and motor neurons.
whyNot.B: A-beta fibres carry touch and vibration.
whyNot.C: A-delta fibres carry the fast, sharp first pain.
whyNot.D: B fibres are preganglionic autonomic fibres.

items.objective: Distinguish the fibre types carrying first and second pain.

items.stemHtml: Five weeks after a distal radius fracture was treated in a cast, a 46-year-old woman has severe burning pain of the whole hand, pain when the bedsheet touches her skin, a swollen, shiny, cooler hand with sweating changes and stiff fingers. Nerve conduction studies are normal. Which of the following best distinguishes her condition from the other subtype of the same syndrome?

options.label: A
options.html: The pain extends beyond a single nerve territory

options.label: B
options.html: Changes in skin temperature and sweating are present

options.label: C
options.html: There is no identifiable injury to a peripheral nerve

options.label: D
options.html: The pain follows a fracture rather than soft-tissue injury

options.label: E
options.html: The symptoms began within 3 months of the injury

items.explanationHtml:
This is complex regional pain syndrome. Type I has no definable nerve lesion; type II follows a confirmed injury to a peripheral nerve. Pain beyond one nerve territory, autonomic changes, the type of inciting injury and the timing are shared by both subtypes.

Takeaway: CRPS type II requires a confirmed nerve injury; type I does not.

whyNot.A: Pain spreading beyond a nerve territory is typical of both types.
whyNot.B: Vasomotor and sudomotor changes occur in both types.
whyNot.D: Both types can follow fractures, sprains, surgery or immobilisation.
whyNot.E: Timing of onset does not separate the two types.

items.objective: Distinguish type I from type II complex regional pain syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman with painful diabetic neuropathy has a good response to duloxetine. Duloxetine's analgesic effect is attributed mainly to enhancing a pathway that begins in which of the following structures?

options.label: A
options.html: Ventral posterolateral nucleus of the thalamus

options.label: C
options.html: Periaqueductal grey and its brainstem relays

items.explanationHtml:
The periaqueductal grey drives descending inhibition through the rostral ventromedial medulla (serotonergic raphe neurons) and the locus coeruleus (noradrenergic neurons), which project to the dorsal horn and suppress pain transmission. By blocking serotonin and noradrenaline reuptake, SNRIs and tricyclics strengthen this descending control.

Takeaway: SNRIs and tricyclics relieve neuropathic pain by boosting descending monoaminergic inhibition from the brainstem.

whyNot.A: The thalamus relays ascending pain signals; it is not the source of descending inhibition.
whyNot.B: The substantia nigra is part of the dopaminergic motor system.
whyNot.D: The somatosensory cortex localises pain; it is not the target of SNRI analgesia.
whyNot.E: The dorsal root ganglion holds first-order sensory neurons; duloxetine does not act there.

items.objective: Explain how SNRIs relieve neuropathic pain through descending pain modulation.

items.stemHtml:
A 44-year-old man comes to the emergency department with 5 days of worsening mid-back pain, fever and, since this morning, weakness of both legs. He injects heroin. Temperature is 38.6°C (101.5°F). There is tenderness over the T8 spinous process. Strength in the hip flexors is 3/5 bilaterally, and pinprick sensation is reduced below the umbilicus. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference range
Leukocytes15,800/mm34,500–11,000/mm3
ESR94 mm/h0–15 mm/h
Glucose, fasting96 mg/dL70–100 mg/dL
Creatinine0.9 mg/dL0.6–1.2 mg/dL

Blood cultures are drawn. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic study?

options.label: A
options.html: Plain radiographs of the thoracic spine

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the whole spine with gadolinium

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, focal spinal pain and a new deficit in a person who injects drugs is a spinal epidural abscess until proved otherwise. MRI with gadolinium of the entire spine defines the abscess and its extent (skip lesions occur) and guides urgent surgical drainage. Empiric IV antibiotics against S. aureus, including MRSA, and gram-negative rods are started after cultures.

Takeaway: back pain + fever + neurological deficit → MRI of the whole spine with contrast, then decompression and antibiotics.

whyNot.A: Radiographs are normal early and would delay the diagnosis.
whyNot.B: Lumbar puncture is avoided: it rarely helps and can spread infection into the subarachnoid space.
whyNot.D: A bone scan is less sensitive and less specific than MRI and does not show cord compression.
whyNot.E: Echocardiography may be needed later to look for endocarditis, but it does not evaluate the spine.

items.objective: Choose MRI with gadolinium to diagnose a spinal epidural abscess.

items.stemHtml: A 68-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer has had increasing mid-back pain for 3 weeks, worse when he lies down. Since yesterday his legs feel heavy and he has stumbled twice. Strength is 4/5 in both legs, knee reflexes are brisk and both plantar responses are extensor. Sensation to pinprick is reduced below the nipple line. Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Oral ibuprofen and review in 1 week

items.explanationHtml:
Back pain with upper motor neuron leg signs and a sensory level in a patient with cancer is metastatic spinal cord compression. High-dose dexamethasone is given immediately to reduce vasogenic oedema, followed by urgent MRI of the whole spine and definitive treatment with radiotherapy and/or surgical decompression. Neurological status at the start of treatment predicts walking ability afterward.

Takeaway: suspected malignant cord compression with a deficit → dexamethasone now, then emergency MRI and decompression.

whyNot.A: Lumbar puncture does not diagnose cord compression and may worsen it.
whyNot.B: Delay risks permanent paralysis; this is an emergency.
whyNot.C: A bone scan shows skeletal metastases but not cord compression and would delay treatment.
whyNot.E: Physical therapy does not treat the compression and wastes critical time.

items.objective: Begin immediate glucocorticoids for suspected metastatic spinal cord compression.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old woman has had low back pain radiating down both legs for 4 days. This morning she could not pass urine and noticed numbness "where she sits". Examination shows weakness of ankle plantar flexion on both sides, absent ankle reflexes and reduced perianal sensation. A bladder scan shows 850 mL of urine after an attempt to void. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Emergency MRI of the lumbosacral spine

options.label: D
options.html: Plain radiographs of the lumbar spine

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral sciatica, saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention and lower motor neuron signs make this cauda equina syndrome, most often from a large central disc herniation. Emergency MRI confirms the compression, and urgent surgical decompression gives the best chance of recovering bladder and leg function.

Takeaway: saddle anaesthesia plus urinary retention → emergency MRI and decompression.

whyNot.B: Conservative care is for radiculopathy without red flags; this is a surgical emergency.
whyNot.C: An epidural injection does not relieve mass compression of the cauda equina.
whyNot.D: Radiographs cannot show a disc herniation or neural compression.
whyNot.E: Waiting for electrodiagnostic studies would delay decompression.

items.objective: Recognise cauda equina syndrome and obtain emergency MRI.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old man has had pain in his left buttock radiating down the back of the thigh and the outside of the calf to the top of his foot for 2 weeks, after lifting furniture. He has no fever, weight loss, bladder or bowel symptoms, or history of cancer. Raising his straightened left leg to 40° reproduces the leg pain. Strength, including great-toe extension, is normal; reflexes are symmetric. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: MRI of the lumbar spine this week

items.explanationHtml:
This is an acute L5 radiculopathy without red flags or motor deficit. Most patients improve within 6 weeks. Recommended care is an NSAID (if no contraindication), heat and staying active. Imaging is reserved for red flags, a progressive or severe motor deficit, or symptoms persisting beyond about 6 weeks in a candidate for injection or surgery.

Takeaway: acute sciatica without red flags: NSAIDs and staying active, no early imaging.

whyNot.A: Early MRI does not improve outcomes without red flags and often shows incidental findings.
whyNot.B: Bed rest slows recovery compared with remaining active.
whyNot.C: Surgery is not indicated without a progressive deficit, cauda equina syndrome or failure of conservative care.
whyNot.D: Opioids give no extra benefit over NSAIDs for most patients and carry harms.

items.objective: Manage acute lumbar radiculopathy without red flags conservatively.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man who has had a complete T4 spinal cord injury for 3 years has a sudden pounding headache during a clinic visit. He is flushed and sweating over the face. Blood pressure is 196/108 mm Hg and pulse is 50/min. He is lying flat on the examination table. Which of the following is the most appropriate first step?

options.label: B
options.html: Sit him upright and check his bladder catheter

options.label: C
options.html: Obtain emergency CT of the head

options.label: D
options.html: Elevate his legs and give an IV fluid bolus

items.explanationHtml:
This is autonomic dysreflexia. Sitting the patient up pools blood in the legs and lowers pressure; then find and remove the trigger, most often bladder distension from a blocked catheter, then bowel impaction or a pressure sore. If systolic pressure stays at about 150 mm Hg or higher after these steps, give a rapid short-acting antihypertensive such as nitrate paste or nifedipine.

Takeaway: autonomic dysreflexia: sit up, loosen clothing, find the trigger (bladder first); drugs only if pressure stays high.

whyNot.A: Drugs come after positioning and removing the trigger; the hypertension usually resolves once the cause is removed.
whyNot.C: The headache is explained by the blood pressure surge; imaging delays effective treatment.
whyNot.D: Elevating the legs and giving fluid would raise his blood pressure further.
whyNot.E: The bradycardia is a baroreflex response and resolves when the pressure falls.

items.objective: Manage autonomic dysreflexia with positioning and removal of the trigger.

items.stemHtml: A 78-year-old man tripped on a step and struck his forehead on the ground. He now cannot grip with either hand and has marked weakness of both arms. He can lift both legs against resistance. He has some difficulty starting to urinate. CT of the cervical spine shows multilevel degenerative changes without fracture. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A hyperextension injury in an older adult with cervical spondylosis typically causes central cord syndrome: weakness worse in the arms than the legs, with the hands most affected, variable sensory loss and bladder dysfunction. MRI shows cord oedema or contusion. Most patients recover some function, with the legs and bladder recovering before the hands.

Takeaway: older adult + hyperextension + hands weaker than legs = central cord syndrome.

whyNot.A: Anterior cord syndrome causes paralysis of the legs as well as arms below the lesion, with preserved vibration sense.
whyNot.B: Brown-Séquard syndrome causes one-sided weakness with opposite-side pain loss.
whyNot.D: A posterior cord syndrome mainly causes loss of vibration and position sense, not weakness.
whyNot.E: A forehead fall does not stretch both plexuses, and bladder difficulty points to the cord.

items.objective: Diagnose central cord syndrome after a hyperextension injury.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman has had progressive weakness and numbness of both legs and urinary retention over 3 days. A year ago she had an episode of severe visual loss in the right eye that partly recovered. Examination shows paraparesis, brisk reflexes in the legs and a sensory level at T6. MRI of the spine shows a contrast-enhancing T2 lesion extending from T2 to T8 without compression. MRI of the brain is normal. Serum testing for which of the following is most likely to establish the diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
A longitudinally extensive myelitis (three or more vertebral segments) with a history of severe optic neuritis and a normal brain MRI strongly suggests neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder. Serum aquaporin-4 IgG confirms it. Acute treatment is high-dose IV methylprednisolone with early plasma exchange if needed; long-term immunotherapy prevents relapses. Some multiple sclerosis disease-modifying drugs can worsen it, which is why the distinction matters.

Takeaway: longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis + optic neuritis → test aquaporin-4 IgG.

whyNot.A: HLA-B27 is associated with spondyloarthritis, not myelitis with optic neuritis.
whyNot.C: Acetylcholine receptor antibodies diagnose myasthenia gravis, which does not cause a sensory level.
whyNot.D: Anti-GM1 antibodies are linked to multifocal motor neuropathy and axonal Guillain–Barré syndrome.
whyNot.E: ANCA-associated vasculitis rarely causes myelitis and would not explain the clinical pattern.

items.objective: Recognise neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder in longitudinally extensive transverse myelitis.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man has had trouble fastening buttons and writing for 8 months, and his walking has become unsteady. Flexing his neck sends an electric sensation down his back. He has wasting of the small hand muscles, brisk reflexes in both legs, a positive Hoffmann sign on both sides and extensor plantar responses. Which of the following studies is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?

options.label: B
options.html: Nerve conduction studies of the arms

items.explanationHtml:
Hand clumsiness, gait imbalance, Lhermitte sign and upper motor neuron signs below the neck in an older adult indicate degenerative cervical myelopathy. MRI of the cervical spine shows the canal narrowing and cord signal change. Moderate or progressive myelopathy is treated with surgical decompression.

Takeaway: hand clumsiness + gait imbalance + upper motor neuron signs below the neck → MRI of the cervical spine.

whyNot.A: Head CT does not image the cervical cord; brisk reflexes and a Hoffmann sign in both arms and legs point below the brain.
whyNot.B: Nerve conduction studies assess peripheral nerves and cannot show cord compression.
whyNot.C: B<sub>12</sub> deficiency can mimic myelopathy and is worth checking, but it cannot confirm cord compression.
whyNot.E: CSF analysis does not show structural compression.

items.objective: Confirm degenerative cervical myelopathy with MRI.

items.stemHtml: A 19-year-old man is brought to the emergency department after diving into a shallow lake. He cannot move his arms or legs. Blood pressure is 76/40 mm Hg and pulse is 48/min. His skin is warm and dry. FAST examination is negative, and a CT of the chest, abdomen and pelvis shows no bleeding. CT of the spine shows a burst fracture of C6. Which of the following is the most likely cause of his hypotension?
items.explanationHtml:
Hypotension with bradycardia and warm skin after a cervical cord injury is neurogenic shock: the injury cuts descending drive to the thoracolumbar sympathetic neurons, so vessels dilate and vagal influence on the heart goes unopposed.

Takeaway: hypotension + bradycardia + warm skin after a cervical cord injury = neurogenic shock.

whyNot.A: Bleeding causes tachycardia and cool skin, and the imaging shows no haemorrhage.
whyNot.B: Tamponade causes tachycardia, raised jugular venous pressure and muffled heart sounds.
whyNot.D: Spinal shock describes the temporary loss of reflexes below the injury; it is not a cause of hypotension.
whyNot.E: Tension pneumothorax causes tachycardia, absent breath sounds and would be seen on chest CT.

items.objective: Recognise neurogenic shock after cervical spinal cord injury.

items.stemHtml: The patient described previously has neurogenic shock from a C6 spinal cord injury. After 2 L of crystalloid, his blood pressure is 82/44 mm Hg (mean arterial pressure 57 mm Hg) and pulse is 46/min. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
When fluids do not restore pressure in neurogenic shock, a vasopressor is needed. Norepinephrine adds β1 chronotropic and inotropic support to its α effect, so it suits hypotension with bradycardia. Many centres target a mean arterial pressure of about 85–90 mm Hg in the first days to support cord perfusion.

Takeaway: neurogenic shock not responding to fluids → norepinephrine.

whyNot.A: Routine high-dose methylprednisolone is not recommended after spinal cord injury; its benefit is doubtful and its harms are real.
whyNot.C: Further large-volume fluid risks pulmonary oedema without fixing the vasodilation.
whyNot.D: A pure α-agonist can worsen the bradycardia through reflex vagal slowing.
whyNot.E: There is no evidence of blood loss.

items.objective: Choose norepinephrine for fluid-refractory neurogenic shock with bradycardia.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with a severe headache that began 6 hours ago and double vision. Her right eyelid droops, and the right eye is turned down and out. The right pupil is 7 mm and does not react to light; the left is 3 mm and reactive. CT of the head without contrast is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: C
options.html: Ice-pack test on the drooping eyelid

options.label: D
options.html: MRI of the orbits as an outpatient

items.explanationHtml:
A painful, pupil-involving third nerve palsy suggests compression by an expanding aneurysm of the posterior communicating artery, which is at high risk of rupture. Emergency vascular imaging (CT or MR angiography; catheter angiography if non-invasive imaging is unclear) is required, followed by neurosurgical or endovascular treatment.

Takeaway: a pupil-involving third nerve palsy needs emergency angiographic imaging.

whyNot.B: Attributing a pupil-involving palsy to diabetes risks missing an aneurysm about to rupture.
whyNot.C: The ice-pack test is for myasthenia gravis, which never affects the pupil.
whyNot.D: An outpatient orbital MRI would not show an intracranial aneurysm and would cause a dangerous delay.
whyNot.E: Glucocorticoids have no role in compressive third nerve palsy.

items.objective: Order emergency vascular imaging for a pupil-involving third nerve palsy.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man has had a painful boil on the side of his nose for a week. For 2 days he has had fever, headache and swelling around both eyes. Temperature is 39.4°C (102.9°F). Both eyes protrude, the conjunctivae are swollen, and he cannot move either eye fully in any direction. Sensation is reduced over the forehead on both sides. Pupils are sluggish. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Infection of the central face drains through valveless veins to the cavernous sinus. Fever, bilateral proptosis and chemosis, ophthalmoplegia from cranial nerves III, IV and VI, and reduced V1 sensation indicate septic cavernous sinus thrombosis, most often from S. aureus. Treatment is high-dose IV antibiotics, usually with anticoagulation; MRI with venography confirms it.

Takeaway: bilateral ophthalmoplegia + V1 numbness + fever after a facial infection = cavernous sinus thrombosis.

whyNot.A: Orbital cellulitis is usually one-sided and does not cause forehead numbness or spread to the other eye.
whyNot.B: Preseptal cellulitis spares eye movements and does not cause proptosis.
whyNot.C: Graves orbitopathy develops slowly without fever or sensory loss.
whyNot.E: A carotid–cavernous fistula causes pulsatile proptosis and a bruit, without fever.

items.objective: Diagnose septic cavernous sinus thrombosis.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman reports 3 months of double vision. She sees two overlapping images when she looks at a distant sign, even when her left eye is covered; the double vision disappears when she covers her right eye. Eye movements are full and the neurological examination is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: MRI of the brain with gadolinium

options.label: C
options.html: Eye examination with refraction and slit lamp

options.label: D
options.html: CT angiography of the head and neck

items.explanationHtml:
Double vision that persists when the other eye is covered is monocular diplopia, here from the right eye. It arises in the eye itself (cataract, refractive error, corneal irregularity, dry eye), not from misaligned eyes, so the next step is an ophthalmological examination rather than neuro-imaging.

Takeaway: monocular diplopia is an eye problem; binocular diplopia is a nerve, muscle or junction problem.

whyNot.A: Brain imaging is not indicated for monocular diplopia with a normal neurological examination.
whyNot.B: Myasthenia gravis causes binocular diplopia that disappears when either eye is covered.
whyNot.D: Vascular imaging is for binocular diplopia from a suspected aneurysm.
whyNot.E: Thyroid eye disease restricts eye movement and causes binocular diplopia.

items.objective: Distinguish monocular from binocular diplopia and choose the right next step.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old boy has had headaches on waking for 3 weeks, often with vomiting, and his parents say he has become clumsy. Today they noticed that his left eye turns inward. He cannot move the left eye outward past the midline. He walks with a wide base and has bilateral optic disc swelling. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Morning headache with vomiting, ataxia, papilledema and a new abducens palsy point to raised intracranial pressure from a posterior fossa tumour with hydrocephalus. The abducens palsy is a false localising sign. MRI of the brain is the test of choice in children.

Takeaway: a new abducens palsy with papilledema and ataxia in a child → MRI for a posterior fossa mass.

whyNot.A: Lumbar puncture before imaging in suspected mass-related raised pressure risks herniation.
whyNot.C: Patching treats amblyopia; it does not address a new acquired palsy with raised intracranial pressure.
whyNot.D: EEG does not evaluate raised intracranial pressure or a mass.
whyNot.E: Delay is dangerous in a child with signs of raised intracranial pressure.

items.objective: Investigate a new abducens palsy with papilledema in a child with brain MRI.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man who has smoked 1 pack of cigarettes daily for 40 years has had a hoarse, breathy voice for 2 months. He has lost 5 kg (11 lb). He has had no neck surgery. Laryngoscopy shows a left vocal fold fixed in the paramedian position without a mass. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Empiric proton pump inhibitor for 8 weeks

options.label: C
options.html: CT of the neck and chest with contrast

options.label: E
options.html: Reassurance and repeat laryngoscopy in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
The left recurrent laryngeal nerve loops under the aortic arch, so its paralysis may be caused by a lung cancer or nodal mass in the aortopulmonary window, an aortic aneurysm, or a neck or thyroid tumour. CT from the skull base through the chest, following the whole nerve, is the next step in a smoker with weight loss.

Takeaway: unexplained left vocal fold paralysis → CT of the neck and chest along the recurrent laryngeal nerve.

whyNot.A: Voice therapy may help later, but the cause must be found first.
whyNot.B: Reflux does not paralyse a vocal fold.
whyNot.D: A lesion of the vagus nucleus would usually cause other brainstem signs; the recurrent nerve course is the higher-yield area.
whyNot.E: Waiting risks missing a treatable cancer.

items.objective: Investigate unexplained recurrent laryngeal nerve palsy with CT of the neck and chest.

items.stemHtml: Two weeks after an excisional biopsy of an enlarged lymph node in the posterior triangle of the right side of her neck, a 42-year-old woman cannot raise her right arm above her head. Her right shoulder droops, shrugging is weak on the right, and the scapula flares slightly outward when she abducts the arm. Sensation is normal. Which of the following nerves was most likely injured?
items.explanationHtml:
The spinal accessory nerve crosses the posterior triangle superficially and is the nerve most often injured in lymph node biopsy there. Trapezius weakness causes shoulder droop, weak shrugging, lateral scapular flaring and difficulty lifting the arm above the head. Early surgical repair gives the best results when the nerve has been cut.

Takeaway: posterior triangle surgery + weak shrug and shoulder droop = spinal accessory nerve injury.

whyNot.A: Long thoracic injury causes medial winging and does not weaken shrugging.
whyNot.B: Axillary nerve injury weakens the deltoid and numbs the lateral shoulder; shrug is normal.
whyNot.C: Suprascapular injury weakens abduction initiation and external rotation, not shrugging.
whyNot.D: A C5 root lesion would weaken the deltoid and biceps and reduce the biceps reflex, often with neck pain.

items.objective: Recognise spinal accessory nerve injury after posterior triangle surgery.

items.stemHtml: On the day after a left carotid endarterectomy, a 71-year-old man has slightly slurred speech. His voice is normal. When he protrudes his tongue, it deviates to the left. Facial movements, palate and limb strength are normal. Which nerve was most likely injured during the operation?

options.label: E
options.html: Marginal mandibular branch of the left facial nerve

items.explanationHtml:
The hypoglossal nerve crosses the internal and external carotid arteries high in the surgical field and can be stretched by retraction. A left lesion lets the intact right genioglossus push the tongue to the left. Most such injuries are neurapraxias that recover.

Takeaway: after carotid surgery, tongue deviation toward the operated side means hypoglossal nerve injury.

whyNot.A: A right hypoglossal lesion would push the tongue to the right, and the right side was not operated on.
whyNot.C: The glossopharyngeal nerve does not move the tongue.
whyNot.D: Vagus or recurrent laryngeal injury would cause hoarseness; his voice is normal.
whyNot.E: The marginal mandibular branch weakens the lower lip, not the tongue.

items.objective: Identify hypoglossal nerve injury after carotid endarterectomy.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with a known non-functioning pituitary macroadenoma develops a sudden, severe headache, vomiting and double vision. Blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg and pulse is 112/min. He has bilateral temporal visual field loss, ptosis of the right eye with the eye turned down and out, and a dilated right pupil. Serum sodium is 129 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L). Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden headache, visual loss and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with a pituitary adenoma is pituitary apoplexy: haemorrhage or infarction expands the tumour into the cavernous sinuses and optic chiasm. Hypotension and hyponatraemia suggest acute adrenal insufficiency from loss of ACTH. High-dose IV hydrocortisone is life-saving and comes first, followed by MRI and neurosurgical review for decompression.

Takeaway: pituitary apoplexy with hypotension → IV hydrocortisone first, then MRI and neurosurgery.

whyNot.B: Dopamine agonists treat prolactinomas over weeks; they do not address acute adrenal crisis.
whyNot.C: Thrombolysis is for ischaemic stroke and would worsen haemorrhage.
whyNot.D: Lumbar puncture does not treat the adrenal crisis or the mass effect.
whyNot.E: Mannitol lowers raised intracranial pressure from cerebral oedema; the danger here is adrenal insufficiency and local mass effect.

items.objective: Give glucocorticoids first in pituitary apoplexy with cranial neuropathy and hypotension.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman at 32 weeks' gestation has had numbness and tingling of the thumb, index and middle fingers of both hands for 3 weeks. The symptoms wake her at night and ease when she shakes her hands. Tapping over the palmar wrist reproduces the tingling. There is no thenar wasting and strength is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Surgical release of the transverse carpal ligament

options.label: E
options.html: Night-time wrist splints in a neutral position

items.explanationHtml:
Fluid retention in pregnancy often causes carpal tunnel syndrome, which usually resolves after delivery. Without weakness or wasting, neutral wrist splints at night are first-line; a local corticosteroid injection is an option if symptoms are troublesome.

Takeaway: mild carpal tunnel syndrome, especially in pregnancy: night splints first.

whyNot.A: Electrodiagnostic testing is not required before conservative treatment of a typical case.
whyNot.B: Surgery is reserved for wasting, weakness, severe conduction findings or failure of conservative care.
whyNot.C: The classic median distribution and nocturnal pattern point to the wrist, not the neck.
whyNot.D: Systemic glucocorticoids are not appropriate for mild carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy.

items.objective: Manage mild carpal tunnel syndrome in pregnancy with night splinting.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old man has had numbness of the thumb, index and middle fingers of the right hand for 2 years despite night splints and two corticosteroid injections. He now drops objects. There is visible wasting of the thenar eminence and weak thumb abduction. Nerve conduction studies show severely prolonged median distal latency with reduced amplitude across the wrist. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: Surgical release of the carpal tunnel

options.label: D
options.html: Continued night splinting for 6 more months

items.explanationHtml:
Thenar wasting, weakness and severe conduction findings mean axonal loss in carpal tunnel syndrome. Surgical decompression should not be delayed, because function lost to prolonged compression may not return.

Takeaway: carpal tunnel syndrome with thenar wasting or severe conduction findings → surgical release.

whyNot.A: Repeated injections have failed and do not reverse axonal loss.
whyNot.C: Gabapentin may ease pain but does not relieve the compression.
whyNot.D: Continued splinting risks permanent loss of median function.
whyNot.E: Transposition treats ulnar neuropathy at the elbow, not median compression at the wrist.

items.objective: Refer carpal tunnel syndrome with axonal loss for surgical release.

items.stemHtml:
A 58-year-old man has had weight loss and fatigue for 4 months. Three weeks ago he developed a painful right wrist drop, and this week a painful left foot drop. He has a lacy, purple rash on his legs. Blood pressure is 172/98 mm Hg. Laboratory results:

TestResultReference range
ESR88 mm/h0–15 mm/h
Creatinine1.7 mg/dL0.6–1.2 mg/dL
Hepatitis B surface antigenPositiveNegative
ANCA (MPO and PR3)NegativeNegative
UrinalysisNo red cell castsNo casts

Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Painful, stepwise failure of separate nerves is mononeuritis multiplex. With hypertension, kidney involvement without glomerulonephritis, livedo, negative ANCA and hepatitis B infection, the cause is polyarteritis nodosa, a necrotising vasculitis of medium-sized arteries. A nerve and muscle biopsy or angiography confirms it. Treatment includes glucocorticoids, antiviral therapy and often plasma exchange for hepatitis B–associated disease.

Takeaway: mononeuritis multiplex + hepatitis B + hypertension + ANCA-negative = polyarteritis nodosa.

whyNot.A: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is usually PR3-ANCA positive and involves the airways and causes glomerulonephritis.
whyNot.B: CIDP is symmetric, demyelinating and progresses over months without systemic features.
whyNot.D: Diabetic radiculoplexus neuropathy affects the thigh in a diabetic patient and does not explain the systemic findings.
whyNot.E: Multiple sclerosis affects the central nervous system, not individual peripheral nerves.

items.objective: Recognise polyarteritis nodosa as a cause of mononeuritis multiplex.

items.stemHtml: A 52-year-old woman is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes today. She has no foot symptoms. When should she first be screened for diabetic peripheral neuropathy?
items.explanationHtml:
Type 2 diabetes may have been present for years before diagnosis, so neuropathy screening starts at diagnosis and is repeated annually. Screening uses the history plus a 10-g monofilament and at least one other test (pinprick, temperature or 128-Hz vibration). People with type 1 diabetes start 5 years after diagnosis.

Takeaway: screen for diabetic neuropathy at diagnosis of type 2 diabetes and every year after.

whyNot.B: Five years after diagnosis is the starting point for type 1 diabetes.
whyNot.C: Neuropathy is often painless; waiting for symptoms misses loss of protective sensation.
whyNot.D: Screening does not depend on glucose control.
whyNot.E: Annual screening is recommended from diagnosis, regardless of age.

items.objective: Apply the timing of diabetic neuropathy screening.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman lost 18 kg (40 lb) after bariatric surgery. She noticed that her right foot slaps the floor when she walks. She often sits with her legs crossed. Ankle dorsiflexion and eversion are 2/5 on the right; inversion and plantar flexion are 5/5. Hip abduction is normal. She has numbness over the dorsum of the right foot and lower lateral leg. Reflexes are normal. Tapping behind the fibular head causes tingling down the leg. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: A
options.html: L5 radiculopathy from a disc herniation

options.label: B
options.html: Sciatic neuropathy at the sciatic notch

options.label: D
options.html: Common fibular neuropathy at the fibular head

options.label: E
options.html: Deep fibular neuropathy at the ankle

items.explanationHtml:
Rapid weight loss reduces the fat padding over the fibular head, and leg crossing compresses the common fibular nerve there. Weak dorsiflexion and eversion with preserved inversion and hip abduction, numbness of the lateral leg and dorsum, and a Tinel sign at the fibular head localise the lesion. Avoiding leg crossing and using an ankle-foot orthosis usually lead to recovery.

Takeaway: foot drop with normal inversion and hip abduction = common fibular neuropathy, not L5.

whyNot.A: L5 radiculopathy weakens inversion and hip abduction as well, usually with back pain.
whyNot.B: A sciatic lesion would also weaken plantar flexion and inversion and the hamstrings.
whyNot.C: Tibial neuropathy weakens plantar flexion and inversion and numbs the sole.
whyNot.E: A deep fibular lesion at the ankle spares eversion and lateral leg sensation.

items.objective: Distinguish common fibular neuropathy from L5 radiculopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old man with obesity has had burning and numbness over the outer front of his left thigh for 2 months. He recently started wearing a heavy tool belt at work. Strength, reflexes and the straight-leg raise test are normal. Pressing just medial to the anterior superior iliac spine reproduces his symptoms. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: C
options.html: Removing the belt, plus weight loss

items.explanationHtml:
Pure sensory symptoms in the anterolateral thigh with a normal motor and reflex examination are meralgia paresthetica, entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve under the inguinal ligament. Removing the compression (belts, tight clothing), weight loss and reassurance resolve most cases.

Takeaway: meralgia paresthetica: remove the compression and reassure.

whyNot.A: Imaging is not needed when strength, reflexes and the straight-leg raise are normal.
whyNot.B: Conduction studies of this small sensory nerve are technically difficult and unnecessary in a typical case.
whyNot.D: Surgery is reserved for rare persistent, disabling cases.
whyNot.E: Systemic glucocorticoids have no role.

items.objective: Manage meralgia paresthetica conservatively.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old truck driver rests his left elbow on the open window during long drives. For 3 months he has had numbness of the little finger and the adjacent half of the ring finger on both the palm and the back of the hand. Finger abduction strength is 5−/5, and there is no wasting. Tapping behind the medial epicondyle reproduces the tingling. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: A
options.html: Avoid pressure on the elbow and splint it in partial extension at night

options.label: B
options.html: Surgical anterior transposition of the ulnar nerve

options.label: C
options.html: Corticosteroid injection into the carpal tunnel

items.explanationHtml:
Sensory-predominant ulnar neuropathy at the elbow without significant weakness or wasting is treated conservatively: stop leaning on the elbow, avoid prolonged elbow flexion, and use a padded night splint holding the elbow fairly straight. Surgery is considered for weakness, wasting or failure after about 3–6 months.

Takeaway: mild ulnar neuropathy at the elbow → avoid pressure and flexion, night splint.

whyNot.B: Surgery is for motor deficits, wasting or failed conservative care.
whyNot.C: The carpal tunnel holds the median nerve, not the ulnar nerve.
whyNot.D: Dorsal and palmar ulnar-side numbness with a Tinel sign at the elbow localises to the elbow, not the neck.
whyNot.E: A neuropathic pain drug does not address the compression.

items.objective: Choose conservative management for mild ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man has had slowly progressive numbness and tingling in both feet for 9 months, now to the ankles. He drinks 1–2 beers per week and takes no medications. Ankle reflexes are absent, and vibration sense is reduced at the toes. Strength is normal. Complete blood count and TSH are normal. Which of the following additional tests has the highest diagnostic yield?

options.label: A
options.html: Sural nerve biopsy and anti-Hu antibodies

options.label: B
options.html: Glucose tolerance test, vitamin B<sub>12</sub> level and serum immunofixation

options.label: C
options.html: MRI of the lumbar spine and CSF protein

options.label: D
options.html: Genetic testing for PMP22 duplication and heavy-metal screen

items.explanationHtml:
In a distal symmetric sensory polyneuropathy, the most productive tests are for glucose dysregulation (an oral glucose tolerance test detects more than fasting glucose alone), vitamin B12 deficiency (with methylmalonic acid if borderline) and a monoclonal protein (serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation). These find a treatable cause in a large share of patients.

Takeaway: first-line tests in distal symmetric polyneuropathy: glucose tolerance, B12 and immunofixation.

whyNot.A: Nerve biopsy and paraneoplastic antibodies are for atypical, rapidly progressive or asymmetric neuropathies.
whyNot.C: A length-dependent symmetric pattern does not point to the lumbar spine.
whyNot.D: Hereditary neuropathy presents earlier with foot deformity, and heavy-metal toxicity is uncommon without exposure.
whyNot.E: These tests target vasculitis and multifocal motor neuropathy, which have asymmetric or motor patterns.

items.objective: Choose the highest-yield tests for distal symmetric polyneuropathy.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old woman has had attacks of severe, stabbing pain in the left lower jaw and chin for 2 months. Each attack lasts a few seconds and is set off by chewing, talking or a breeze on her face. Between attacks she is pain-free. Neurological examination, including facial sensation and the corneal reflex, is normal. MRI of the brain shows no lesion. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?
items.explanationHtml:
Brief, triggered, electric pains in the mandibular division with a normal examination are classic trigeminal neuralgia. Carbamazepine (or oxcarbazepine) is first-line; monitor sodium and blood counts.

Takeaway: carbamazepine is first-line for trigeminal neuralgia.

whyNot.A: Indomethacin treats paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua, which are not triggered by touch.
whyNot.B: Opioids are ineffective for the paroxysmal pain of trigeminal neuralgia.
whyNot.C: Triptans treat migraine and cluster headache.
whyNot.D: Glucocorticoids are not used for trigeminal neuralgia.

items.objective: Treat classic trigeminal neuralgia with carbamazepine.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman has had brief, electric-shock pains in the right cheek, set off by touching her face, for 3 weeks. Two years ago she had blurred vision and pain on moving her left eye, which resolved over 6 weeks. Examination shows mildly reduced pinprick sensation over the right cheek. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: B
options.html: MRI of the brain with gadolinium

options.label: D
options.html: Reassurance and carbamazepine with no further testing

items.explanationHtml:
Trigeminal neuralgia in a young patient with sensory loss and a past episode suggestive of optic neuritis raises concern for multiple sclerosis (a demyelinating plaque at the trigeminal entry zone in the pons) or another secondary cause. MRI of the brain with contrast is needed; it is in fact advised for all patients with trigeminal neuralgia.

Takeaway: young age, sensory loss or bilateral pain in trigeminal neuralgia → MRI for MS or a structural cause.

whyNot.A: Surgery is considered only after imaging and failure of drug treatment.
whyNot.C: The triggered, electric pain is neuropathic, not dental.
whyNot.D: Her red flags call for imaging before treatment alone.
whyNot.E: ESR is used to screen for giant cell arteritis, which causes jaw claudication in older adults, not electric pains.

items.objective: Recognise red flags for secondary trigeminal neuralgia and obtain MRI.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old man has had trigeminal neuralgia in the right maxillary division for 4 years. Carbamazepine controlled it until he developed hyponatraemia; oxcarbazepine caused the same problem, and other drugs have not helped. He is otherwise healthy. MRI shows a loop of the superior cerebellar artery compressing the right trigeminal root. Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: B
options.html: Microvascular decompression of the trigeminal root

options.label: D
options.html: Extraction of the right upper molars

items.explanationHtml:
For a fit patient with drug-refractory trigeminal neuralgia and a compressing vessel on MRI, microvascular decompression gives the most durable relief while preserving facial sensation. Percutaneous ablation or stereotactic radiosurgery suits older or higher-risk patients.

Takeaway: drug-refractory trigeminal neuralgia with neurovascular compression in a fit patient → microvascular decompression.

whyNot.A: Opioids do not control trigeminal neuralgia and add risk.
whyNot.C: Aspirin has no effect on trigeminal neuralgia.
whyNot.D: Dental extraction does not help neuropathic facial pain and is a common error.
whyNot.E: Occipital nerve blocks are used for some headaches, not for trigeminal neuralgia.

items.objective: Choose microvascular decompression for refractory trigeminal neuralgia.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman has burning pain and sensitivity to clothing in a band on her right chest wall where she had shingles 4 months ago. She has narrow-angle glaucoma, orthostatic hypotension and a history of falls. Creatinine is 1.0 mg/dL (0.6–1.2 mg/dL). Which of the following is the most appropriate initial treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
This is postherpetic neuralgia: pain persisting 3 months or more after the rash. For localised pain in an older adult, a topical lidocaine patch is a first-line choice with minimal systemic effects. Gabapentinoids are an alternative but cause dizziness and sedation that raise fall risk.

Takeaway: localised postherpetic neuralgia in an older adult → topical lidocaine.

whyNot.A: Tricyclics worsen orthostatic hypotension and falls and can precipitate angle-closure glaucoma.
whyNot.B: Opioids are not first-line and raise the risk of falls, confusion and constipation.
whyNot.D: Antivirals treat acute zoster; they do not relieve established postherpetic neuralgia.
whyNot.E: Glucocorticoids do not treat postherpetic neuralgia.

items.objective: Choose topical lidocaine for postherpetic neuralgia in a frail older adult.

items.stemHtml: A healthy 55-year-old man asks how to avoid shingles; his father had severe nerve pain after it. He had chickenpox as a child and has never received a zoster vaccine. He takes no medications. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation?

options.label: C
options.html: Recombinant zoster vaccine, 2 doses 2–6 months apart

options.label: D
options.html: Serology for varicella antibodies before deciding

options.label: E
options.html: A single dose of recombinant zoster vaccine now

items.explanationHtml:
The recombinant zoster vaccine is recommended as a 2-dose series (2–6 months apart) for adults aged 50 or older, and for immunocompromised adults aged 19 or older. It markedly reduces shingles and postherpetic neuralgia. Prior chickenpox, prior shingles or unknown history do not change the recommendation, and serology is not needed.

Takeaway: adults ≥50: recombinant zoster vaccine, 2 doses.

whyNot.A: The recommended starting age is 50.
whyNot.B: The varicella vaccine prevents primary chickenpox in non-immune people; it is not the zoster prevention vaccine.
whyNot.D: Serologic testing is not needed before zoster vaccination.
whyNot.E: One dose gives incomplete protection; the series is 2 doses.

items.objective: Recommend the recombinant zoster vaccine for adults aged 50 and older.

items.stemHtml: Seven weeks after a distal radius fracture was treated with a cast, a 45-year-old woman has severe burning pain throughout her right hand. Light touch is painful.
