items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man taking sertraline for depression is treated for a vancomycin-resistant enterococcal infection. On the third day of the antibiotic he becomes agitated, sweaty and tremulous. He has a temperature of 38.6°C (101.5°F), dilated pupils, hyperactive reflexes and inducible clonus at both ankles. Which property of the antibiotic best explains this reaction?

options.label: A
options.html: Inhibition of the bacterial 50S ribosomal subunit

options.label: B
options.html: Inhibition of CYP2D6, raising sertraline levels

items.explanationHtml:
Linezolid, used for VRE, is a weak, nonselective, reversible MAO inhibitor. Combined with an SSRI it can cause serotonin syndrome: agitation, hyperthermia, mydriasis, hyperreflexia and clonus, worse in the legs.

Takeaway: linezolid is an MAO inhibitor; with SSRIs it can cause serotonin syndrome.

whyNot.A: This is its antibacterial action and does not affect serotonin.
whyNot.B: The reaction is not explained by a pharmacokinetic interaction.
whyNot.C: D<sub>2</sub> blockade causes rigidity and neuroleptic malignant syndrome, not clonus.
whyNot.D: GABA<sub>A</sub> antagonism by some antibiotics lowers the seizure threshold, but does not cause this syndrome.

items.objective: Explain linezolid-associated serotonin syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old man with schizophrenia was started on haloperidol 5 days ago. He is brought to the emergency department because he has become confused and stiff. Temperature is 40.1°C (104.2°F), pulse is 124/min and blood pressure fluctuates between 150/95 and 190/110 mm Hg. He is diaphoretic, with generalized lead-pipe rigidity and reduced reflexes. There is no clonus. Creatine kinase is 18,500 U/L. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial step in management?

options.label: E
options.html: Stop haloperidol; cool, hydrate and monitor

items.explanationHtml:
Fever, lead-pipe rigidity, autonomic instability, altered mental status and a very high CK after starting an antipsychotic are neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Management: stop the dopamine antagonist, cool, give IV fluids (to protect the kidneys from rhabdomyolysis) and benzodiazepines in intensive care. Dantrolene or bromocriptine are added for severe or persistent cases.

Takeaway: neuroleptic malignant syndrome: stop the antipsychotic, cool, hydrate; dantrolene or bromocriptine if severe.

whyNot.A: Cyproheptadine treats serotonin syndrome, which causes clonus and hyperreflexia rather than rigidity.
whyNot.B: Any dopamine antagonist can sustain the syndrome; all must be stopped.
whyNot.C: Physostigmine is for anticholinergic toxicity, which causes dry skin and normal tone.
whyNot.D: Hyperthermia here comes from muscle rigidity and central dysregulation; antipyretics do not address it, and he needs active treatment.

items.objective: Manage neuroleptic malignant syndrome.

items.stemHtml: A 44-year-old woman taking escitalopram for depression was given tramadol for back pain 2 days ago. She now has agitation, shivering, sweating and diarrhea. Temperature is 38.4°C (101.1°F) and pulse is 118/min. Pupils are dilated. Reflexes are brisk with sustained clonus at both ankles and inducible clonus at the wrists. Muscle tone is otherwise normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial management?

options.label: C
options.html: Continue escitalopram and stop tramadol only

options.label: D
options.html: Stop both drugs and give a benzodiazepine

items.explanationHtml:
Clonus, hyperreflexia, mydriasis, diarrhea and fever after combining an SSRI with tramadol are serotonin syndrome. Initial management is to stop all serotonergic drugs, give supportive care and benzodiazepines for agitation. Cyproheptadine is added if symptoms persist. Severe hyperthermia needs ICU care, sedation and paralysis.

Takeaway: serotonin syndrome: stop serotonergic drugs, give benzodiazepines; cyproheptadine if not settling.

whyNot.A: Dantrolene is used for severe neuroleptic malignant syndrome and malignant hyperthermia, not serotonin toxicity.
whyNot.B: Antipsychotics are not first-line and risk confusion with neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
whyNot.C: Both serotonergic drugs should be stopped until the syndrome settles.
whyNot.E: Bromocriptine is a dopamine agonist for neuroleptic malignant syndrome and can worsen serotonin toxicity.

items.objective: Manage serotonin syndrome caused by an SSRI-tramadol interaction.

items.stemHtml: A 22-year-old woman receives IV metoclopramide in the emergency department for vomiting from gastroenteritis. Three hours later her head pulls to one side, her jaw clenches and her tongue protrudes. She is alert and frightened. Temperature is 37.0°C (98.6°F). Which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?
items.explanationHtml:
Sudden sustained muscle contractions within hours of a dopamine-blocking antiemetic are acute dystonia. IV or IM diphenhydramine or benztropine relieves it within minutes. Continue an oral antimuscarinic for a day or two to prevent recurrence.

Takeaway: acute dystonia after a dopamine antagonist: IV diphenhydramine or benztropine.

whyNot.A: Another dopamine antagonist would worsen the dystonia.
whyNot.C: Propranolol treats akathisia, not acute dystonia.
whyNot.D: Dantrolene is for neuroleptic malignant syndrome or malignant hyperthermia; she has neither.
whyNot.E: VMAT2 inhibitors treat tardive dyskinesia, which develops over months to years.

items.objective: Treat drug-induced acute dystonia.

items.stemHtml: A 55-year-old man with schizophrenia has been stable for 15 years on risperidone. His sister notices constant lip pursing, tongue movements and grimacing, which have increased over 2 years. He is not distressed by his psychosis, which has been well controlled, and a previous attempt to reduce the dose led to relapse. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
Slow-onset involuntary orofacial movements after years of antipsychotic treatment are tardive dyskinesia. When the antipsychotic must continue, add a VMAT2 inhibitor (valbenazine or deutetrabenazine). Switching to clozapine is another option for some patients.

Takeaway: tardive dyskinesia on a needed antipsychotic: add a VMAT2 inhibitor; avoid anticholinergics.

whyNot.A: Antimuscarinic drugs do not help tardive dyskinesia and may worsen it.
whyNot.B: Stopping risks relapse of his schizophrenia, as before.
whyNot.D: A stronger D<sub>2</sub> antagonist carries a higher risk of worsening tardive dyskinesia.
whyNot.E: Propranolol treats akathisia and tremor, not tardive dyskinesia.

items.objective: Manage tardive dyskinesia in a patient who must remain on an antipsychotic.

items.stemHtml:
A 72-year-old woman with epilepsy who takes phenytoin is admitted with pneumonia. Over 3 days she becomes unsteady and drowsy, with coarse nystagmus on lateral gaze. She has no new neurological deficit. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Total phenytoin16 µg/mL (therapeutic 10–20 µg/mL)
Albumin2.0 g/dL (3.5–5.5 g/dL)
Creatinine1.0 mg/dL (0.6–1.2 mg/dL)
Sodium139 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L)
Glucose108 mg/dL (70–100 mg/dL fasting)

Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Hold phenytoin and measure the free phenytoin level

options.label: C
options.html: Continue the same dose because the level is therapeutic

options.label: D
options.html: Obtain an urgent MRI of the brain

items.explanationHtml:
Phenytoin is about 90% bound to albumin. With an albumin of 2.0 g/dL the free (active) fraction rises, so a normal total level can hide toxicity. Nystagmus, ataxia and drowsiness fit. Hold the drug and measure the free level; if it is unavailable, a corrected total level estimates the free drug.

Takeaway: in hypoalbuminemia, phenytoin toxicity can occur with a normal total level: check the free level.

whyNot.A: Her symptoms are those of toxicity; a higher dose would worsen them.
whyNot.C: The total level understates the active free drug when albumin is low.
whyNot.D: Nystagmus and ataxia with a likely high free level are explained by toxicity; imaging is not the first step.
whyNot.E: An abrupt switch is not needed; first confirm toxicity and hold doses until it resolves.

items.objective: Recognize phenytoin toxicity hidden by hypoalbuminemia.

items.stemHtml: A 39-year-old woman is found unresponsive at home with an empty bottle of her alprazolam and an empty bottle of her amitriptyline. She has taken alprazolam daily for 6 years. Respirations are 9/min and shallow, blood pressure is 102/64 mm Hg and oxygen saturation is 91% on room air. The ECG shows a QRS duration of 128 ms. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Airway support and IV sodium bicarbonate

items.explanationHtml:
She has mixed sedative and tricyclic toxicity. Support her airway and breathing, and treat the QRS widening from tricyclic sodium channel blockade with IV sodium bicarbonate. Flumazenil is avoided: in chronic benzodiazepine users and after proconvulsant co-ingestion it can provoke seizures that are hard to control.

Takeaway: avoid flumazenil in benzodiazepine dependence or tricyclic co-ingestion; support the airway and treat the tricyclic.

whyNot.A: Flumazenil can trigger seizures here because she is benzodiazepine-dependent and has taken a tricyclic.
whyNot.B: There is no evidence of opioid ingestion, and the wide QRS needs specific treatment.
whyNot.C: Lavage without a protected airway risks aspiration and is rarely indicated.
whyNot.E: Physostigmine is contraindicated in tricyclic overdose with QRS widening because it can cause asystole.

items.objective: Avoid flumazenil and manage mixed benzodiazepine-tricyclic overdose safely.

items.stemHtml: A 48-year-old man had a kidney transplant 4 weeks ago and takes tacrolimus, mycophenolate and prednisone. He develops a severe headache, confusion and blurred vision, followed by a generalized seizure. Blood pressure is 196/112 mm Hg. MRI of the brain shows symmetrical T2 hyperintensity in the white matter of both occipital and parietal lobes, without restricted diffusion. In addition to seizure control, which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Start IV acyclovir for herpes encephalitis

options.label: D
options.html: Start IV heparin for venous sinus thrombosis

options.label: E
options.html: Lower the blood pressure and reduce or replace tacrolimus

items.explanationHtml:
Headache, confusion, visual loss and seizures with posterior, symmetrical vasogenic edema in a hypertensive patient on a calcineurin inhibitor are posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome. Treat by controlling blood pressure and reducing or switching tacrolimus. It usually resolves if recognized early.

Takeaway: PRES (calcineurin inhibitor, hypertension, posterior edema): lower BP and stop or change the drug.

whyNot.A: Herpes encephalitis affects the temporal lobes asymmetrically and does not match this symmetrical posterior pattern.
whyNot.B: There is no ischemic stroke; the lesions are vasogenic edema without restricted diffusion.
whyNot.C: Steroids do not treat this syndrome; the causes are the blood pressure and the calcineurin inhibitor.
whyNot.D: The imaging and setting point to PRES, not venous thrombosis.

items.objective: Recognize and manage tacrolimus-associated PRES.

items.stemHtml: An 81-year-old woman is brought to the physician because she has become confused over 2 weeks. She was recently started on oxybutynin for urge incontinence and has also been taking diphenhydramine at night for sleep. She has a dry mouth, constipation and a palpable bladder. Temperature is 37.1°C (98.8°F). She is inattentive and disoriented to date. There are no focal neurological signs. Urinalysis is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Add lorazepam at night for sleep

items.explanationHtml:
She has delirium from anticholinergic burden (oxybutynin plus diphenhydramine), with dry mouth, constipation and urinary retention. Both drugs are on lists of medications to avoid in older adults. Stop them, relieve urinary retention, and use non-drug sleep measures. Behavioural therapy or a non-anticholinergic option can manage the incontinence.

Takeaway: in older adults, new confusion with anticholinergic signs calls for deprescribing the culprits.

whyNot.B: Antipsychotics do not treat the cause and add risk in older adults.
whyNot.C: This is delirium from anticholinergic drugs, not dementia; donepezil is not the next step.
whyNot.D: Benzodiazepines worsen delirium and fall risk in older adults.
whyNot.E: A clear drug cause and no focal signs make imaging a low priority; stop the drugs first.

items.objective: Manage anticholinergic delirium in an older adult by deprescribing.

items.stemHtml: A 57-year-old woman completed 6 months of adjuvant paclitaxel chemotherapy for breast cancer 2 months ago. She now has persistent burning pain and numbness in both feet and fingertips that disturb her sleep. Examination shows reduced pinprick and vibration sense in a stocking-glove pattern and absent ankle reflexes. Her strength is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate drug for her pain?
items.explanationHtml:
This is painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy from a taxane. Duloxetine, a serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor, is the drug with the best evidence for this pain. Prevention depends mainly on dose reduction or delay during chemotherapy.

Takeaway: duloxetine is the drug of choice for painful chemotherapy-induced neuropathy.

whyNot.A: Opioids are not first-line for chemotherapy-induced neuropathic pain and carry dependence risk.
whyNot.B: Vitamin E has not been shown to prevent or treat this neuropathy.
whyNot.D: Corticosteroids do not treat toxic axonal neuropathy.
whyNot.E: Acetyl-L-carnitine is not recommended and may worsen taxane neuropathy.

items.objective: Choose duloxetine for painful chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has latent tuberculosis infection. He will start a 9-month course of isoniazid, because rifamycin regimens are unsuitable owing to drug interactions with his other medications. He drinks 2–3 beers on most days. Which of the following should be added to his isoniazid?
items.explanationHtml:
Isoniazid depletes pyridoxine and can cause peripheral neuropathy. Pyridoxine is given with isoniazid to people at higher risk: diabetes, alcohol use, malnutrition, HIV, chronic kidney disease, pregnancy and breastfeeding. He has two risk factors.

Takeaway: give pyridoxine with isoniazid when there are risk factors for neuropathy.

whyNot.A: Folic acid does not prevent isoniazid neuropathy.
whyNot.C: Thiamine prevents Wernicke encephalopathy, not isoniazid neuropathy.
whyNot.D: Vitamin B<sub>12</sub> does not counter isoniazid's effect on pyridoxine.
whyNot.E: Riboflavin has no role in isoniazid toxicity.

items.objective: Prevent isoniazid neuropathy with pyridoxine in high-risk patients.

items.stemHtml:
A 31-year-old man with bipolar disorder has taken valproate for 2 months. His wife brings him in because he has become increasingly drowsy and confused over 3 days. He has no fever or focal neurological signs. Asterixis is present. Laboratory studies show:

TestResult
Valproate level88 µg/mL (therapeutic 50–100 µg/mL)
Ammonia186 µg/dL (normal under 50 µg/dL)
AST24 U/L (12–38 U/L)
ALT30 U/L (10–40 U/L)
Bilirubin, total0.6 mg/dL (0.1–1.0 mg/dL)
Sodium140 mEq/L (136–145 mEq/L)

Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: B
options.html: Continue valproate because the level is therapeutic

options.label: E
options.html: Increase the valproate dose to treat a mixed episode

items.explanationHtml:
Drowsiness, confusion and asterixis with high ammonia and normal liver tests on valproate are valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy. Valproate impairs urea cycle function, partly through carnitine depletion. Stop the drug; levocarnitine is given to symptomatic patients. Choose another mood stabilizer.

Takeaway: valproate can cause hyperammonemic encephalopathy with normal liver tests: stop it and give levocarnitine.

whyNot.B: Hyperammonemic encephalopathy can occur at therapeutic levels and requires stopping the drug.
whyNot.C: Lactulose lowers ammonia but leaves the cause in place.
whyNot.D: Liver tests and bilirubin are normal; this is not hepatotoxicity.
whyNot.E: His confusion is from hyperammonemia, not mood; more valproate would worsen it.

items.objective: Recognize and manage valproate-induced hyperammonemic encephalopathy.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis, controlled on pyridostigmine, develops acute bacterial cystitis. She is allergic to sulfonamides. Two days after starting an oral antibiotic, she develops drooping eyelids, double vision and difficulty swallowing. Which of the following antibiotics was she most likely given?
items.explanationHtml:
Fluoroquinolones carry a warning that they can exacerbate myasthenia gravis, sometimes severely, by impairing neuromuscular transmission. Aminoglycosides, magnesium and some β-blockers do the same. For cystitis in this patient, nitrofurantoin or fosfomycin would be a better choice.

Takeaway: fluoroquinolones and aminoglycosides can trigger myasthenic crises.

whyNot.A: Nitrofurantoin is not known to worsen myasthenia.
whyNot.B: Fosfomycin is not associated with myasthenic exacerbations.
whyNot.C: β-lactams are generally considered safe in myasthenia.
whyNot.D: Penicillins are generally considered safe in myasthenia.

items.objective: Identify drugs that exacerbate myasthenia gravis.

items.stemHtml: A 4-day-old boy is brought to the emergency department because both of his eyes have become swollen and are draining thick yellow pus that reappears within minutes of being wiped away. He was born at home, and his mother had no prenatal care. A Gram stain of the discharge shows gram-negative diplococci inside neutrophils. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Hyperacute, copious, rapidly reaccumulating pus in the first days of life with gram-negative intracellular diplococci is gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum, acquired during birth from an infected mother. It can perforate the cornea within days and is treated as an emergency.

Takeaway: neonatal conjunctivitis in days 2–5 with gram-negative diplococci is gonococcal.

whyNot.B: Chlamydia is an obligate intracellular bacterium that does not show on Gram stain, and neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis usually starts later, around days 5–14.
whyNot.C: Haemophilus is a gram-negative coccobacillus, not a diplococcus, and it is not a typical cause of hyperacute neonatal conjunctivitis.
whyNot.D: Pseudomonas is a gram-negative rod; it causes keratitis in contact lens wearers and infections in sick premature infants, not this picture.
whyNot.E: S. aureus is a gram-positive coccus in clusters.

items.objective: Identify Neisseria gonorrhoeae as the cause of hyperacute neonatal conjunctivitis from its timing and Gram stain.

items.stemHtml: An 11-day-old girl is brought to the clinic because of swelling of both eyelids and a watery discharge that has become mucopurulent over 3 days. She received erythromycin ointment in both eyes at birth. She is feeding well and is afebrile. Giemsa staining of conjunctival scrapings shows intracytoplasmic inclusions within epithelial cells. Without systemic treatment, this infant is at greatest risk for which of the following over the next several weeks?

options.label: B
options.html: Afebrile pneumonia with a staccato cough

items.explanationHtml:
Onset in the second week and intracytoplasmic inclusion bodies point to Chlamydia trachomatis, acquired at delivery. Erythromycin ointment does not reliably prevent it. The organism also colonises the nasopharynx, and untreated infants can develop an afebrile pneumonia at about 1–3 months with a repetitive staccato cough, tachypnoea and sometimes eosinophilia. That is why treatment is systemic.

Takeaway: neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis needs systemic treatment because it can be followed by afebrile pneumonia.

whyNot.A: Neonatal meningitis is caused mainly by group B streptococci, E. coli and Listeria, not by Chlamydia trachomatis.
whyNot.C: Septic arthritis can complicate disseminated gonococcal infection, not chlamydial infection.
whyNot.D: Hearing loss follows congenital infections such as CMV and rubella, not chlamydial conjunctivitis.
whyNot.E: Hepatosplenomegaly fits congenital infections such as CMV, syphilis or toxoplasmosis.

items.objective: Recognise neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis and its association with later afebrile pneumonia.

items.stemHtml: A 24-year-old woman comes to the emergency department with severe pain, redness and blurred vision in her right eye that began yesterday. She wears soft contact lenses and often sleeps in them. Slit-lamp examination shows a white corneal infiltrate with an overlying epithelial defect and a layer of pus in the anterior chamber. Culture of corneal scrapings grows an oxidase-positive, gram-negative rod that makes a blue-green pigment. Which of the following organisms is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Contact lens–related keratitis, especially with overnight wear, is classically caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa: an oxidase-positive, gram-negative rod that makes blue-green pyocyanin and pyoverdine. Its proteases can melt the cornea within a day, so this is an ophthalmic emergency.

Takeaway: contact lens wearer plus rapidly progressive corneal ulcer equals Pseudomonas until proven otherwise.

whyNot.A: Serratia can infect contact lens wearers but is oxidase negative and makes a red pigment.
whyNot.B: E. coli is oxidase negative, makes no pigment and is an uncommon cause of keratitis.
whyNot.D: Klebsiella is an oxidase-negative, mucoid, nonpigmented rod.
whyNot.E: Moraxella is oxidase positive but is a gram-negative diplococcus without pigment.

items.objective: Identify Pseudomonas aeruginosa as the classic cause of contact lens–associated bacterial keratitis.

items.stemHtml: A 27-year-old man comes to the clinic because of pain, redness and sensitivity to light in his left eye for 2 days. For the past year he has had low back pain and stiffness that are worst in the morning and improve with exercise. Examination shows redness concentrated around the edge of the cornea, a small left pupil, and white cells floating in the anterior chamber. Which of the following genetic markers is most strongly associated with this patient's condition?
items.explanationHtml:
Acute anterior uveitis (pain, photophobia, ciliary flush, miosis, anterior chamber cells) in a young man with inflammatory back pain suggests ankylosing spondylitis. Acute anterior uveitis is the most common extra-articular feature of the HLA-B27–associated spondyloarthritides.

Takeaway: anterior uveitis plus inflammatory back pain points to HLA-B27 spondyloarthritis.

whyNot.A: HLA-DR3 is linked to type 1 diabetes, Graves disease and celiac disease, not to spondyloarthritis with uveitis.
whyNot.B: HLA-DR4 is linked to rheumatoid arthritis and type 1 diabetes.
whyNot.C: HLA-DQ2 is linked to celiac disease.
whyNot.E: HLA-B51 is linked to Behçet disease, which causes uveitis with oral and genital ulcers rather than inflammatory back pain.

items.objective: Associate acute anterior uveitis with HLA-B27 spondyloarthritis.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy has had nasal congestion and purulent nasal discharge for 10 days. Over the past day his left eyelids have become red and swollen, his left eye bulges forward, and it hurts when he moves the eye. Eye movements are limited in all directions. Spread of infection into the orbit most likely occurred through which of the following structures?

options.label: A
options.html: Roof of the orbit from the frontal sinus

options.label: B
options.html: Floor of the orbit from the maxillary sinus

options.label: C
options.html: Superior orbital fissure from the sphenoid sinus

options.label: D
options.html: Nasolacrimal duct from the nasal cavity

options.label: E
options.html: Medial orbital wall from the ethmoid air cells

items.explanationHtml:
Orbital cellulitis in children most often follows ethmoid sinusitis. The ethmoid air cells are separated from the orbit only by the thin lamina papyracea of the medial wall, which has small perforations for vessels and nerves. Pain on eye movement, proptosis and ophthalmoplegia show the infection is behind the orbital septum.

Takeaway: orbital cellulitis in a child usually comes from the ethmoid sinus through the medial orbital wall.

whyNot.A: The frontal sinus develops late and is a less common source in young children.
whyNot.B: The orbital floor is thicker, and the maxillary sinus is a less common source than the ethmoid air cells.
whyNot.C: Sphenoid sinusitis is uncommon and tends to threaten the optic canal and cavernous sinus rather than causing typical orbital cellulitis.
whyNot.D: Infection of the nasolacrimal system causes dacryocystitis at the medial canthus, not orbital cellulitis with restricted eye movement.

items.objective: Explain the usual route of spread of sinus infection into the orbit.

items.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man is admitted with right orbital cellulitis. Two days later he has a temperature of 39.6°C (103.3°F) and is drowsy. His right eye cannot move in any direction, his left eye now bulges with swollen conjunctiva, and he cannot abduct the left eye. Sensation is reduced over the forehead on both sides. Spread of infection by which of the following routes best explains the progression?

options.label: A
options.html: Valveless ophthalmic veins draining into the cavernous sinus

options.label: B
options.html: Ophthalmic artery branches feeding the internal carotid artery

options.label: C
options.html: Subarachnoid space around the optic nerve sheath

options.label: D
options.html: Facial lymphatics draining to the preauricular nodes

options.label: E
options.html: Pterygoid plexus draining into the sigmoid sinus

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral orbital signs, palsies of the nerves running through the sinus (III, IV, V1 and VI; the abducens nerve lies free within the sinus and is often hit first) and systemic toxicity indicate septic cavernous sinus thrombosis. The superior and inferior ophthalmic veins have no valves, so infected thrombus passes from the orbit into the cavernous sinus, and then to the other side through the intercavernous sinuses.

Takeaway: orbital or mid-face infection reaches the cavernous sinus through valveless ophthalmic veins.

whyNot.B: Infection does not spread backward along arteries against the flow; the cavernous sinus is reached through veins.
whyNot.C: Spread along the optic nerve sheath would cause meningitis and optic neuropathy, not bilateral palsies of nerves III, IV, V1 and VI.
whyNot.D: Lymphatic spread to preauricular nodes would not produce cranial nerve palsies in both orbits.
whyNot.E: The sigmoid sinus is in the posterior fossa; thrombosis there causes signs of raised pressure and mastoid involvement, not bilateral orbital signs.

items.objective: Describe the venous route by which orbital infection causes cavernous sinus thrombosis.

items.stemHtml: A 41-year-old woman has a red, watery, painful right eye for 3 days. She had a similar episode in the same eye 2 years ago. Fluorescein staining shows a branching linear ulcer with terminal bulbs on the corneal epithelium, and corneal sensation is reduced on that side. Between episodes, the causative virus most likely persists in which of the following locations?
items.explanationHtml:
A dendritic ulcer with reduced corneal sensation is herpes simplex keratitis, usually HSV-1. The virus travels up the sensory axons of the ophthalmic division and stays latent in the trigeminal ganglion, from which it reactivates. Recurrences cause stromal scarring and are a major infectious cause of corneal blindness.

Takeaway: HSV keratitis recurs from latency in the trigeminal ganglion.

whyNot.A: The geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve is linked with herpes zoster oticus, not corneal herpes.
whyNot.C: The ciliary ganglion is a parasympathetic ganglion and is not the site of herpes simplex latency for the cornea.
whyNot.D: The superior cervical ganglion is sympathetic and does not carry corneal sensation.
whyNot.E: Epithelial cells are lysed during active infection; latency is in sensory neurons.

items.objective: State the site of latency of herpes simplex virus that causes recurrent keratitis.

items.stemHtml: A 10-month-old girl is evaluated because her mother noticed a white glow in both of the child's pupils in photographs. Examination under anaesthesia shows several white, partly calcified tumours in both retinas. Genetic testing of blood shows a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation in a gene on chromosome 13q14. In normal cells, the protein encoded by this gene has which of the following functions?

options.label: A
options.html: Inactivates RAS by stimulating its GTPase activity

options.label: C
options.html: Binds E2F transcription factors until it is phosphorylated in G1

options.label: D
options.html: Repairs base mismatches after DNA replication

options.label: E
options.html: Senses DNA damage and induces transcription of p21

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral, multifocal retinoblastoma with a germline mutation at 13q14 is heritable retinoblastoma due to RB1. Hypophosphorylated RB protein binds and inhibits E2F, preventing transcription of S-phase genes. Cyclin D–CDK4/6 phosphorylates RB in late G1 and releases E2F. Losing both copies removes this brake on the G1–S transition.

Takeaway: RB holds E2F in check at the G1–S checkpoint until it is phosphorylated.

whyNot.A: This is the function of neurofibromin (NF1).
whyNot.B: This is the function of the APC protein, which is lost in familial adenomatous polyposis.
whyNot.D: Mismatch repair proteins (MLH1, MSH2 and others) are lost in Lynch syndrome.
whyNot.E: This is p53, encoded on chromosome 17p and lost in Li–Fraumeni syndrome.

items.objective: Describe the normal function of the RB protein in cell cycle control.

items.stemHtml: A 7-year-old boy was treated at 1 year of age for retinoblastoma in both eyes. He carries a germline RB1 mutation. Which of the following cancers is he at greatest increased risk of developing later in childhood or adolescence?
items.explanationHtml:
People with a germline RB1 mutation have a high lifelong risk of second primary cancers, most characteristically osteosarcoma, along with soft-tissue sarcomas and melanoma. Radiation to the orbit raises the risk further, which is why imaging and treatment try to avoid radiation.

Takeaway: survivors of heritable retinoblastoma are at risk of osteosarcoma.

whyNot.A: Wilms tumour is linked to WT1 and to overgrowth syndromes, not to RB1.
whyNot.B: Medulloblastoma is linked to Gorlin and Turcot syndromes.
whyNot.C: Neuroblastoma is associated with MYCN amplification and ALK mutations, not RB1.
whyNot.E: Hepatoblastoma is linked to Beckwith–Wiedemann syndrome and familial adenomatous polyposis.

items.objective: Recognise osteosarcoma as the characteristic second cancer after heritable retinoblastoma.

items.stemHtml: A paediatric oncologist explains retinoblastoma genetics to the parents of a newly diagnosed child. Which of the following findings in a child with retinoblastoma most strongly suggests that the child carries a germline mutation in RB1?

options.label: B
options.html: A single tumour in one eye

items.explanationHtml:
In heritable retinoblastoma every retinal cell already carries one mutant allele, so one further somatic hit in any cell produces a tumour. This makes bilateral or multifocal tumours and early onset likely. In nonheritable disease, both hits must happen in the same cell, so a single tumour in one eye is the rule. Some children with one-sided disease still carry a germline mutation, so all affected children are offered testing.

Takeaway: bilateral or multifocal retinoblastoma implies a germline RB1 mutation.

whyNot.A: Leukocoria is the most common presenting sign of both heritable and nonheritable disease.
whyNot.B: A single unilateral tumour is typical of the nonheritable form, in which both hits occur in one retinal cell.
whyNot.C: Later diagnosis is more typical of nonheritable disease; germline cases present earlier.
whyNot.D: Strabismus occurs with any tumour that affects central vision, heritable or not.

items.objective: Apply the two-hit model to distinguish heritable from nonheritable retinoblastoma.

items.stemHtml: A 63-year-old man with blue eyes has painless blurring in his left eye. Ophthalmoscopy shows a dome-shaped, brown, elevated mass arising from the choroid. Tumour testing shows a GNAQ mutation. If this tumour metastasises, which of the following is the most likely first site of distant spread?
items.explanationHtml:
A pigmented choroidal mass in an adult with light eyes is uveal melanoma, the most common primary intraocular malignancy in adults. Its drivers (GNAQ or GNA11) differ from those of skin melanoma. With no intraocular lymphatics, it spreads through the blood and shows a strong preference for the liver, which is the first and often the only site of metastasis.

Takeaway: uveal melanoma metastasises to the liver.

whyNot.B: The inside of the globe has no lymphatic drainage, so intraocular melanoma rarely spreads to lymph nodes.
whyNot.C: Brain metastases are much less common for uveal melanoma than for skin melanoma.
whyNot.D: The lung can be involved, but far less often than the liver.
whyNot.E: Bone metastases occur but are uncommon as the first site.

items.objective: State the characteristic metastatic site of uveal melanoma and the reason it spreads through blood.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old man who worked outdoors for 40 years has a slowly enlarging nodule on his right lower eyelid near the inner corner. It is 7 mm across, pearly, with fine surface vessels, rolled edges and a small central ulcer, and the lashes over it have fallen out. Which of the following findings is most likely on histological examination of a biopsy specimen?

options.label: B
options.html: Nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading

options.label: D
options.html: Atypical melanocytes along the dermoepidermal junction

items.explanationHtml:
A pearly, telangiectatic, ulcerated nodule with lash loss on the lower lid of a sun-exposed older adult is basal cell carcinoma, the most common eyelid malignancy. Histology shows nests of basaloid cells with peripheral palisading and retraction artefact around the nests. It invades locally and rarely metastasises.

Takeaway: the most common eyelid cancer is basal cell carcinoma, with palisading basaloid nests.

whyNot.A: These are features of squamous cell carcinoma, which is less common on the eyelid.
whyNot.C: Foamy, lipid-rich cells suggest sebaceous carcinoma, which tends to involve the upper lid and mimic a chalazion.
whyNot.D: This describes melanoma in situ, a pigmented lesion.
whyNot.E: This is a chalazion, which is not ulcerated or pearly and does not cause lash loss.

items.objective: Recognise eyelid basal cell carcinoma and its histological features.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old woman has a firm, painless lump in her left upper eyelid. It was diagnosed as a chalazion and removed twice in the past year, but it recurred in the same place each time. Her left eye has also been red and irritated for months, despite lid hygiene. Examination shows a yellowish nodule at the lid margin, thickening of the lid and loss of lashes over the lesion. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Sebaceous gland carcinoma arises from the meibomian glands, often on the upper lid of older women. It masquerades as a recurrent chalazion or a chronic one-sided blepharoconjunctivitis, so the diagnosis is delayed. It can spread to regional lymph nodes and is more aggressive than basal cell carcinoma. Any recurrent chalazion in an older adult needs a full-thickness biopsy.

Takeaway: a chalazion that keeps recurring in an older adult is sebaceous carcinoma until a biopsy says otherwise.

whyNot.A: A hordeolum is acute and painful and does not recur in the same place with lash loss.
whyNot.B: Basal cell carcinoma usually affects the lower lid and has a pearly, telangiectatic border.
whyNot.D: Xanthelasma forms soft yellow plaques near the inner canthus, not a firm nodule at the lid margin.
whyNot.E: Molluscum causes small umbilicated papules, sometimes with a follicular conjunctivitis, and is not firm or recurrent after excision.

items.objective: Recognise sebaceous gland carcinoma as a mimic of recurrent chalazion.

items.stemHtml: A 58-year-old woman was treated 4 years ago for invasive ductal carcinoma of the breast. She now has blurred vision in both eyes. Dilated fundus examination shows several flat, creamy-yellow lesions deep to the retina in both eyes. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Metastasis to the choroid is the most common intraocular malignancy in adults overall. The choroid has rich blood flow, and breast (in women) and lung cancers are the usual primaries. The lesions are typically creamy yellow, often multiple and bilateral.

Takeaway: multiple creamy choroidal lesions in a patient with cancer are metastases.

whyNot.A: Uveal melanoma is usually a single pigmented, dome-shaped mass in one eye.
whyNot.B: A nevus is a flat, stable, usually pigmented lesion that does not cause symptoms in both eyes.
whyNot.C: Retinoblastoma is a childhood tumour.
whyNot.E: Toxoplasma retinochoroiditis causes a fluffy white focus with vitreous inflammation, often next to an old pigmented scar.

items.objective: Recognise choroidal metastasis as the most common intraocular malignancy in adults.

items.stemHtml: A 12-year-old girl cannot read the board from the back of the classroom but reads her book easily. Visual acuity improves with a pinhole. Where do parallel rays from a distant object come to a focus in her uncorrected eye, and which lens corrects it?

options.label: A
options.html: Behind the retina; a converging lens

options.label: B
options.html: In front of the retina; a converging lens

options.label: C
options.html: Behind the retina; a diverging lens

options.label: D
options.html: On the retina in one meridian only; a cylindrical lens

options.label: E
options.html: In front of the retina; a diverging lens

items.explanationHtml:
Good near vision with poor distance vision that improves with a pinhole is myopia. The eye is usually too long, so parallel light from distant objects focuses in front of the retina. A diverging (concave, minus) lens spreads the rays so the focus moves back onto the retina. Myopia usually appears in school-age children and progresses through adolescence.

Takeaway: myopia focuses in front of the retina and is corrected with a minus lens.

whyNot.A: This describes hyperopia, which makes near vision harder than distance vision.
whyNot.B: A converging lens would move the focus further forward and worsen myopia.
whyNot.C: Light focused behind the retina needs more converging power, not less.
whyNot.D: This describes astigmatism, which blurs both near and distant vision.

items.objective: Explain the optics of myopia and its correction.

items.stemHtml: A 47-year-old accountant has had increasing difficulty reading small print over the past year and now holds her phone at arm's length to read it. Her distance vision is unchanged, and the eye examination is otherwise normal. Which of the following best explains her symptoms?

options.label: A
options.html: Loss of elasticity of the lens

options.label: B
options.html: Weakness of the ciliary muscle from loss of sympathetic input

items.explanationHtml:
For near focus, the ciliary muscle contracts, the zonules slacken and the elastic lens becomes rounder. From the 40s onward the lens stiffens and can no longer round up enough: presbyopia. Reading glasses (plus lenses) compensate.

Takeaway: presbyopia is age-related loss of lens elasticity, which limits accommodation.

whyNot.B: The ciliary muscle is driven by parasympathetic fibres for accommodation, and its strength is largely preserved with age.
whyNot.C: An elongating globe causes myopia, which blurs distance rather than near vision.
whyNot.D: A cataract causes glare and blurring at all distances, and the lens would look abnormal.
whyNot.E: Corneal curvature changes cause astigmatism or a change in refraction, not age-related loss of near focus.

items.objective: Explain the mechanism of presbyopia.

items.stemHtml: A 66-year-old man with primary open-angle glaucoma has used one eye drop every night in his right eye only for 18 months. His wife notices that the right iris has become darker brown than the left and that the right eyelashes are longer and thicker. The drug he is using lowers intraocular pressure mainly by which of the following mechanisms?

options.label: A
options.html: Blocking β-adrenergic receptors on the ciliary epithelium

options.label: B
options.html: Increasing uveoscleral outflow of aqueous humour

options.label: C
options.html: Inhibiting carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body

options.label: D
options.html: Contracting the ciliary muscle to open the trabecular meshwork

options.label: E
options.html: Stimulating α2 receptors to decrease aqueous production

items.explanationHtml:
Iris darkening (more melanin in iris melanocytes) and longer, thicker lashes are characteristic of prostaglandin F2α analogues such as latanoprost. They are first-line drops for open-angle glaucoma and lower pressure by increasing uveoscleral outflow through the ciliary muscle.

Takeaway: prostaglandin analogues raise uveoscleral outflow and can darken the iris and lengthen lashes.

whyNot.A: β-Blockers such as timolol reduce aqueous production but do not darken the iris or lengthen lashes.
whyNot.C: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce aqueous production; they do not change iris colour.
whyNot.D: Pilocarpine works this way and causes a small pupil and brow ache, not iris darkening.
whyNot.E: Brimonidine and apraclonidine work this way; their typical problem is allergic conjunctivitis.

items.objective: Describe the mechanism and adverse effects of prostaglandin analogue eye drops.

items.stemHtml: A 61-year-old woman who is long-sighted applies a transdermal scopolamine patch for motion sickness before a cruise. That evening she develops severe pain in her right eye, a headache, nausea and halos around lights. Her right eye is red, the cornea is hazy and the pupil is mid-dilated and unreactive. Which of the following actions of the drug most directly led to her eye condition?

options.label: A
options.html: Stimulation of muscarinic receptors in the ciliary muscle

options.label: B
options.html: Blockade of α1 receptors on the iris dilator muscle

options.label: C
options.html: Blockade of muscarinic receptors on the iris sphincter muscle

options.label: D
options.html: Blockade of β2 receptors on the ciliary epithelium

options.label: E
options.html: Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the ciliary body

items.explanationHtml:
Scopolamine is a muscarinic antagonist. Blocking M3 receptors on the iris sphincter dilates the pupil. In a hyperopic eye with a shallow anterior chamber, the mid-dilated, relaxed peripheral iris bunches into the angle and blocks the trabecular meshwork, producing acute angle-closure glaucoma.

Takeaway: anticholinergic mydriasis can precipitate angle closure in a narrow-angled eye.

whyNot.A: Muscarinic stimulation (pilocarpine) contracts the ciliary muscle and opens the angle; scopolamine blocks these receptors.
whyNot.B: α1 blockade would constrict the pupil and would not precipitate angle closure.
whyNot.D: β blockade reduces aqueous production and lowers pressure.
whyNot.E: Carbonic anhydrase inhibition lowers intraocular pressure.

items.objective: Explain how anticholinergic drugs precipitate acute angle-closure glaucoma.

items.stemHtml: A 13-year-old boy is evaluated for blurred vision. He is tall and thin with long limbs, and he has mild intellectual disability. A year ago he had a deep vein thrombosis of the left leg. Slit-lamp examination shows both lenses displaced downward. Plasma concentrations of homocysteine and methionine are both increased. Deficiency of which of the following enzymes is the most likely cause?
items.explanationHtml:
Downward lens dislocation, a marfanoid build, intellectual disability and thrombosis are the picture of classic homocystinuria from cystathionine β-synthase deficiency. Homocysteine cannot be converted to cystathionine, so it builds up and is remethylated to methionine, which rises too. Excess homocysteine damages zonular fibres and the vascular endothelium.

Takeaway: lens dislocation with thrombosis and high methionine points to cystathionine β-synthase deficiency.

whyNot.A: Methionine synthase deficiency raises homocysteine but lowers methionine and causes megaloblastic anaemia.
whyNot.B: This causes phenylketonuria: intellectual disability and fair skin, without lens dislocation or thrombosis.
whyNot.C: This causes alkaptonuria: dark urine, pigmented cartilage and arthritis.
whyNot.E: This causes classic galactosaemia, with cataracts rather than lens dislocation.

items.objective: Distinguish cystathionine β-synthase deficiency from other causes of lens disease and hyperhomocysteinaemia.

items.stemHtml: A 3-month-old boy has bilateral cataracts found at a routine examination. He is feeding well, growing normally and is not jaundiced, and his liver is not enlarged. His urine tests positive for a reducing substance, but a glucose-specific dipstick is negative. Accumulation of which of the following substances in the lens most directly caused his cataracts?
items.explanationHtml:
Isolated cataracts with galactose in the urine and an otherwise well infant suggest galactokinase deficiency. Galactose that cannot be phosphorylated is reduced by aldose reductase to galactitol, which is trapped in the lens and draws in water by osmosis. Classic galactosaemia also causes galactitol cataracts, but adds liver failure, jaundice and E. coli sepsis.

Takeaway: galactitol formed by aldose reductase causes the cataracts of galactose disorders.

whyNot.A: Sorbitol forms from glucose and causes cataracts in diabetes, not in disorders of galactose metabolism.
whyNot.B: Galactose-1-phosphate accumulates in classic galactosaemia and damages the liver, brain and kidneys; this infant has no such signs.
whyNot.C: This accumulates in hereditary fructose intolerance, which causes hypoglycaemia and liver injury after fructose intake.
whyNot.D: Glucose-6-phosphate accumulates in von Gierke disease, which causes hypoglycaemia and hepatomegaly.

items.objective: Explain the biochemical basis of cataracts in disorders of galactose metabolism.

items.stemHtml: A 38-year-old woman has taken prednisone 15 mg daily for 3 years for systemic lupus erythematosus. She now has glare from oncoming headlights and difficulty reading, which are worse in bright light. Which of the following lens changes is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Long-term corticosteroid use, systemic or topical, causes posterior subcapsular cataract. The opacity sits near the eye's optical centre, so it causes glare and early loss of near vision, worst in bright light when the pupil is small. Steroids can also raise intraocular pressure in susceptible patients.

Takeaway: chronic glucocorticoids cause posterior subcapsular cataract.

whyNot.B: Nuclear sclerosis is the usual age-related cataract of older adults and tends to cause a myopic shift.
whyNot.C: Anterior polar cataracts are usually congenital, small and stable.
whyNot.D: Subluxation occurs with zonular weakness, as in Marfan syndrome or trauma, not with steroids.
whyNot.E: This crystalline cataract is classically associated with myotonic dystrophy.

items.objective: Associate long-term corticosteroid use with posterior subcapsular cataract.

items.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man has bumped into door frames on both sides for several months. Confrontation testing shows loss of the outer half of the visual field in each eye. MRI shows a sellar mass extending upward. Refer to the diagram of the visual pathway. A lesion at which of the labelled sites best explains his visual fields?
items.explanationHtml:
Loss of both temporal fields is a bitemporal hemianopia, caused by compression of the crossing nasal fibres at the optic chiasm (site B). A pituitary macroadenoma pressing up from below typically affects the upper temporal fields first.

Takeaway: bitemporal hemianopia localises to the chiasm, most often a pituitary adenoma.

whyNot.A: Site A is the left optic nerve; a lesion there blinds the left eye only.
whyNot.C: Site C is the left optic tract, which causes a right homonymous hemianopia.
whyNot.D: Site D is the left Meyer loop, which causes a right upper quadrantanopia.
whyNot.E: Site E is the left parietal radiation, which causes a right lower quadrantanopia.
whyNot.F: Site F is the left occipital cortex, which causes a right homonymous hemianopia, often sparing the macula.

items.objective: Localise a bitemporal hemianopia to the optic chiasm.

items.stemHtml: A 34-year-old woman underwent resection of the anterior left temporal lobe for drug-resistant epilepsy. Afterward she notices that she cannot see objects in the upper right part of her vision with either eye. Refer to the diagram of the visual pathway. Damage at which of the labelled sites best explains her finding?
items.explanationHtml:
Fibres from the lower retina, which carry the upper visual field, sweep forward around the temporal horn in Meyer loop before turning back to the occipital lobe. Anterior temporal lobe surgery or a temporal stroke damages them, causing a contralateral upper homonymous quadrantanopia.

Takeaway: a temporal lobe lesion causes a contralateral upper quadrantanopia.

whyNot.A: An optic nerve lesion affects one eye only.
whyNot.B: A chiasmal lesion causes a bitemporal hemianopia.
whyNot.C: An optic tract lesion causes a complete homonymous hemianopia.
whyNot.E: The parietal radiation carries the lower field; damage there causes a lower quadrantanopia.
whyNot.F: An occipital cortex lesion causes a homonymous hemianopia, often with macular sparing.

items.objective: Localise a contralateral upper quadrantanopia to Meyer loop in the temporal lobe.

items.stemHtml: A 72-year-old man with atrial fibrillation suddenly cannot see things to his right. Examination shows a right homonymous hemianopia in which central vision is preserved, and the defects in the two eyes match exactly. Strength, sensation and language are normal. Refer to the diagram of the visual pathway. A lesion at which of the labelled sites best explains these findings?
items.explanationHtml:
An isolated, congruous right homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing localises to the left occipital cortex. An embolus to the left posterior cerebral artery is the usual cause. The occipital pole, which represents the macula, often receives extra supply from the middle cerebral artery, so central vision survives.

Takeaway: homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing means occipital cortex, usually a posterior cerebral artery stroke.

whyNot.A: An optic nerve lesion affects one eye and causes a relative afferent pupillary defect.
whyNot.B: A chiasmal lesion causes a bitemporal defect.
whyNot.C: An optic tract lesion causes a homonymous hemianopia that is often incongruous and does not spare the macula.
whyNot.D: A Meyer loop lesion causes an upper quadrantanopia only.
whyNot.E: A parietal radiation lesion causes a lower quadrantanopia and usually other parietal signs.

items.objective: Localise a congruous homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing to the occipital cortex.

items.stemHtml: A 29-year-old woman has blurred vision in her left eye and pain when she moves it. In a dim room, a light shone into her right eye makes both pupils constrict. When the light is swung quickly to her left eye, both pupils dilate. Moving the light back to the right eye makes both pupils constrict again. Damage to which of the following structures best explains this pupillary finding?
items.explanationHtml:
This is a relative afferent pupillary defect in the left eye. Both pupils share their efferent supply (each Edinger–Westphal nucleus receives input from both eyes), so they always change together. When the light moves to the eye with a damaged optic nerve, less signal reaches the midbrain and both pupils dilate. Painful monocular vision loss in a young woman suggests optic neuritis.

Takeaway: both pupils dilating when light swings to one eye means an afferent lesion of that eye's optic nerve.

whyNot.A: A right optic nerve lesion would make both pupils dilate when the light moves to the right eye.
whyNot.C: An oculomotor lesion affects the efferent limb: the left pupil would be large and react poorly whichever eye is lit, while the right pupil reacts normally.
whyNot.D: A chiasmal lesion affects both eyes' crossing fibres and does not usually cause this one-sided afferent defect.
whyNot.E: Pupillary fibres leave the tract before the lateral geniculate nucleus, so lesions here do not cause an afferent pupillary defect.

items.objective: Interpret the swinging-flashlight test to localise an afferent pupillary defect.

items.stemHtml: A 62-year-old man who has smoked for 45 years has had pain in his left shoulder and inner arm for 3 months. Examination shows mild drooping of the left upper eyelid, a small left pupil that dilates slowly in dim light, and a dry left side of the face. A chest radiograph shows a mass at the apex of the left lung. Which of the following neurons is most likely damaged?

options.label: A
options.html: Hypothalamospinal neurons in the lateral medulla

options.label: B
options.html: Postganglionic fibres on the internal carotid artery

options.label: C
options.html: Preganglionic sympathetic fibres crossing the lung apex

options.label: D
options.html: Parasympathetic fibres travelling with the oculomotor nerve

options.label: E
options.html: Postganglionic fibres in the short ciliary nerves

items.explanationHtml:
Ptosis, miosis and facial anhidrosis are Horner syndrome. Second-order (preganglionic) sympathetic fibres leave the cord at T1, pass over the lung apex and ascend to the superior cervical ganglion. An apical (Pancoast) tumour damages them and often the lower brachial plexus, causing shoulder and inner-arm pain. Anhidrosis of the face fits a lesion before the sweat fibres branch off with the external carotid.

Takeaway: Horner syndrome with an apical lung mass is a second-order (preganglionic) lesion.

whyNot.A: These first-order neurons would be damaged by a brainstem stroke, which causes other brainstem signs.
whyNot.B: These third-order fibres lie in the neck and skull base, away from the lung apex, and their damage spares most facial sweating.
whyNot.D: Loss of these fibres causes a large pupil, not a small one.
whyNot.E: Damage to these parasympathetic fibres causes a tonic, dilated pupil.

items.objective: Localise Horner syndrome from a Pancoast tumour to the second-order sympathetic neuron.

items.stemHtml: A 49-year-old woman has a severe headache and drooping of her right eyelid that began 2 days ago. Her right eye rests down and out, and the right pupil is 7 mm and does not react to light. CT angiography shows an aneurysm at the junction of the right internal carotid and posterior communicating arteries. Why is the pupil involved in this patient?

options.label: A
options.html: Ischaemia of the central core of the nerve

options.label: B
options.html: Damage to the Edinger–Westphal nucleus only

options.label: C
options.html: Interruption of sympathetic fibres on the carotid artery

options.label: E
options.html: Injury to the pretectal nucleus of the midbrain

items.explanationHtml:
Parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres run on the outside of the oculomotor nerve. An external mass such as a posterior communicating artery aneurysm compresses them early, producing a fixed, dilated pupil along with ptosis and a down-and-out eye. Microvascular ischaemia, as in diabetes, damages the core of the nerve and typically spares the pupil.

Takeaway: a “blown” pupil with an oculomotor palsy means compression until proven otherwise.

whyNot.A: Central ischaemia from small-vessel disease typically spares the peripheral pupillary fibres.
whyNot.B: A nuclear lesion in the midbrain would not explain ptosis and eye position from an aneurysm outside the brainstem.
whyNot.C: Sympathetic loss causes a small pupil, not a dilated one.
whyNot.E: A pretectal lesion causes light–near dissociation without ptosis or a down-and-out eye.

items.objective: Explain why compressive oculomotor palsies involve the pupil.

items.stemHtml: A 26-year-old woman has had double vision for 4 days. When she looks to the right, her left eye does not move past the midline, and her right eye shows jerking nystagmus. When she looks to the left, both eyes move normally. When she focuses on a near target, both eyes turn inward normally. A lesion of which of the following structures is most likely?
items.explanationHtml:
Failure of the left eye to adduct on right gaze, with nystagmus of the abducting right eye, is a left internuclear ophthalmoplegia. The left MLF carries signals from the right abducens nucleus to the left medial rectus subnucleus. Convergence uses a separate pathway, so it is preserved. In a young woman, multiple sclerosis is the most likely cause.

Takeaway: an INO is named by the eye that fails to adduct; the lesion is in that side's MLF.

whyNot.A: A right MLF lesion would impair adduction of the right eye on gaze to the left.
whyNot.B: An abducens nucleus lesion causes a palsy of gaze toward the left in both eyes.
whyNot.C: An oculomotor nerve lesion would also impair convergence and cause ptosis and other eye movement problems.
whyNot.D: A right PPRF lesion would prevent both eyes from looking to the right.

items.objective: Localise internuclear ophthalmoplegia to the medial longitudinal fasciculus.

items.stemHtml: A 32-year-old woman noticed in a mirror that her right pupil is larger than her left. The right pupil reacts very little to light but slowly constricts and stays constricted during prolonged near focus. One drop of very dilute pilocarpine (0.1%) constricts the right pupil but not the left. Her ankle reflexes are absent on both sides. Damage to which of the following structures is most likely?

options.label: C
options.html: Oculomotor nerve in the cavernous sinus

options.label: D
options.html: Pretectal area of the dorsal midbrain

items.explanationHtml:
A large pupil with a poor light reaction, a slow, tonic near response and constriction to dilute pilocarpine is a tonic (Adie) pupil. Damage to the ciliary ganglion or short ciliary nerves leaves the sphincter denervated and supersensitive. Aberrant regrowth of fibres meant for the ciliary muscle explains the better near response. With absent tendon reflexes, it is Holmes–Adie syndrome.

Takeaway: a large pupil that constricts to dilute pilocarpine is a tonic pupil from ciliary ganglion damage.

whyNot.B: A preganglionic lesion would not produce denervation supersensitivity of the iris sphincter to dilute pilocarpine.
whyNot.C: An oculomotor lesion would cause ptosis and eye movement problems, and dilute pilocarpine would not usually constrict the pupil.
whyNot.D: Dorsal midbrain lesions cause bilateral light–near dissociation with upgaze palsy, not a single large supersensitive pupil.
whyNot.E: Damage to this sympathetic ganglion causes a small pupil (Horner syndrome).

items.objective: Recognise a tonic pupil and localise it to the ciliary ganglion.

items.stemHtml: A 23-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of pain, redness, light sensitivity and blurred vision in his left eye since yesterday. He wears extended-wear soft contact lenses and removed them this morning. Visual acuity is 20/60 in the left eye and 20/20 in the right. There is a 2-mm white corneal opacity with an overlying epithelial defect that stains with fluorescein. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Pressure patch and recheck in 24 hours

options.label: D
options.html: Oral cephalexin and lens hygiene advice

options.label: E
options.html: Artificial tears and a 1-week lens holiday

items.explanationHtml:
A corneal infiltrate with an epithelial defect in a contact lens wearer is bacterial keratitis until proven otherwise, and Pseudomonas is the main concern. Stop lens wear, start intensive topical antibiotic drops with antipseudomonal cover (a fluoroquinolone), and arrange same-day ophthalmology for corneal scrapings and possibly fortified antibiotics.

Takeaway: contact lens ulcer: no patch, no steroid, antipseudomonal drops and same-day ophthalmology.

whyNot.A: Patching a contact lens–related ulcer creates a warm, closed space that favours Pseudomonas and is contraindicated.
whyNot.C: A steroid can worsen an infectious ulcer and is not started before an ophthalmologist confirms the diagnosis.
whyNot.D: Oral antibiotics do not reach adequate corneal levels and cephalexin does not cover Pseudomonas.
whyNot.E: A corneal infiltrate with an epithelial defect in a lens wearer is presumed bacterial keratitis and needs antibiotics.

items.objective: Manage suspected contact lens–associated bacterial keratitis.

items.stemHtml: A 3-day-old boy born at term has marked swelling of both eyelids and copious purulent discharge from both eyes. His mother had no prenatal care. He is feeding normally, is not jaundiced, and his temperature is 37.2°C (99.0°F). Gram staining of the exudate reveals paired gram-negative cocci within polymorphonuclear cells. Cultures have been sent. In addition to saline irrigation of the eyes and an evaluation for disseminated infection, which of the following is the most appropriate treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: A single parenteral dose of ceftriaxone

items.explanationHtml:
Hyperacute purulent conjunctivitis in the first days of life with gram-negative intracellular diplococci is gonococcal ophthalmia neonatorum. Treat with a single dose of ceftriaxone given IV or IM, irrigate the eyes, hospitalise and look for disseminated infection (blood and CSF cultures as indicated). Test the infant for chlamydia, and test and treat the mother and her partners. In a jaundiced or premature infant, another third-generation cephalosporin is used instead of ceftriaxone.

Takeaway: neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis needs systemic ceftriaxone, not drops alone.

whyNot.A: Topical treatment alone is inadequate for gonococcal ophthalmia, which needs systemic therapy.
whyNot.B: Topical treatment alone does not treat the systemic infection and is not recommended.
whyNot.D: Oral erythromycin treats neonatal chlamydial conjunctivitis, not gonococcal infection.
whyNot.E: Gonococcal ophthalmia can perforate the cornea within days; waiting is unsafe.

items.objective: Treat neonatal gonococcal conjunctivitis with systemic ceftriaxone.

items.stemHtml: A 56-year-old woman with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis has had a deep, boring pain in her right eye for 1 week. The pain wakes her at night and spreads to her forehead and jaw. The globe is tender to touch, and the inferior sclera has a violet hue. Instilling 2.5% phenylephrine drops does not blanch the deep vessels. Visual acuity is 20/30. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: B
options.html: Topical antibiotic drops and a recheck in 1 week

options.label: D
options.html: Urgent ophthalmology and a systemic anti-inflammatory drug

options.label: E
options.html: Topical corticosteroid drops from the primary clinic

items.explanationHtml:
Severe pain that wakes the patient, a tender globe, a violet hue and deep vessels that do not blanch with phenylephrine indicate scleritis, which is linked to rheumatoid arthritis and vasculitides such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis. It threatens sight through scleral thinning. Management is urgent ophthalmology and systemic treatment: an NSAID for milder disease, then systemic corticosteroids or immunosuppressive therapy.

Takeaway: scleritis needs urgent ophthalmology and systemic anti-inflammatory therapy.

whyNot.A: These treat allergic conjunctivitis, which itches and does not cause deep pain or a tender globe.
whyNot.B: There is no infection, and delay risks scleral thinning and perforation.
whyNot.C: Reassurance suits episcleritis, which is mild and blanches with phenylephrine.
whyNot.E: Topical steroids alone do not control scleritis, and steroid drops should not be started without an ophthalmologist.

items.objective: Distinguish scleritis from episcleritis and arrange urgent systemic treatment.

items.stemHtml: A 6-year-old girl has had a cold for 1 week. Over the past day her right eyelids have become red and swollen. Her temperature is 38.9°C (102.0°F). The right eye bulges slightly, she has pain when looking in any direction, and upward and outward movements of the right eye are limited. Visual acuity is 20/25 in each eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: A
options.html: Oral amoxicillin–clavulanate and review in 48 hours

options.label: B
options.html: Warm compresses and topical antibiotic ointment

options.label: D
options.html: Outpatient MRI of the brain in 1 week

options.label: E
options.html: IV antibiotics and contrast CT of the orbits and sinuses

items.explanationHtml:
Pain with eye movement, restricted movement and proptosis show infection behind the orbital septum: orbital cellulitis, usually from ethmoid sinusitis. Admit, start intravenous broad-spectrum antibiotics, and obtain CT of the orbits and sinuses with contrast to look for a subperiosteal or orbital abscess. Involve ophthalmology and ENT; drain an abscess if vision is threatened or it does not respond.

Takeaway: orbital signs mean IV antibiotics and contrast CT, not oral treatment.

whyNot.A: Oral treatment is for preseptal cellulitis with normal eye movements; this child has orbital signs.
whyNot.B: Topical treatment does not reach orbital infection.
whyNot.C: There are no meningeal signs, and delaying antibiotics for a lumbar puncture is not indicated.
whyNot.D: Orbital cellulitis needs imaging and intravenous antibiotics now.

items.objective: Distinguish orbital from preseptal cellulitis and manage orbital cellulitis.

items.stemHtml: A 31-year-old woman with Crohn disease has had a painful red left eye for 2 days. Bright light is painful, and her vision is slightly blurred. There is no discharge. The redness is most intense in a ring around the cornea. The left pupil is smaller than the right and reacts sluggishly. Shining a light into the right eye causes pain in the left eye. Intraocular pressure is normal. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
items.explanationHtml:
Pain, photophobia (including pain when light enters the other eye, from consensual pupil movement), a perilimbal ciliary flush, a small sluggish pupil from sphincter spasm and normal pressure indicate anterior uveitis. Inflammatory bowel disease is a recognised association. She needs same-day ophthalmology for slit-lamp confirmation and treatment with topical corticosteroids and a cycloplegic.

Takeaway: ciliary flush plus photophobia plus a small pupil is anterior uveitis.

whyNot.B: Angle closure gives a mid-dilated pupil, a hazy cornea and a very high pressure.
whyNot.C: Conjunctivitis causes diffuse redness with discharge, not a small pupil, photophobia or reduced vision.
whyNot.D: Episcleritis causes sectoral redness with mild discomfort and no photophobia or pupil change.
whyNot.E: A subconjunctival haemorrhage is a painless flat patch of blood with normal vision.

items.objective: Diagnose anterior uveitis and recognise its association with inflammatory bowel disease.

items.stemHtml: A 74-year-old man had uncomplicated cataract surgery on his right eye 4 days ago. Since last night he has had increasing pain in that eye and his vision has dropped to counting fingers. The eyelids are swollen, the conjunctiva is intensely red, and a 2-mm layer of white cells is visible at the bottom of the anterior chamber. The view of the fundus is hazy. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?
items.explanationHtml:
Pain, falling vision, a hypopyon and vitreous haze days after intraocular surgery are acute postoperative endophthalmitis, most often from the patient's own skin flora (coagulase-negative staphylococci). Management is emergency vitreous sampling (tap) with injection of intravitreal antibiotics, typically vancomycin for gram-positive and ceftazidime for gram-negative cover. Vitrectomy is considered when vision is reduced to light perception.

Takeaway: postoperative endophthalmitis needs intravitreal antibiotics immediately.

whyNot.A: Topical antibiotics do not reach therapeutic levels in the vitreous.
whyNot.C: Oral antibiotics alone do not achieve reliable vitreous levels against the likely organisms.
whyNot.D: Steroids alone would leave an infection untreated.
whyNot.E: Intravenous antibiotics penetrate the vitreous poorly; intravitreal delivery is required.

items.objective: Manage acute postoperative endophthalmitis with intravitreal antibiotics.

items.stemHtml: A 71-year-old woman has had burning pain over the right side of her forehead for 3 days. Today she developed clusters of vesicles on a red base over the right forehead and upper eyelid, and a few vesicles on the tip of her nose. Her right eye is mildly red and watery, and visual acuity is 20/25. Which of the following is the most appropriate management?

options.label: A
options.html: Topical acyclovir cream to the rash only

options.label: C
options.html: Oral valacyclovir and prompt eye examination

items.explanationHtml:
Vesicles in the distribution of V1 are herpes zoster ophthalmicus. Lesions on the tip or side of the nose (the nasociliary branch, Hutchinson sign) predict eye involvement such as keratitis or uveitis. Start an oral antiviral (valacyclovir, famciclovir or acyclovir) ideally within 72 hours of the rash, and arrange prompt ophthalmology examination.

Takeaway: zoster in V1, especially on the nose, needs an oral antiviral and an eye examination.

whyNot.A: Topical cream does not treat the infection of the nerve or protect the eye.
whyNot.B: A steroid without an antiviral is not appropriate.
whyNot.D: Steroid drops are started only by an ophthalmologist after examination, if at all.
whyNot.E: Nose-tip involvement predicts eye involvement, and an antiviral should be started within 72 hours.

items.objective: Manage herpes zoster ophthalmicus with oral antiviral therapy and ophthalmology review.

items.stemHtml: The parents of a 9-month-old boy bring photographs in which his left pupil looks white instead of red. He is otherwise well and developing normally. On examination, the red reflex is present in the right eye but absent in the left. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step?

options.label: A
options.html: Repeat the red reflex check at the next well-child visit

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the orbits with contrast

options.label: E
options.html: Reassurance that the photographs show an artefact

items.explanationHtml:
Leukocoria with an absent red reflex needs an urgent dilated examination by an ophthalmologist, usually under anaesthesia. Retinoblastoma is the diagnosis that must not be missed; the differential includes congenital cataract, persistent fetal vasculature and Coats disease.

Takeaway: an absent or white red reflex means urgent ophthalmology referral.

whyNot.A: Delay risks spread of a retinoblastoma outside the eye.
whyNot.B: CT exposes the child to radiation and is not the first step; examination comes first, and MRI is used for staging.
whyNot.C: Patching treats amblyopia; the cause of the abnormal reflex must be found first.
whyNot.E: An absent red reflex on examination confirms a real abnormality.

items.objective: Refer urgently a child with leukocoria.

items.stemHtml: A 14-month-old girl is diagnosed with retinoblastoma in both eyes. Her parents have no history of eye cancer, and they also have a 6-week-old son. Which of the following is the most appropriate recommendation for the family?

options.label: A
options.html: No testing, because the disease is sporadic in this family

options.label: C
options.html: Yearly CT of the brother's orbits

options.label: D
options.html: Testing of the brother only if a second tumour occurs

options.label: E
options.html: RB1 testing of the girl and eye screening of her brother

items.explanationHtml:
Bilateral retinoblastoma implies a germline RB1 mutation, either new or inherited from a parent with mild disease or mosaicism. Test the affected child to find the mutation. Then test the parents and siblings for that mutation, and give at-risk siblings serial dilated fundus examinations from birth until the risk is excluded.

Takeaway: bilateral retinoblastoma calls for germline testing and screening of siblings.

whyNot.A: Bilateral disease implies a germline mutation, which the brother may have inherited.
whyNot.B: A karyotype detects only large deletions of 13q and misses most point mutations.
whyNot.C: CT exposes a child who may carry a germline mutation to radiation; screening is by fundus examination.
whyNot.D: Screening should start now: tumours found early are more treatable.

items.objective: Arrange germline testing and sibling screening after a diagnosis of bilateral retinoblastoma.

items.stemHtml: A 2-year-old boy has a calcified white mass in his right eye found on examination under anaesthesia, consistent with retinoblastoma. The left eye is normal. Which of the following is the most appropriate imaging study to assess for optic nerve involvement and intracranial disease?

options.label: A
options.html: MRI of the brain and orbits

options.label: B
options.html: CT of the brain and orbits

items.explanationHtml:
MRI of the brain and orbits shows optic nerve invasion, extension outside the globe and a pineal tumour (trilateral retinoblastoma) without radiation. CT is avoided because radiation increases later cancer risk in children with germline RB1 mutations, and germline status is often unknown at diagnosis. Ocular ultrasound complements the examination.

Takeaway: stage retinoblastoma with MRI, not CT.

whyNot.B: CT adds ionising radiation, which raises the risk of second cancers in children who may carry a germline RB1 mutation, and shows the optic nerve less well.
whyNot.C: PET-CT is not used for routine staging of intraocular retinoblastoma and adds radiation.
whyNot.D: Radiographs cannot assess the optic nerve or brain.
whyNot.E: A bone scan is reserved for suspected metastatic disease.

items.objective: Choose MRI rather than CT to stage retinoblastoma.

items.stemHtml: A 64-year-old woman has painless blurring of vision in her right eye. Dilated examination shows an elevated, dome-shaped, brown choroidal mass 12 mm across and 6 mm thick, with orange pigment on its surface. Ultrasound shows low internal reflectivity. The ophthalmologist plans plaque brachytherapy. Which of the following studies is most important for staging before treatment?

options.label: C
options.html: Ultrasound of the cervical lymph nodes

items.explanationHtml:
A thick, dome-shaped pigmented choroidal mass with orange pigment and low internal reflectivity on ultrasound is choroidal melanoma. It spreads through the blood and shows a strong preference for the liver, so staging, and surveillance afterwards, centre on liver imaging (MRI or ultrasound) with liver function tests.

Takeaway: uveal melanoma staging and follow-up focus on the liver.

whyNot.A: Brain metastases from uveal melanoma are uncommon at presentation.
whyNot.C: Intraocular melanoma has no lymphatic drainage and rarely spreads to nodes.
whyNot.D: Bone metastases are uncommon at presentation.
whyNot.E: Marrow involvement is not a typical early site and biopsy is not part of staging.

items.objective: Stage uveal melanoma with liver imaging.

items.stemHtml: A 69-year-old man who farmed for 50 years has a painless lump on his left lower eyelid that has grown slowly over 8 months. It is a 6-mm pearly nodule with rolled borders, surface telangiectasia and a small crusted centre, and the lashes over it are missing. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.label: D
options.html: Incision and curettage as for a chalazion

options.label: E
options.html: Observation with a recheck in 6 months

items.explanationHtml:
A pearly, telangiectatic, ulcerated nodule with lash loss is typical of basal cell carcinoma, the most common eyelid cancer. Confirm with a biopsy, then excise with margin control (Mohs micrographic surgery or frozen-section control) to remove the tumour while preserving the lid.

Takeaway: an eyelid lesion with lash loss, ulceration or pearly edges needs a biopsy.

whyNot.A: Warm compresses treat a chalazion, which is not pearly, ulcerated or associated with lash loss.
whyNot.B: There is no infection, and treatment would delay the diagnosis of a cancer.
whyNot.D: Curettage would not diagnose or adequately remove a tumour.
whyNot.E: A growing lesion with features of cancer needs tissue diagnosis now.

items.objective: Biopsy an eyelid lesion with features of basal cell carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 70-year-old woman has a lump in her right upper eyelid that has been incised and drained as a chalazion three times in 10 months; each time it recurred in the same place. The lid margin is now thickened, there is loss of lashes, and she has a persistent red, irritated right eye. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
items.explanationHtml:
A chalazion that keeps recurring in the same place in an older adult, especially with lid thickening, lash loss and chronic one-sided irritation, raises concern for sebaceous gland carcinoma. A full-thickness biopsy with histological examination is needed, and the pathologist should be told of the suspicion.

Takeaway: biopsy a recurrent chalazion in an older adult.

whyNot.A: A fourth curettage would delay the diagnosis of a possible carcinoma.
whyNot.B: Steroid injection treats a true chalazion and would delay diagnosis.
whyNot.C: Doxycycline helps meibomian gland dysfunction and rosacea, not a recurrent lesion with lash loss.
whyNot.E: Conservative measures have already failed, and malignancy must be excluded.

items.objective: Biopsy a recurrent chalazion in an older adult to exclude sebaceous carcinoma.

items.stemHtml: A 67-year-old man has had a slowly increasing, painless bulging of his left eye for 6 months. He has no double vision, fever or weight loss. Examination shows 4 mm of left proptosis and a smooth, salmon-pink, fleshy patch under the upper conjunctiva. Thyroid function is normal. Biopsy shows small lymphocytes with plasmacytic differentiation and a clonal B-cell population. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.label: D
options.html: Cavernous venous malformation of the orbit

items.explanationHtml:
